sounds.name: Screaming Acid Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Aphex Twin — early ambient-techno bass lines
sounds.blurb: A snarling, resonant bass line that squeals as the filter closes on each note.
sounds.how: One reverse sawtooth into a low-pass filter with PEAK almost at its limit, so the filter rings at its own pitch. Envelope 2 flicks the cutoff open at the start of every note and lets it fall back. The FILTER 2 circuit is the more aggressive of the two, which is what gives the squeal its edge.

steps.title: One reverse sawtooth, low down
steps.why:
One reverse sawtooth, an octave down, gives the filter plenty to bite on. Oscillator 2 is kept silent so the pitch stays single and clean for the squeal later.
- VCO1 WAVE FORM reverse saw: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator, the part that makes the raw tone. A reverse sawtooth has every harmonic, so it is the brightest, buzziest wave on the switch. A triangle would leave the filter far less to work on.
- SCALE 16′: Korg’s octave switch, marked in organ-pipe feet. 16′ is an octave below 8′, down in bass territory.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 8 / 0: the mixer. Oscillator 1 goes in fairly hot and Oscillator 2 is off. Its waveform is set back to reverse saw so nothing odd is waiting if you bring it up.
- Listen for: a raw, buzzy saw, because the low-pass is still at its starting 2.3 kHz. Hold a low note and remember it; the next step takes most of that buzz away.

steps.title: Close the filter and wind up PEAK
steps.why:
The low-pass filter takes the top off the saw and PEAK makes it ring. This is where the squeal comes from, before anything moves.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 3.2 (176 Hz): the low-pass filter keeps what is below the cutoff and removes what is above. At 176 Hz only the body of the note gets through, so on its own it is a thud. Raise it and the bass gets buzzier and less controlled.
- Low-pass PEAK 8.6: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost right at the cutoff. Near the top the filter rings at its own pitch. Below about 7 this turns into an ordinary filtered bass.
- FILTER 2: the harder of the two filter circuits, and the switch covers both filters. It distorts sooner and sounds angrier; FILTER 1 gives a rounder, more polite version.
- High-pass CUTOFF 0 (12 Hz): the high-pass filter removes bass below its cutoff. At 12 Hz it lets everything through.
- Listen for: a dark thud with a whistle on top. Flip between FILTER 1 and 2 on a held note to hear the edge change.

steps.title: Flick it open on each note
steps.why:
Envelope 2 now kicks the cutoff up at the start of every note and lets it fall back. The sweep past the resonant peak is the “wow” of an acid line.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 6.4: EG2 is envelope generator 2, which shapes each note over time. This knob sets how far it pushes the low-pass cutoff; it is the size of the sweep and the knob to ride by hand while a pattern plays.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: the cutoff jumps up the instant you play and starts falling straight away, so the squeal lands on the beat.
- DECAY 4.4 (190 ms): how long the squeal lasts. Short is percussive; long turns each note into a slow sweep.
- SUSTAIN 1.5, RELEASE 2 (140 ms): the envelope settles low while held and dies quickly after. It also drives the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier), so held notes get quieter too.
- Listen for: a sharp “wow” at the front of each note. Sweep DECAY while a riff plays to hear it tighten and loosen.

steps.title: Keep the notes short
steps.why:
The level is set and nothing is allowed to slide between notes. With the short release from the last step, notes stop before the next one starts, which keeps a fast pattern readable.
- VOLUME 9: the overall output level. The squeal is loud at its peak, so set this by ear against the rest of the track.
- Portamento TIME 0: no glide, so each note jumps straight to its pitch. Turning it up would make the line slide from note to note.
- Listen for: clean gaps between notes in a fast riff. Then drop the low-pass PEAK below 7 and hear the squeal turn into a plain filtered bass.

context.lpf.peak: This is the squeal. Below about 7 the sound turns into an ordinary filtered bass.
context.lpf.cutoff: Where the note sits between flicks. Raise it and the bass gets buzzier and less controlled.
context.lpmod.eg2: The size of the sweep. This is the knob to ride by hand while a pattern plays.
context.eg2.decay: How long the squeal lasts. Short is percussive; long turns each note into a slow sweep.
context.lpf.type: FILTER 2 is the harder-edged circuit. Switch to FILTER 1 for a rounder, more polite version of the same patch.

tweaks.try: Sweep between 3 and 8 while the pattern runs
tweaks.hear: The classic acid build, from a muted thump to a full screaming sweep.
Same shape, less bite: the resonance is smoother and the distortion backs off.
The bottom drops out and the squeal is left on its own — thinner, more piercing.

sounds.name: Two-Filter Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Vangelis — Blade Runner era leads
sounds.blurb: A singing lead with a hollow, vocal middle, made by squeezing both filters together.
sounds.how: This is the patch that shows what two filters in series are for. The high-pass takes the bass out from below and the low-pass takes the top off from above, leaving a narrow band in the middle. With a little PEAK on each, that band takes on a vocal quality no single filter can give you.

steps.title: Two sawtooths, half a semitone apart
steps.why:
Two sawtooths make the raw material for the lead. Both are on 8′, so they play the same octave, and the offset on Oscillator 2 keeps them from locking into one tone.
- Reverse saw on both: VCO stands for voltage-controlled oscillator, the part that makes the raw tone. A sawtooth has every harmonic, which the two filters need to carve a band from.
- SCALE 8′ on both: Korg’s octave switch in organ-pipe feet. 8′ is the pitch of the key you play, and on this synth the same footage means the same octave on both oscillators.
- PITCH 0.2 (about +0.5 semitone): tunes Oscillator 2 against Oscillator 1. Half a semitone gives a fast beat that thickens the tone. Back it towards 0 for a cleaner note.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 7 / 6: the mixer. The second saw sits a little lower so the first defines the pitch.
- Listen for: hold a note and bring VCO2 LEVEL down to 0 and back. The tone goes from thin and still to wide and moving.

steps.title: Cut the bass with the high-pass
steps.why:
The high-pass filter strips the bass from under the saws. On its own that sounds weedy; it is the lower half of a squeeze the next step completes.
- High-pass CUTOFF 3.6 (144 Hz): a high-pass filter removes everything below its cutoff. This is the bottom edge of the band. Raise it and the lead gets thinner and more nasal; at 0 it turns back into an ordinary low-pass lead.
- High-pass PEAK 4.2: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost right at the cutoff. A little gives the bottom edge some body; a lot makes it honk.
- Listen for: sweep the high-pass CUTOFF between 0 and 6 while a note rings. The body drains out and the sound goes from full to reedy.

steps.title: Cut the top with the low-pass
steps.why:
Now the low-pass filter closes in from above. With 144 Hz as the floor and 788 Hz as the ceiling, what survives is a narrow band with a resonant edge at each end: the hollow, vocal middle of this lead.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 5.4 (788 Hz): the low-pass removes everything above its cutoff. Bring it closer to the high-pass and the band narrows, more vocal and more hollow; raise it and the saw’s buzz comes back.
- Low-pass PEAK 4.6: resonance at the top edge. The two peaks together behave like the formants of a voice.
- FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits, and it applies to both filters. It keeps the peaks singing rather than tearing.
- Listen for: move the low-pass CUTOFF slowly down towards 4 and back while holding a note. The vowel shifts from open to closed and nasal.

steps.title: Let it bloom
steps.why:
Envelope 2 shapes each note over time, and here it also nudges the low-pass open, so each note opens up slightly after it starts instead of arriving all at once.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 3.4: EG2 is envelope generator 2. This knob sets how far it lifts the low-pass above 788 Hz, widening the band at the front of each note.
- ATTACK 2.2 (28 ms): a slightly soft start for brightness and loudness, since envelope 2 also opens the amplifier. It takes the click off without making the lead slow.
- DECAY 5.5 (460 ms), SUSTAIN 7: the bloom settles back over about half a second to a level that keeps held notes full.
- RELEASE 4.5 (630 ms): notes fade out over more than half a second, so a phrase joins up.
- Listen for: held notes open, then settle a little. Set EG2/EXT to 0 and the band goes static.

steps.title: Vibrato and a little glide
steps.why:
Vibrato and a little glide make the lead sound played rather than programmed. Both are kept small on purpose.
- MG WAVE FORM 5 (triangle): MG is the modulation generator, Korg’s name for an LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a slow wave that moves other controls. At the centre it is a triangle, which rises and falls evenly for smooth vibrato.
- FREQUENCY 5.4 (1.84 Hz): the vibrato speed, just under two wobbles a second.
- Pitch MG/T.EXT 1.1: how far the MG moves the pitch of both oscillators. Keep it under about 2 or it stops sounding like a player. The mod wheel adds to this knob, so vibrato can come in part-way through a note.
- Portamento TIME 2.4: the pitch slides from the previous note instead of jumping. At 0 notes jump; higher gives long swoops.
- Listen for: play a slow legato phrase. Each note slides in and then wavers gently. Push the mod wheel on a long note to deepen the vibrato.

context.hpf.cutoff: The bottom edge of the band. Raise it and the lead gets thinner and more nasal; drop it to 0 and the patch turns into an ordinary low-pass lead.
context.lpf.cutoff: The top edge. Bring the two cutoffs closer together and the band narrows, which makes the tone more vocal and more hollow.
context.hpf.peak: Emphasis at the bottom edge. A little gives the tone body; a lot makes it honk.
context.lpf.peak: Emphasis at the top edge.
context.fmod.mg: Vibrato depth. Keep it under about 2 or it stops sounding like a player.

tweaks.try: Sweep between 0 and 6 while a note rings
tweaks.hear: The body drains out of the sound and it goes from full to reedy — a whole tonal range one filter cannot reach.
The top edge starts to whistle, moving the lead towards a flute or a bottle.
A hollow, organ-like lead. Small offsets thicken; big ones harmonise.

sounds.name: Ring Mod Bell
sounds.ref: In the style of 1970s sci-fi television stings
sounds.blurb: A metallic, inharmonic bell that rings out and fades.
sounds.how: The RING position on Oscillator 2’s waveform switch multiplies the two oscillators together instead of adding them. The result is the sum and difference of their frequencies, which are not whole-number harmonics — so it sounds like metal rather than a note. Tuning the oscillators to an odd interval makes it more bell-like.

steps.title: Turn Oscillator 2 into the ring modulator
steps.why:
Switching Oscillator 2 to RING turns it into a ring modulator: instead of a second tone you get the two oscillators multiplied together. That is the source of the metallic clang.
- VCO1 triangle, SCALE 8′: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. The triangle is soft and hollow, a simple input for the ring modulator; a pulse would give a rougher, more gong-like clang.
- VCO2 RING, SCALE 8′: RING replaces Oscillator 2’s output with the two oscillators multiplied, which gives their sum and difference frequencies rather than the notes themselves.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 3.5 / 9: with RING selected, VCO2 LEVEL is the amount of ring modulation, so it leads. Oscillator 1 is still one of the two inputs, so it stays in the patch; its level sets how much plain triangle is heard beside the metal.
- Listen for: with both on 8′ and no detune, the ring output is fairly plain and still sounds like a note. The next step makes it metal.

steps.title: Tune to an awkward interval
steps.why:
Detuning Oscillator 2 by an odd interval pushes the ring modulator’s sum and difference tones off the harmonic series. The note stops sounding like a note and starts sounding like struck metal.
- PITCH 1.7 (about +4.1 semitones): just over a major third, not an octave or a fifth, so the new tones land between the harmonics. Every position sounds like a different piece of metal; this is the main control of the patch.
- Listen for: hold a note and turn PITCH slowly. Near 2.9 (a fifth) and 4.9 (an octave) the tone settles and turns more musical; in between it clangs. Turn VCO1 LEVEL to 0 for only the metal, and up for a clearer pitch.

steps.title: Open the filter and take the bass out
steps.why:
Bells live in the upper middle. The low-pass is opened to let the clang through, and the high-pass takes out the weight that would make it sound like a note rather than a strike.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 8 (4.6 kHz), PEAK 1.5: the low-pass removes what is above the cutoff. Opened this far it keeps the bright inharmonic tones. A touch of PEAK, Korg’s word for resonance, adds a slight edge without a whistle.
- High-pass CUTOFF 3.2 (109 Hz), PEAK 1: the high-pass removes what is below the cutoff. It takes the body out so the sound reads as metal. Drop it to 0 and a thicker, bassier tone comes back under the clang.
- Listen for: the sound getting lighter and brighter, with less weight under it on low keys.

steps.title: Strike and ring
steps.why:
Envelope 2 now gives the shape of anything struck: all the energy at the start, then a slow fade. It also opens the amplifier, so it sets the bell’s loudness over time.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: EG2, envelope generator 2, jumps to full at once with no pause at the top. That is the strike.
- DECAY 7.4 (2.2 s): how long the bell rings as it fades. Long decay with zero sustain is what makes it a strike rather than a held note.
- SUSTAIN 0: nothing is held, so the bell dies away on its own even with the key down.
- RELEASE 5.5 (1.2 s): let go early and the ring still tails off over about a second instead of stopping dead.
- Listen for: tap a key, then hold one. Both ring out and fade. Shorten DECAY and it turns from a bell into a clank.

context.vco2.pitch: The interval between the two oscillators sets which inharmonic tones appear. Every position sounds like a different piece of metal — this is the main control of the patch.
context.mix.vco1: How much plain Oscillator 1 is heard alongside the ring output. At 0 you get only the metal; turn it up and a recognisable pitch comes back.
context.eg2.decay: How long the bell rings. Long decay with zero sustain is what makes it a strike rather than a held note.
context.hpf.cutoff: Takes the body out so it reads as metal rather than as a bass note.

tweaks.hear: Every position is a different bell. Around 1.5 and 3.5 are the most metallic.
More harmonics into the ring modulator, so a rougher, more gong-like clang.
A short metallic tick rather than a bell — the start of synthetic percussion.

sounds.name: Random Step Burble
sounds.ref: In the style of 1960s and 70s computer sound effects
sounds.blurb: A chattering, random melody that plays itself while you hold one key.
sounds.how: The sample and hold reads the noise generator on every tick of its clock and holds the reading until the next one. Patched to oscillator pitch, that gives a new random note on every tick. This is what the patch panel is for: nothing on the front panel can do it, and it takes two cables.

steps.title: One plain oscillator
steps.why:
A single pulse wave gives a clear, simple tone, so each random step will be easy to pick out at speed.
- WAVE FORM pulse, PW 5: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. PW is pulse width: near 0 a hollow square, towards 10 a thin, nasal pulse. 5 sits between, bright but not harsh.
- SCALE 8′: Korg’s octave switch in organ-pipe feet; 8′ is the pitch of the key you play.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 7 / 0: only Oscillator 1 in the mixer, so the random notes come out as single, clear pitches.
- Listen for: an ordinary buzzy note for now, with the filter at its starting 2.3 kHz.

steps.title: Open the filter
steps.why:
The steps are the interest here, so the filter stays fairly open. A bit of resonance gives each new step a ping as it lands.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 6.6 (1.8 kHz): the low-pass removes what is above the cutoff. At 1.8 kHz most of the pulse gets through. This is how bright the chatter is.
- Low-pass PEAK 4.4: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. With it up, each step pings at its own pitch, the classic “computer thinking” sound.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1.5 (34 Hz): the high-pass trims only the lowest rumble; the body of the note stays.
- Listen for: a slightly hollow, ringing edge on a held note. Once the steps are running, push PEAK to 9 and each step rings out.

steps.title: Hold the note open
steps.why:
Envelope 2 opens the amplifier on every note. Here it stays fully open while a key is held, so one held key keeps the sound running and the stepping is left to the sample and hold.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms): EG2, envelope generator 2, reaches full straight away.
- DECAY 6 (690 ms), SUSTAIN 10: with sustain at maximum there is nothing to decay to, so the level stays at full for as long as you hold.
- RELEASE 2 (140 ms): the sound stops quickly when you let go.
- Listen for: a held note that does not change at all. Later, lower SUSTAIN and the pattern fades out under you.

steps.title: Clock the sample and hold from the modulation generator
steps.why:
The modulation generator becomes the clock for the sample and hold, so its speed will be the speed of the burble. The sound does not change yet: the sample and hold is ticking, but its output goes nowhere.
- FREQUENCY 6.4 (3.16 Hz): MG is the modulation generator, Korg’s name for an LFO (low-frequency oscillator). About three ticks a second; faster chatters, slower wanders.
- MG WAVE FORM 5: at the centre the pulse output is a square, so the ticks are evenly spaced.
- Cable MG OUT (pulse) → CLOCK: the pulse output only swings one way, which makes it a clean clock. CLOCK tells the S&H (sample and hold) when to take a reading, which it holds until the next tick.
- Listen for: nothing new yet. The next cable makes the ticks audible.

steps.title: Send the steps to pitch
steps.why:
Now the random readings reach pitch. Each tick lands on a new random note, and one held key plays a chattering melody by itself.
- Cable S&H OUT → VCO 1+2 CV IN: with nothing patched into S&H IN, the sample and hold reads noise, so every held value is random. VCO 1+2 CV IN is the pitch CV (control voltage) input for both oscillators; here it adds to the note you play.
- Listen for: a new pitch about three times a second, each one pinging through the resonant filter. Turn FREQUENCY to speed the burble up or slow it down, and play other keys: the random steps move with the key.

context.mg.freq: The speed of the burble, because the modulation generator is clocking the sample and hold.
context.lpf.peak: With resonance up, each step pings at its own pitch — the classic "computer thinking" sound.
context.lpf.cutoff: How bright the chatter is.
context.eg2.sustain: Full sustain keeps the sound running so you can hear the steps; lower it and the pattern fades under you.

tweaks.hear: Slow gives a lazy random melody; fast turns into a rattle where the steps blur into a texture.
The steps slide into each other rather than jumping — a drunken siren instead of a computer.
Each step rings out. Try turning the oscillator level down so the filter is nearly all you hear.

sounds.name: Delayed Pitch Sweep
sounds.ref: In the style of early electronic library music
sounds.blurb: Each note sits still, then slides upward part way through.
sounds.how: Envelope 1 has a DELAY stage before its attack, and it is wired to oscillator pitch through the EG1/EXT knob. Set a delay of a second or so and the note starts normally, waits, then climbs. Very few synths can do this without a cable; here it is two knobs.

steps.title: A simple held tone
steps.why:
A plain, steady tone is enough here, because the point is a pitch move that arrives later. Two oscillators give it a little movement so a long held note does not sound dead.
- VCO1 reverse saw, VCO2 square, both 8′: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. The bright saw carries the tone and the hollow square adds body. 8′ is the pitch of the key played, the same octave on both.
- PITCH −0.1 (about −0.4 semitone): Oscillator 2 sits a touch flat, so the two beat slowly against each other.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 7 / 4: the square sits well under the saw as support.
- Listen for: a slow swirl on a held note from the detune. Nothing else moves yet.

steps.title: Filter it warm
steps.why:
A medium filter setting keeps the tone warm, so when the pitch climbs later it stays pleasant rather than piercing.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 5.6 (902 Hz), PEAK 3: the low-pass removes what is above 902 Hz, taking the fizz off the saw. PEAK, Korg’s word for resonance, adds a little colour at the cutoff.
- High-pass CUTOFF 0.8 (21 Hz): the high-pass is almost out of the way, only trimming sub-bass rumble.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 1.6: EG2 is envelope generator 2. A small amount lifts the cutoff at the start of each note for a little brightness on the front.
- Listen for: a rounder, darker note than before, with a faint brighter start.

steps.title: Hold the note
steps.why:
Envelope 2 opens the amplifier, and here it keeps the note sounding for as long as the key is held, so it is still there when the delayed sweep arrives.
- ATTACK 1.5 (16 ms): a slightly soft start that takes the click off the front.
- DECAY 6 (690 ms), SUSTAIN 9: the level barely drops after the start, so held notes stay nearly full. The small filter lift from the last step settles over the same time.
- RELEASE 4 (460 ms): notes fade over about half a second after you let go.
- Listen for: an even, held note. Hold it for a couple of seconds; in the next steps something happens part way through.

steps.title: Set envelope 1 to wait, then rise
steps.why:
Envelope 1 is the simpler of the two envelopes, and it is wired to oscillator pitch. This step sets its shape; nothing is heard yet, because its depth knob is still at 0.
- DELAY TIME 7 (830 ms): EG1, envelope generator 1, waits this long after you press a key before it starts to rise. That wait is the whole trick, and a delay stage is rare on a monosynth.
- ATTACK TIME 5 (220 ms): once the wait is over, how long the climb takes. Short is a jump; long is a slide.
- RELEASE TIME 5 (690 ms): after you let go, how long the pitch takes to come back down.
- Listen for: no change yet. The next step connects this envelope to pitch.

steps.title: Send envelope 1 to pitch
steps.why:
The EG1/EXT knob in the frequency modulation section is how envelope 1 reaches the pitch of both oscillators. Turning it up makes the delayed climb audible.
- EG1/EXT 3.4: how far envelope 1 moves the pitch. Around 3 is a few semitones, a musical lift; past 6 it leaves the keyboard behind and becomes a siren. The EXT half of the name means a cable in the FREQ socket would take the envelope’s place here.
- Listen for: hold a note. It sits still for a little under a second, climbs over about a quarter of a second, then stays up. Let go and it falls back as it fades. Notes shorter than 830 ms never climb at all.

context.eg1.delay: How long the note waits before it starts to climb. This is the whole trick.
context.eg1.attack: How long the climb takes. Short is a jump, long is a slide.
context.fmod.eg1: How far the pitch climbs. Around 3 is a few semitones; past 6 it leaves the keyboard behind.
context.eg1.release: How the pitch comes back down when you let go.
context.eg2.sustain: High sustain keeps the note alive long enough for the delayed sweep to arrive.

tweaks.hear: A dramatic rising whistle instead of a musical interval — the classic tape-machine-speeding-up effect.
The sweep happens at the front of the note instead, which is the usual synth pitch blip.

tweaks.try: Set to 0 with delay still at 7
tweaks.hear: The pitch jumps in one step part way through the note.

sounds.name: Wind and Weather
sounds.ref: In the style of 1970s radio drama atmospheres
sounds.blurb: No oscillators at all: a resonant band of noise that rises and falls like wind.
sounds.how: The fourth position on Oscillator 1’s waveform switch replaces the oscillator with the noise generator. Noise holds every frequency at once, so the two filters can pick out a narrow band of it, and the ear hears that band as a pitch — like wind across a gap. The modulation generator moves the band slowly so the wind gusts on its own.

steps.title: Noise instead of an oscillator
steps.why:
There are no oscillators in this sound. The fourth position on Oscillator 1’s waveform switch swaps the oscillator for the noise generator, and noise holds every frequency at once: the raw material for wind.
- VCO1 WAVE FORM noise: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator, but in this position there is no oscillator at all, just noise. It costs you an oscillator, where most synths give noise its own mixer channel.
- VCO1 LEVEL 9.5: now the noise level, set high so there is plenty for the filters to pick from.
- VCO2 LEVEL 0: Oscillator 2 is silent, so nothing pitched is heard.
- Listen for: a steady hiss, slightly dulled by the low-pass at its starting 2.3 kHz. It is the same on every key, because noise has no pitch.

steps.title: Squeeze a band out of it
steps.why:
The two filters close in on the noise from both sides and leave a narrow band. With resonance on both edges the ear hears that band as a howl with a rough pitch, like wind across a gap.
- High-pass CUTOFF 3.4 (126 Hz), PEAK 6: the high-pass removes everything below 126 Hz; PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. Raising this cutoff turns weather into steam.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 5 (600 Hz), PEAK 6.8: the low-pass removes everything above 600 Hz. Its PEAK is how whistly the wind is: lower for distant surf, higher for a howling gale.
- FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits, applied to both filters, so the peaks whistle without tearing.
- Listen for: the hiss turning into a hollow, whistling band. Move the low-pass CUTOFF by hand to hear the wind’s pitch change.

steps.title: Let it swell
steps.why:
Envelope 2 opens the amplifier on every note. A long attack and a long release make each gust fade in and out rather than switching on.
- ATTACK 6.4 (620 ms): EG2, envelope generator 2, takes over half a second to reach full, so a gust arrives slowly when you press a key.
- DECAY 6 (690 ms), SUSTAIN 10: at full sustain the level simply stays up while you hold.
- RELEASE 6.6 (2.3 s): the wind dies away over a couple of seconds after you let go.
- VOLUME 9: the overall output. A narrow band of noise is quiet, so it needs more level here.
- Listen for: press and release a key. The wind rises, holds, then trails away.

steps.title: Move the band slowly
steps.why:
The modulation generator now moves the band up and down by itself, so the wind gusts without you touching anything.
- MG WAVE FORM 5 (triangle): MG is the modulation generator, Korg’s name for an LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a slow wave that moves other controls. A triangle rises and falls evenly, like a gust.
- FREQUENCY 1.2 (0.19 Hz): about one rise and fall every five seconds. This is how often the wind swells.
- Low-pass MG/T.EXT 4.4: how far the MG moves the top edge of the band, which is how far each gust travels.
- High-pass MG/T.EXT 2.4: a smaller move on the bottom edge, so the whole band shifts rather than just stretching.
- Listen for: hold a key for ten seconds. The whistle rises and falls in pitch. Set both MG/T.EXT knobs to 0 and it goes static.

context.lpf.peak: How whistly the wind is. Lower it for distant surf; raise it for a howling gale.
context.hpf.cutoff: The bottom of the band. Raising it turns weather into steam.
context.mg.freq: How often the wind rises and falls.
context.eg2.attack: How slowly a gust arrives when you press a key.

tweaks.try: Drop to 2 and lower the cutoff to 3
tweaks.hear: The whistle goes and distant surf is left.
Fast flutter instead of wind — closer to a helicopter or a flag.
A snare-like burst. Noise plus a fast envelope is how synth percussion starts.

sounds.name: Rubber Funk Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Daft Punk — Homework-era basslines
sounds.blurb: A round, bouncing bass with a soft quack on the front of every note.
sounds.how: Two oscillators an octave apart give weight and definition at once. The low-pass sits fairly closed with moderate resonance, and envelope 2 flicks it open for a fraction of a second on each note — that flick is the quack. FILTER 1 is the rounder of the two circuits, which keeps it warm rather than harsh.

steps.title: Saw plus square, an octave apart
steps.why:
Two oscillators an octave apart give weight and definition at once. The sawtooth carries the harmonics the filter will work on, and the square an octave above it adds a clear, hollow tone that helps the line read.
- VCO1 reverse saw, SCALE 16′: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. The saw has every harmonic, and 16′ puts it an octave below the key played, in bass range.
- VCO2 square, SCALE 8′: on this synth the same footage means the same pitch on both oscillators, so 8′ here is an octave above Oscillator 1. The square is hollow and solid.
- PITCH −0.1 (about −0.2 semitone): a slight flat offset so the two drift against each other instead of locking.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 8 / 6.5: the saw leads. Turn the square down and the bass gets thinner but more defined.
- Listen for: mute VCO2 LEVEL and bring it back. The note gains a firmer, hollow middle.

steps.title: Close the low-pass part way
steps.why:
This is the resting tone between the envelope’s flicks: dark and round.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 3.6 (232 Hz): the low-pass removes what is above the cutoff, so at 232 Hz the bass is mostly body. Raise it and the quack turns into a buzz.
- Low-pass PEAK 4.4: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. A moderate amount gives the coming sweep a vocal edge without screaming; past about 7 the low end starts to disappear.
- FILTER 1: the rounder of the two circuits, covering both filters. It keeps the bass warm rather than harsh.
- High-pass CUTOFF 0 (12 Hz), PEAK 0: the high-pass is fully out of the way, so none of the low end is lost.
- Listen for: a muffled, round bass note. The front edge comes in the next step.

steps.title: Flick it open
steps.why:
Envelope 2 now flicks the filter open at the start of every note and lets it close again. That quick flick is the rubbery quack.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 5.4: EG2 is envelope generator 2. This knob sets how far it opens the low-pass above 232 Hz: lower for a smooth dub bass, higher for a sharper funk bass.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: the filter opens instantly and starts closing at once, so the quack sits right on the beat.
- DECAY 4.6 (220 ms), SUSTAIN 3: the filter closes over about a fifth of a second to a low level. The same envelope drives the amplifier, so held notes also settle quieter.
- RELEASE 2.2 (150 ms): notes stop quickly after you let go.
- Listen for: a soft “wow” on the front of each note. Sweep DECAY while playing a line to hear the bounce get shorter or longer.

steps.title: Keep it tight
steps.why:
The shape is done; this step makes sure notes neither slide nor run into each other, which keeps a bassline funky rather than muddy.
- Portamento TIME 0: no glide, so every note jumps straight to pitch and the quack lands in time.
- VOLUME 8.5: the overall output level.
- Listen for: the gaps in a syncopated line, kept clean by the 150 ms release. Raise RELEASE to about 5 and the notes blur into each other.

context.lpf.cutoff: How dark the bass sits between flicks. Raise it and the quack turns into a buzz.
context.lpmod.eg2: The size of the quack. Lower for a smooth dub bass, higher for a sharper funk bass.
context.eg2.decay: How long the quack lasts. Around a fifth of a second is the sweet spot.
context.lpf.peak: Adds the vocal edge. Past about 7 the low end starts to disappear.
context.mix.vco2: The octave-up square is the weight. Turn it down and the bass gets thinner but more defined.

tweaks.hear: Short is a percussive pluck; long turns each note into a slow opening sweep.
Notes slide into each other — a lazier, more slurred groove.
Harder and dirtier. The same patch moves from house towards techno.

sounds.name: Wobble Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of late-2000s dubstep
sounds.blurb: A heavy bass note that opens and closes in time, all by itself.
sounds.how: The modulation generator is sent to the low-pass cutoff instead of to pitch. At a few cycles a second the filter opens and shuts repeatedly while you hold one note, and high resonance makes each pass across the cutoff growl. The WAVE FORM knob decides whether the wobble is smooth or jerky.

steps.title: A thick low pair
steps.why:
Two sawtooths low down fill out the bottom. They sit an octave apart, and the upper one is tuned a little sharp so the pair beats and the note never sounds still.
- Reverse saw on both: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. Saws have every harmonic, which gives the filter something to sweep past.
- SCALE 32′ and 16′: Korg’s octave switch in organ-pipe feet. 32′ on Oscillator 1 is two octaves below the key played; 16′ on Oscillator 2 is one octave below.
- PITCH 0.3 (about +0.6 semitone): Oscillator 2 sits slightly sharp of the octave, which gives a rough, fast beat.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 8 / 7: both in almost equally.
- Listen for: a deep, grinding low note with some movement in it.

steps.title: Low cutoff, high resonance
steps.why:
The wobble will be the cutoff sweeping past the harmonics, so the filter starts low, with plenty of resonance to exaggerate each pass.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 3 (154 Hz): the low-pass removes what is above the cutoff. This is the bottom of the sweep, how dark it gets at the closed end.
- Low-pass PEAK 7.4: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. This high, each pass across the harmonics growls; that is what turns a filter sweep into a wobble.
- FILTER 2: the harder of the two circuits, covering both filters. It distorts sooner and adds grit.
- High-pass CUTOFF 0 (12 Hz): the high-pass is out of the way, so the sub stays.
- Listen for: a dark note with a whistle on top. Sweep CUTOFF by hand; that is the movement the last step automates.

steps.title: Hold the note open
steps.why:
Envelope 2 opens the amplifier. Full sustain keeps the note at a steady level while held, so the filter does all the moving.
- ATTACK 0.5 (8 ms): nearly instant, with the click just softened.
- DECAY 6 (690 ms), SUSTAIN 10: no drop at all while the key is down.
- RELEASE 2.4 (170 ms): a short tail so notes stop cleanly.
- VOLUME 8.5: the overall output.
- Listen for: an unchanging held note. EG2/EXT is still at 0, so the envelope does not touch the filter.

steps.title: Send the modulation generator to the cutoff
steps.why:
The modulation generator goes to the low-pass cutoff instead of to pitch. The filter now opens and shuts about twice a second while you hold one note: the wobble.
- MG WAVE FORM 5 (triangle): MG is the modulation generator, Korg’s name for an LFO (low-frequency oscillator). At the centre it is a triangle, a smooth sweep up and down. Turn it to either end for a sawtooth that ramps and snaps back.
- FREQUENCY 5.6 (2.05 Hz): the wobble speed. Match it to the track by ear.
- Low-pass MG/T.EXT 5.4: the wobble depth, how far the cutoff travels. Too little is a tremble; too much sounds like a siren.
- Listen for: hold a low note and the growl opens and closes on its own. Turn FREQUENCY while holding to hear the wobble go from half-time to fast.

context.mg.freq: The speed of the wobble. Match it to the track by ear.
context.lpmod.mg: How far the filter travels on each wobble. Too little and it is a tremble; too much and it sounds like a siren.
context.lpf.peak: The growl. This is what turns a filter sweep into a wobble.
context.mg.wave: At the centre the wobble is a smooth triangle. Turned to either end it becomes a sawtooth, so the filter ramps and then snaps back.
context.lpf.cutoff: The bottom of the sweep — how dark it gets at the closed end.

tweaks.hear: The smooth wobble becomes a ramp that resets sharply — more aggressive, more rhythmic.
The wobble speeds past rhythm into a buzzing growl on the note itself.
The bass thins into a mid-range talking sound — the two filters chasing each other.

sounds.name: Filter Kick Drum
sounds.ref: In the style of 1980s electro and 1990s techno
sounds.blurb: A deep kick drum made from the filter alone, with no oscillators at all.
sounds.how: Wind PEAK up until the low-pass whistles on its own: the filter has become an oscillator, and the cutoff is its pitch. A fast envelope on the cutoff drops that pitch sharply at the start of each hit, and a fast envelope on the amplifier cuts it short. That pitch drop is what the ear reads as a drum.

steps.title: Almost nothing in the mixer
steps.why:
The filter is going to make this sound itself, so the mixer is almost empty. A whisper of triangle stays in so each hit has something to strike the filter with: from cold, a resonant filter takes a moment to get going, and the first kick would be missing.
- VCO1 triangle, SCALE 32′: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. A triangle has very few harmonics, and 32′, two octaves below the key, keeps it low and out of the way.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 3.5 / 0: just enough of Oscillator 1 to kick the filter. Turn it up and you hear the note as well as the drum. Oscillator 2 is off, its switch back on reverse saw.
- Listen for: a quiet, soft low tone. The drum appears in the next two steps.

steps.title: Make the filter sing
steps.why:
With PEAK near maximum the low-pass filter rings on its own at the cutoff frequency: the filter has become an oscillator, and the cutoff is its pitch.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 2.4 (102 Hz): the low-pass normally removes what is above the cutoff. Ringing, it is now the pitch of the drum: lower for a deeper kick, higher for a tom.
- Low-pass PEAK 9.8: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. Anything below about 9 and the filter stops ringing, so the drum disappears. This is the sound source.
- FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits, covering both filters, so the tone stays round rather than distorted.
- High-pass CUTOFF 0 (12 Hz), PEAK 0: the high-pass is fully open so none of the low end is lost.
- Listen for: hold a key and a steady, deep hum rings under the triangle. It is the filter itself.

steps.title: Drop the pitch on every hit
steps.why:
Envelope 2 pushes the cutoff up sharply on every hit and lets it fall back. Because the cutoff is the pitch, that is a pitch drop, and the ear reads a fast pitch drop as the click and thump of a kick.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 3.8: EG2 is envelope generator 2. This knob is the size of the drop: a little gives a soft thud; a lot gives a hard electro click.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: the cutoff jumps up the instant you play and starts falling straight away.
- DECAY 5 (300 ms): the length of the hit. Longer turns the kick into a tom or a bass note.
- SUSTAIN 0: envelope 2 also opens the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier), so with nothing sustained every hit dies away by itself, however long you hold the key.
- Listen for: the hum is gone, replaced by a “boom” with a click at the front. Sweep EG2/EXT while tapping a key.

steps.title: Cut it short
steps.why:
The last step sets the tail after you let go and the overall level. Most of the length already comes from the decay, so this is a tidy-up.
- RELEASE 2 (140 ms): if you let go during the hit, it still fades over about a seventh of a second rather than cutting off with a click.
- VOLUME 9: the overall output. A kick needs level to hit.
- Listen for: tap a steady four-to-the-floor on one low key. Every hit is identical. Try the low-pass CUTOFF at 3.5 for a tom.

context.lpf.peak: Anything below about 9 and the filter stops ringing, so the drum disappears. This is the sound source.
context.mix.vco1: Just enough oscillator to strike the filter on each hit. Turn it up and you hear the note as well as the drum.
context.lpf.cutoff: The pitch of the drum. Lower for a deeper kick, higher for a tom.
context.lpmod.eg2: The size of the pitch drop. A little gives a soft thud; a lot gives a hard electro click.
context.eg2.decay: The length of the hit. Longer turns the kick into a tom or a bass note.

tweaks.hear: The kick becomes a tom. Try playing a pattern up and down the keyboard.
A long booming 808-style kick with a tail.
The oscillator comes through under the thump — a bass note with a kick on the front of it.

sounds.name: Noise Snare
sounds.ref: In the style of early drum machines and electro
sounds.blurb: A short, bright crack of filtered noise.
sounds.how: A snare drum is mostly noise with a little pitch underneath. The waveform switch puts the noise generator where Oscillator 1 was, the high-pass takes the weight out so it cracks rather than thumps, and envelope 2 is set short so the whole thing is over in about a fifth of a second.

steps.title: Noise instead of an oscillator
steps.why:
A snare is mostly noise with a little pitch under it. The fourth waveform position swaps Oscillator 1 for the noise generator, which is the raw material.
- VCO1 WAVE FORM noise: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator, but in this position there is no oscillator, only noise, every frequency at once.
- VCO1 LEVEL 9: now the noise level, set high.
- VCO2 LEVEL 0: Oscillator 2 stays off, so there is no pitched note.
- Listen for: a steady hiss while the key is held. The envelope that turns it into a hit comes last.

steps.title: Take the weight out
steps.why:
A snare lives in the upper middle. The two filters trim the noise from both ends, so it cracks rather than thumps or hisses.
- High-pass CUTOFF 4.6 (288 Hz), PEAK 3.2: the high-pass removes everything below 288 Hz, taking out the rumble. Lower is a deep, wet snare; higher a tight rimshot. PEAK, Korg’s word for resonance, gives it a pitch of its own so it cuts through.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 8 (4.6 kHz), PEAK 2.6: the low-pass takes the very top off, so it is a crack rather than a hiss. This is how bright the crack is.
- FILTER 2: the harder of the two circuits, covering both filters, for a slightly rougher edge.
- Listen for: the hiss narrowing into a brighter, papery band with a faint ring in it.

steps.title: Make it a hit, not a note
steps.why:
Envelope 2 opens the amplifier, and here it is set as short as a drum: every press gives the same burst however long you hold the key.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: EG2, envelope generator 2, jumps straight to full. That instant start is the crack.
- DECAY 4.4 (190 ms), SUSTAIN 0: the burst dies away in under a fifth of a second. Longer becomes a cymbal or a hi-hat wash.
- RELEASE 1.6 (110 ms): a short tail if you let go early.
- VOLUME 9: the overall output.
- Listen for: a short crack on every tap. Play it on the off-beats against the filter kick for a basic electro pattern.

context.hpf.cutoff: How thin the snare is. Low is a deep, wet snare; high is a tight rimshot.
context.eg2.decay: The length of the hit. Longer becomes a cymbal or a hi-hat wash.
context.lpf.cutoff: How bright the crack is.
context.hpf.peak: A little resonance gives the snare a pitch of its own, which helps it cut through.

tweaks.hear: A cymbal or open hi-hat instead of a snare.
A fatter, deeper hit — closer to a tom than a snare.
The noise takes on a pitch, moving it towards a metallic ting.

sounds.name: Laser Zap
sounds.ref: In the style of 1970s and 80s arcade machines
sounds.blurb: A falling whistle that drops out of the top of the keyboard.
sounds.how: Envelope 1 is wired to oscillator pitch. Set it to snap up instantly and fall back slowly, wind the EG1/EXT knob a long way up, and every note starts far above where you played it and slides down. A simple tone works best — the point is the movement, not the timbre.

steps.title: One plain oscillator
steps.why:
A simple tone works best here: the point is the pitch movement, not the timbre.
- WAVE FORM pulse, PW 4: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. PW is pulse width, from a hollow square near 0 to thin and nasal towards 10. At 4 it is bright enough to follow as it falls without being harsh.
- SCALE 8′: Korg’s octave switch in organ-pipe feet; 8′ is the pitch of the key you play.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 8 / 0: one oscillator only, so the fall is one clear line.
- Listen for: a plain, buzzy note.

steps.title: Leave the filter open
steps.why:
Nothing should get in the way of the pitch drop, so both filters are left mostly out of the way.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 8 (4.6 kHz), PEAK 2.4: the low-pass removes what is above the cutoff. This high, the pulse comes through bright, even when the pitch is far up. A little PEAK, Korg’s word for resonance, adds some edge.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1.5 (34 Hz): the high-pass removes only the lowest rumble.
- Listen for: the note a little brighter and harder than before.

steps.title: Set envelope 1 to fall
steps.why:
Envelope 1 is the simpler of the two envelopes and is wired to oscillator pitch. It rises, holds while the key is down, and falls when you let go. Here it is set to jump up at once and fall back fairly slowly.
- DELAY TIME 0: EG1, envelope generator 1, starts the moment you press a key, with no wait.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (3 ms): it reaches the top at once, so the pitch will jump to its peak instantly. Raise it for a rise-then-fall instead.
- RELEASE TIME 4 (370 ms): how fast it falls after you let go. Quick is an arcade laser; slow is a falling bomb.
- Listen for: no change yet; the depth knob is still at 0.

steps.title: Wind the pitch depth up
steps.why:
The EG1/EXT knob in the frequency modulation section sets how far envelope 1 moves the pitch of both oscillators. Wound up high, every note starts far above where you played it.
- EG1/EXT 7.6: how far above the played note the zap starts. This is the main control. High settings take it well off the top of the keyboard.
- Listen for: tap a key briefly. The note starts as a high whistle and falls as you let go. Hold a key instead and it stays up there, because envelope 1 holds until release.

steps.title: Short notes
steps.why:
The amplifier envelope is set so the sound ends while the pitch is still falling. It never settles on a note, which is what makes it read as a zap rather than a bend.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms): EG2, envelope generator 2, opens the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) at once.
- DECAY 5.2 (350 ms), SUSTAIN 0: the sound fades out over about a third of a second, even if you hold the key.
- RELEASE 2.2 (150 ms): a quick tail after you let go.
- VOLUME 8.5: the overall output.
- Listen for: short taps. Each one is a falling “pew” that is gone before it lands. Raise DECAY and you hear the pitch settle, which turns the zap into a bend.

context.fmod.eg1: How far above the played note the zap starts. This is the main control.
context.eg1.release: How fast it falls. Quick is an arcade laser; slow is a falling bomb.
context.eg2.decay: How long the whole sound lasts. It should end before the pitch settles.
context.eg1.attack: At 0 the pitch is at the top instantly. Raise it and you get a rise-then-fall instead.

tweaks.hear: The pitch sweeps up before it falls — a rising whistle rather than a drop.
The note sits still on its own pitch, then leaps up part way through before it fades.

tweaks.try: Push to 9 and drop the cutoff to 4
tweaks.hear: The resonance whistles along with the drop, adding a second falling tone.

sounds.name: Vocal Band Pad
sounds.ref: In the style of 1970s library and television music
sounds.blurb: A slow, breathy pad with a voice-like formant in the middle.
sounds.how: Two resonant filters closed in on each other leave a narrow band, and a resonant peak at each edge of that band behaves like the formants in a human voice. A slow attack and release make it a pad; a slow sweep of the high-pass makes the vowel change as the note holds.

steps.title: Two detuned sawtooths
steps.why:
Two sawtooths give the filters every harmonic to shape, and a slight detune gives the slow drift a pad wants.
- Reverse saw on both, SCALE 8′: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. A sawtooth has every harmonic. 8′ on both is the same octave, the pitch of the key played.
- PITCH 0.2 (about +0.4 semitone): Oscillator 2 sits a little sharp, so the pair beats and swirls on a held chord or note.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 7.5 / 7: both in almost equally, for the widest effect.
- Listen for: a bright, moving buzz. The filters will turn it into a voice.

steps.title: Close the two filters in
steps.why:
The two filters close in on each other and leave a narrow band. A resonant peak at each edge behaves like the formants in a human voice, which is where the vocal quality comes from.
- High-pass CUTOFF 4 (190 Hz), PEAK 6.2: the high-pass takes away everything below 190 Hz. This is the lower formant: around 3 sounds like “aw”, around 5 like “ee”. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance; too much and the pad honks.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 6 (1.2 kHz), PEAK 5.8: the low-pass takes the top off above 1.2 kHz. This is the upper formant. Bring the two cutoffs closer for a narrower, more nasal voice.
- FILTER 1: the smoother circuit, covering both filters, which suits a pad.
- Listen for: the buzz turning into a hollow “ah”. Move the high-pass CUTOFF between 3 and 5 to change the vowel.

steps.title: Slow in, slow out
steps.why:
A long attack and a long release is most of what makes a pad a pad. Envelope 2 opens the amplifier, so these settings decide how each chord arrives and leaves.
- ATTACK 6 (460 ms): EG2, envelope generator 2, fades each note in over about half a second.
- HOLD 3 (88 ms): keeps the envelope at full for a moment before the decay begins.
- DECAY 6.5 (1.1 s), SUSTAIN 8: a gentle settle to a level that stays full while held.
- RELEASE 7 (2.9 s): chords fade out over nearly three seconds, so changes overlap.
- VOLUME 8.5: the overall output.
- Listen for: notes swelling in and trailing away. Play a slow line and hear each note blend into the next.

steps.title: Let the vowel move
steps.why:
A very slow modulation generator moves the lower formant, so the vowel changes while the note holds.
- MG WAVE FORM 5 (triangle): MG is the modulation generator, Korg’s name for an LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a slow wave that moves other controls. A triangle rises and falls evenly.
- FREQUENCY 0.9 (0.16 Hz): about one cycle every six seconds. Keep it well under one cycle a second.
- High-pass MG/T.EXT 2.6: how far the MG moves the lower formant, the main source of the vowel change.
- Low-pass MG/T.EXT 1.2: a smaller move on the upper formant, so the band shifts as a whole.
- Listen for: hold a note for ten seconds. The vowel slides from “aw” towards “ee” and back.

context.hpf.cutoff: The lower formant. Moving it changes the vowel — around 3 sounds like "aw", around 5 like "ee".
context.lpf.cutoff: The upper formant. Bring the two closer together for a narrower, more nasal voice.
context.hpf.peak: How strongly the lower formant sings. Too much and the pad honks.
context.eg2.attack: How slowly the chord arrives.
context.mg.freq: How slowly the vowel drifts. Keep it well under one cycle a second.

tweaks.try: Sweep between 2 and 6 while a chord holds
tweaks.hear: The pad moves through a set of vowels. This is the sound two filters make that one cannot.
Wider detune, faster beating — a bigger, more washed-out pad.
The formant softens and the pad turns into a plain warm string sound.

sounds.name: Hollow Fifth Stab
sounds.ref: In the style of Detroit techno chord stabs
sounds.blurb: A short, hollow stab with a fifth built into the sound.
sounds.how: Tuning Oscillator 2 a fifth above Oscillator 1 means a single key plays an interval, so a one-finger line sounds like a chord. Oscillator 2 is a square wave, which is hollow because it has no even harmonics, and Oscillator 1 a pulse. A short envelope on both filter and amplifier makes it a stab rather than a held note.

steps.title: Tune a fifth into the sound
steps.why:
Tuning Oscillator 2 a fifth above Oscillator 1 builds an interval into every key, so a one-finger line sounds like a chord. Hollow waves give it the classic organ-like stab.
- VCO1 pulse, PW 5: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. PW is pulse width: near 0 a hollow square, towards 10 thin and reedy. 5 is in between; narrower makes the stab thinner.
- VCO2 square, both SCALE 8′: a square is hollow because it has no even harmonics. Same footage means same octave on both.
- PITCH 2.9 (+7 semitones): the PITCH knob moves Oscillator 2 about an octave either way, so near 2.9 is a fifth. Near 4.9 is an octave; small values just detune.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 8 / 6.5: the root leads and the fifth sits slightly under it.
- Listen for: every key sounds a two-note chord. Set PITCH to 0 and it collapses back into one note.

steps.title: Thin it out from below
steps.why:
A little high-pass keeps the stab out of the way of a bassline, and the low-pass sits open enough for the hollow tone to read.
- High-pass CUTOFF 2.8 (83 Hz), PEAK 2: the high-pass removes what is below 83 Hz, leaving room underneath for the bass. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, here just a touch.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 6.4 (1.6 kHz), PEAK 4.8: the low-pass removes what is above 1.6 kHz. Moderate resonance gives the stab a slight bark.
- FILTER 2: the harder of the two circuits, covering both filters, for a bit more bite.
- Listen for: a less boomy chord on low keys, with a firmer middle.

steps.title: Stab it
steps.why:
Envelope 2 shapes both brightness and loudness here: every press is a short, bright hit that closes at once.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 4: EG2 is envelope generator 2. This is the brightness flick at the front of each stab.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: the stab hits instantly with no pause at the top.
- DECAY 5 (300 ms), SUSTAIN 0: it rings for under a third of a second and dies away even if you hold. Short keeps it percussive.
- RELEASE 2.2 (150 ms): a quick tail if you let go early.
- VOLUME 8.5: the overall output.
- Listen for: a stabbing off-beat chord. Play a syncopated one-finger pattern and lengthen DECAY to hear it turn into a pad.

context.vco2.pitch: The interval built into every note. Near 2.9 is a fifth; near 4.9 is an octave; small values just detune.
context.lpmod.eg2: The brightness flick at the front of each stab.
context.eg2.decay: How long the stab rings. Short keeps it percussive.
context.hpf.cutoff: How much room is left underneath for a bassline.
context.vco1.pw: Narrower pulse makes the stab thinner and more reedy.

tweaks.hear: The stab turns minor and darker without touching the keyboard.
A held organ chord instead of a stab.
A thin, nasal, almost oboe-like stab that cuts through a mix.

sounds.name: Stepped Bass Sequence
sounds.ref: In the style of Tangerine Dream — sequencer-driven albums
sounds.blurb: A running pattern that plays itself from one held key.
sounds.how: Three cables. The modulation generator’s pulse output clocks the sample and hold, the sample and hold reads noise and sends random voltages to Oscillator 2 only, and the same clock retriggers envelope 1. Oscillator 1 holds the root while Oscillator 2 wanders, which is why the result sounds like a pattern rather than noise.

steps.title: A root and a wanderer
steps.why:
Oscillator 1 will hold the note you play, and Oscillator 2 will be the one moved around by the sample and hold later. That split is why the result sounds like a pattern rather than noise.
- Reverse saw on both: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. Saws have every harmonic, so both parts read through the filter.
- SCALE 16′ and 8′: Korg’s octave switch in organ-pipe feet. Oscillator 1 is an octave below the key as the root; Oscillator 2 sits an octave above it.
- PITCH 0: Oscillator 2 in tune for now.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 6.5 / 7.5: the wanderer is a little louder than the root so its steps stand out.
- Listen for: a plain octave pair on a held note.

steps.title: Filter with a ping
steps.why:
A moderate cutoff and enough resonance that each new step pings as it arrives.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 5 (600 Hz): the low-pass removes what is above 600 Hz, rounding off the saws.
- Low-pass PEAK 6: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. This is how much each step will ping as it lands.
- FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits, covering both filters.
- High-pass CUTOFF 0.5 (17 Hz): the high-pass is practically out of the way.
- Listen for: a darker octave pair with a slight ring.

steps.title: Hold the note
steps.why:
Envelope 2 opens the amplifier. Full sustain means a single held key keeps the sequence running.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms): EG2, envelope generator 2, reaches full at once.
- DECAY 5 (300 ms), SUSTAIN 10: at full sustain the level simply stays up while held.
- RELEASE 2.5 (180 ms): a short tail after you let go.
- VOLUME 8.5: the overall output.
- Listen for: a steady note. The pattern comes in the next steps.

steps.title: Clock the sample and hold
steps.why:
The modulation generator’s pulse output becomes the clock for the sample and hold, so its FREQUENCY knob is now the tempo of the sequence.
- FREQUENCY 6.8 (3.92 Hz): MG is the modulation generator, Korg’s name for an LFO (low-frequency oscillator). Just under four steps a second.
- MG WAVE FORM 5: at the centre the pulse output is an even square, so the steps are evenly spaced.
- Cable MG OUT (pulse) → CLOCK: the pulse output only swings one way, a clean clock. CLOCK tells the S&H (sample and hold) when to take a new reading and hold it.
- Listen for: nothing new yet. The sample and hold is ticking, but its output is not connected.

steps.title: Send the steps to Oscillator 2 only
steps.why:
The random steps go to Oscillator 2 only. The root stays put and only the upper oscillator moves, which keeps the pattern anchored to the note you hold.
- Cable S&H OUT → VCO 2 CV IN: the sample and hold reads noise when nothing is in S&H IN, so each step is a random voltage. VCO 2 CV IN is the pitch CV (control voltage) input for Oscillator 2 alone. VCO 1+2 CV IN would move both and lose the anchor.
- Listen for: the upper line jumping to a new pitch about four times a second over a steady root. Change key and the whole pattern moves with you.

steps.title: Retrigger envelope 1 on every step
steps.why:
The same clock now fires envelope 1 on every step. A small amount of it on pitch gives each step a blip, so you hear the rhythm arrive.
- Cable MG OUT (pulse) → EG1 TRIG IN: fires envelope 1 in time with the clock rather than the keyboard.
- EG1 ATTACK 0 (3 ms), RELEASE 1.5 (77 ms): EG1 is envelope generator 1. It jumps up at once and falls back quickly after each tick.
- EG1/EXT 1.2: how far envelope 1 moves the pitch of both oscillators. Keep it under about 2 so it is a blip, not a bend.
- Listen for: a small “bip” at the front of each step. Set EG1/EXT to 0 and the rhythm goes vaguer; keep portamento TIME at 0 or the steps smear.

context.mg.freq: The tempo of the sequence, because the modulation generator is the clock.
context.lpf.peak: How much each step pings as it lands.
context.mix.vco2: How prominent the wandering oscillator is against the held root.
context.fmod.eg1: The small blip on each step that makes the rhythm audible. Keep it under about 2.
context.porta.time: At 0 the steps jump. Any glide at all smears them into a slide.

tweaks.hear: The steps slide into each other, turning the sequence into a burbling drift.
A slow, deliberate pattern instead of a chatter.
The anchor disappears and the whole thing becomes random — which is why the root note matters.

sounds.name: Feedback Howl
sounds.ref: In the style of industrial and noise records
sounds.blurb: The synth listens to itself and the filter chases its own output.
sounds.how: This is what the external signal processor is for. Patch the main output back into SIGNAL IN, and the envelope follower produces a voltage that rises with how loud the synth currently is. Send that to the low-pass cutoff and you have a loop: louder opens the filter, which makes it louder still, until the filter shuts it down again. It never settles, which is the point.

steps.title: A rough starting tone
steps.why:
The feedback loop needs harmonics to work on. Two sawtooths an octave apart and badly detuned give it plenty and start the sound off unstable.
- Reverse saw on both: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. Saws have every harmonic.
- SCALE 16′ and 8′: Korg’s octave switch in organ-pipe feet. Oscillator 1 an octave below the key, Oscillator 2 at the key.
- PITCH 0.6 (about +1.4 semitones): Oscillator 2 pulled well out of its octave, so the pair sounds sour and rough.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 7.5 / 6.5: both in fairly hot.
- Listen for: a harsh, beating drone.

steps.title: Set the filter low and angry
steps.why:
The cutoff starts almost closed so there is somewhere for the feedback to push it. FILTER 2 and high PEAK give the loop its bite.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 2.8 (134 Hz): the low-pass removes what is above 134 Hz. This is where the filter sits before the feedback pushes it anywhere.
- Low-pass PEAK 7.8: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. This is the peak the loop will chase, and it sets how violent the howl is.
- FILTER 2: the harder of the two circuits, covering both filters. It distorts sooner.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1.2 (27 Hz), PEAK 3: the high-pass trims sub rumble, with a little resonance at the bottom.
- Listen for: a dark, growling thud with a whistle on top.

steps.title: Hold it open
steps.why:
Envelope 2 opens the amplifier. The loop needs time to run, so the note is held fully open.
- ATTACK 1.5 (16 ms): EG2, envelope generator 2, starts with a slightly soft front.
- DECAY 6 (690 ms), SUSTAIN 10: the level stays at full for as long as you hold.
- RELEASE 4 (460 ms): about half a second of tail.
- VOLUME 8.5: the overall output.
- Listen for: a steady held growl.

steps.title: Feed the output back to the signal processor
steps.why:
The main output goes back into the external signal processor, which turns an incoming sound into voltages the synth can use. Its envelope follower makes a voltage that rises with how loud the synth is right now.
- Cable SIGNAL OUT → SIGNAL IN: the synth’s own output into the processor’s input.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 6.5: the preamp gain, how hard the output drives the follower. Turn it down and the loop goes quiet; up and it never settles.
- Listen for: no change yet. The follower is working, but its output goes nowhere.

steps.title: Close the loop
steps.why:
ENV OUT, the envelope follower, goes to the low-pass cutoff. Louder opens the filter, which makes it louder still, until the filter shuts it down again. It never settles, which is the point.
- Cable ENV OUT → CUTOFF FREQ (low-pass): that socket takes envelope 2’s place at the low-pass EG2/EXT knob.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 4.6: EG2 is envelope generator 2, but with the cable in, this knob is the feedback amount. Small values give a slow, heaving movement; large ones make it howl and tear.
- Listen for: hold a note and the tone surges and chokes by itself. Ride EG2/EXT from 2 to 7 to hear it go from growl to scream.

context.lpmod.eg2: The feedback amount, because the CUTOFF FREQ cable replaced envelope 2 at this knob. Small values give a slow breathing; large ones make it howl and tear.
context.esp.level: How hard the output is driven into the follower. Turn it down and the loop goes quiet; up and it never settles.
context.lpf.peak: The resonance the loop is chasing. This sets how violent the howl is.
context.lpf.cutoff: Where the filter starts before the feedback pushes it anywhere.

tweaks.hear: Low is a slow breathing swell; high is an unstable tearing howl that fights itself.
The loop is too weak to sustain itself and the sound settles into an ordinary filtered tone.
A second resonant peak joins in and the howl gains a hollow, throat-like quality.

sounds.name: Held Drone with Tremolo
sounds.ref: In the style of 1970s minimal and drone records
sounds.blurb: A continuous tone that swells and fades on its own.
sounds.how: The INITIAL GAIN socket adds to whatever envelope 2 is doing at the amplifier. Send the modulation generator there and the sound pulses without you touching anything. Here the modulation generator does two jobs at once: it opens the amplifier rhythmically and moves both filters, so the swell and the tone change together.

steps.title: A wide detuned pair
steps.why:
Two sawtooths an octave apart and a good way off in tuning drift against each other slowly, which keeps a drone alive rather than static.
- Reverse saw on both: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. Saws have every harmonic for the filters to shape.
- SCALE 16′ and 8′: Korg’s octave switch in organ-pipe feet. Oscillator 1 an octave below the key, Oscillator 2 at the key.
- PITCH 0.4 (about +0.8 semitone): the drift between the two. Small offsets give a slow beat; larger ones give an interval.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 7.5 / 7: both in almost equally.
- Listen for: a thick, restless held tone.

steps.title: Warm and narrow
steps.why:
A little high-pass stops the drone becoming muddy, and a moderate low-pass with some resonance gives it a centre.
- High-pass CUTOFF 2.2 (55 Hz), PEAK 3.6: the high-pass removes everything below 55 Hz, clearing out the mud. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 5.2 (687 Hz), PEAK 5.2: the low-pass takes the top off above 687 Hz. Its resonance gives the drone a pitch centre of its own, under the oscillators.
- FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits, covering both filters.
- Listen for: a warmer, rounder drone with a faint ring in the middle.

steps.title: Long envelope
steps.why:
Envelope 2 opens the amplifier. Slow in, slow out and full sustain, so the keyboard fades the drone in and out rather than switching it.
- ATTACK 7 (970 ms): EG2, envelope generator 2, takes about a second to fade the drone in.
- DECAY 7 (1.6 s), SUSTAIN 10: at full sustain the drone simply stays up while held.
- RELEASE 8 (5.3 s): after you let go it dies away over five seconds.
- VOLUME 8.5: the overall output.
- Listen for: press and release a key. The drone swells in and takes a long time to fade.

steps.title: Pulse the amplifier
steps.why:
The INITIAL GAIN socket adds to whatever envelope 2 is doing at the amplifier. With the modulation generator patched there, the drone swells and fades on its own.
- MG WAVE FORM 5 (triangle): MG is the modulation generator, Korg’s name for an LFO (low-frequency oscillator). A triangle rises and falls evenly, a smooth swell.
- FREQUENCY 2.2 (0.33 Hz): about one swell every three seconds.
- Cable MG OUT (triangle) → INITIAL GAIN: the MG’s first output, marked reverse saw / triangle / saw, which swings both ways, into the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) control.
- Listen for: a slow pulse in the level while the note holds.

steps.title: Move the filters at the same time
steps.why:
The same modulation generator also reaches both cutoffs through the panel knobs. Because it is one source, the loudness and the tone move together, which sounds deliberate rather than like two unrelated wobbles.
- Low-pass MG/T.EXT 3.2: how much the MG moves the low-pass cutoff, so how much the tone changes on each pulse.
- High-pass MG/T.EXT 1.4: a smaller move on the high-pass, so the bottom shifts slightly too.
- Listen for: each swell now also gets brighter. Turn low-pass MG/T.EXT to 0 to hear the loudness move on its own.

context.mg.freq: The speed of the pulse, since the modulation generator is driving both the amplifier and the filters.
context.lpmod.mg: How much the tone changes on each pulse, as against how much the loudness does.
context.eg2.attack: How slowly the drone fades in when you press a key.
context.vco2.pitch: The drift between the two oscillators. Small offsets give a slow beat; larger ones give an interval.
context.lpf.peak: Gives the drone a pitch centre of its own, under the oscillators.

tweaks.hear: A very long swell, closer to breathing than tremolo.
The pulse becomes a reverse sawtooth: each swell jumps up at once and fades away slowly.
A fifth instead of a detune. The drone turns from one thick note into an open interval.

sounds.name: Audio-Rate Growl
sounds.ref: In the style of industrial synth textures
sounds.blurb: A harsh, metallic lead made by shaking the pitch faster than the ear can follow.
sounds.how: Push the modulation generator up to audio rate and send it to pitch. Below about twenty cycles a second that is vibrato; above it, the ear stops hearing the wobble and starts hearing new frequencies instead, which is frequency modulation. The result is inharmonic and metallic, and the two filters shape what survives.

steps.title: One oscillator to be shaken
steps.why:
The source is kept simple: with FM (frequency modulation) the interest comes from the modulation, not from stacking oscillators.
- WAVE FORM reverse saw, SCALE 8′: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. A saw has every harmonic, so there is plenty for the modulation to smear. 8′ is the pitch of the key played.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 8.5 / 0: one oscillator only.
- Listen for: a plain, bright buzz.

steps.title: Run the modulation generator flat out
steps.why:
The modulation generator is pushed to the top of its range. At about twenty-two cycles a second it is just into the range the ear hears as tone rather than wobble.
- FREQUENCY 10 (22 Hz): MG is the modulation generator, Korg’s name for an LFO (low-frequency oscillator), normally a slow wave that moves other controls. Up here every position gives a different set of inharmonic tones, so it acts as a tone control, not a speed control.
- MG WAVE FORM 5 (triangle): a smooth shape, so the modulation adds fewer extra harsh tones than a saw would.
- Listen for: no change yet. The MG is running but not yet sent anywhere.

steps.title: Send it to pitch, hard
steps.why:
The MG now shakes the pitch of the oscillator. Below about twenty cycles a second that would be vibrato; this fast the ear hears new frequencies instead, which is what FM means.
- Pitch MG/T.EXT 4.2: how far the MG moves the pitch of both oscillators, so it is the FM amount and the whole sound. At 1 it is a rasp, at 4 a metallic growl, past 7 the note is gone and only clang is left.
- Listen for: the clean buzz turning rough and metallic. Sweep MG/T.EXT from 0 to 7 on a held note, then try FREQUENCY between 8 and 10.

steps.title: Filter the mess
steps.why:
FM throws off a lot of harsh upper harmonics. The two filters tame them and pick out a band so it sounds intentional rather than broken.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 5.6 (902 Hz), PEAK 5.6: the low-pass removes what is above 902 Hz; this is how much of the harshness survives. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance.
- FILTER 2: the harder of the two circuits, covering both filters. It adds its own grit.
- High-pass CUTOFF 2.4 (63 Hz), PEAK 4: the high-pass trims the low rumble, and its resonance picks out a band of the clang and emphasises it.
- Listen for: the fizz gone from the top, and a honking, nasal growl left in the middle.

steps.title: Shape each note
steps.why:
Envelope 2 opens the amplifier and, through EG2/EXT, gives the filter a short sweep at the front of each note, so it bites and then settles.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 3.4: EG2 is envelope generator 2. This sets how far it opens the low-pass on each note.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms): the bite lands at once.
- DECAY 3.6 (97 ms), SUSTAIN 6: the sweep falls back within a tenth of a second to a level that keeps held notes growling.
- RELEASE 2.4 (170 ms), VOLUME 8: a short tail, and the overall output.
- Listen for: a brighter snarl on the front of each note, then a steady growl. Play short, spaced notes to hear the bite.

context.fmod.mg: The FM amount. This is the whole sound: at 1 it is a rasp, at 4 a metallic growl, past 7 the note is gone and only clang is left.
context.mg.freq: The modulating frequency. Every position gives a different set of inharmonic tones, so up here it is a tone control, not a speed control.
context.lpf.cutoff: How much of the harshness survives.
context.hpf.peak: Picks out a band of the clang and emphasises it, which makes the sound read as deliberate.

tweaks.hear: The metallic character changes completely with each position, like retuning a bell.
A gritty rasp on an otherwise normal lead — a useful amount for a mix.
The resonance picks one of the clang tones and sings it, turning the growl into a metallic lead.

sounds.name: Fat Buzzing Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Mr Oizo — "Flat Beat"
sounds.blurb: A thick, buzzing bass that sits low and refuses to move.
sounds.how: Almost all of this is in the mixer and the filter type. Both oscillators are run high enough to push the filter into distortion, FILTER 2 is the circuit that distorts soonest, and the cutoff stays put rather than sweeping. What movement there is comes from a small flick of envelope 2, just enough to give each note a front edge.

steps.title: A pulse and a sawtooth, same octave
steps.why:
A pulse and a sawtooth in the same octave make one fat tone rather than two notes. The pulse gives the hollow body, and the saw fills in the harmonics between.
- VCO1 pulse, PW 3: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. PW is pulse width; near 0 is a fat square and higher values thin it out. 3 is a slightly narrowed square.
- VCO2 reverse saw, both SCALE 16′: Korg’s octave switch in organ-pipe feet. 16′ is an octave below the key, and the same footage means the same octave on both.
- PITCH −0.1 (about −0.2 semitone): a slight flat offset so the pair moves a little instead of locking.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 8.5 / 7: both high on purpose. Next step, this drives the filter into distortion.
- Listen for: a thick, hollow buzz.

steps.title: Overload the filter
steps.why:
With both mixer levels up, the filter is fed more than it can take cleanly. FILTER 2, the circuit that distorts soonest, gives the buzz its dirt.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 4.2 (348 Hz): the low-pass removes what is above 348 Hz. Low is a thud; past about 6 it turns harsh. It stays put here rather than sweeping.
- Low-pass PEAK 5.6: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. A little emphasis; too much and the low end drains away.
- FILTER 2: the harder-edged circuit, covering both filters. On FILTER 1 the same patch is clean and much politer.
- High-pass CUTOFF 0 (12 Hz), PEAK 0: the high-pass is fully out of the way.
- Listen for: flip FILTER 1 and 2 on a held note. FILTER 2 fuzzes; FILTER 1 is round. Then turn VCO1 LEVEL down to hear the dirt go.

steps.title: A small flick, not a sweep
steps.why:
Only a small flick of envelope on the cutoff. The note should arrive already buzzing, with a short edge on the front rather than a filter sweep.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 3.2: EG2 is envelope generator 2. A small amount, just enough for a front edge.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: the edge lands at once.
- DECAY 5.2 (350 ms), SUSTAIN 6: the edge falls back over a third of a second. High sustain keeps the note buzzing for its whole length; envelope 2 also sets loudness, so the level holds too.
- RELEASE 2.2 (150 ms): notes stop quickly.
- Listen for: a slight “dt” on the front of each note, then steady buzz.

steps.title: No glide, plenty of level
steps.why:
Nothing slides and the level is up. This kind of bass works by being blunt.
- Portamento TIME 0: no glide, so each note starts where it means to.
- VOLUME 8.5: the overall output.
- Listen for: a stubborn, flat riff on one or two notes. The sound barely changes over the length of a note, which is the character.

context.lpf.type: FILTER 2 is where the dirt comes from. On FILTER 1 the same patch is clean and much politer.
context.mix.vco1: How hard the filter is driven. This is a distortion control as much as a level control.
context.lpf.cutoff: How buzzy the bass sits. Low is a thud; past about 6 it turns harsh.
context.lpf.peak: A little emphasis at the cutoff. Too much and the low end drains away.
context.eg2.sustain: High sustain keeps the note buzzing for its whole length instead of dying back.
context.vco1.pw: Near 0 the pulse is a square and the tone is fat. Turn it up and the bass thins out.

tweaks.hear: Thin and nasal instead of fat — the same line but pushed up out of the bottom.
The buzz takes over and the bass starts to sound like a lead.
The dirt goes. Useful for hearing how much of this sound is the filter circuit.
A short plucked bass rather than a held buzz.

sounds.name: Distorted Riff Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of The Prodigy — the fuzzed synth lines of "Girls"
sounds.blurb: A snarling riff bass, badly detuned and driven until it fuzzes.
sounds.how: Two sawtooths tuned far enough apart to fight each other, both run hard into FILTER 2 so the filter clips. A slow movement from the modulation generator keeps the tone shifting, so a repeated riff never sounds quite the same twice. The high-pass takes out the rumble that all that detuning creates.

steps.title: Detune the two oscillators hard
steps.why:
Two sawtooths in the same octave, detuned hard. A small detune thickens; this much makes them beat fast enough to sound rough before the filter has done anything.
- Reverse saw on both, SCALE 16′: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. Saws have every harmonic. 16′ is an octave below the key, the same octave on both.
- PITCH 0.4 (about +1 semitone): the amount of fight between the two. Deliberately rough.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 9 / 8.5: both near the top. This is level and distortion at once, since it overloads the filter next.
- Listen for: a sour, grinding pair that sounds slightly out of tune.

steps.title: Drive the filter and take the rumble out
steps.why:
Both levels near the top overload FILTER 2. The high-pass then removes the low beating from the detune, which stops the riff turning to mud.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 5 (600 Hz), PEAK 6: the low-pass removes what is above 600 Hz. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance: the edge on the fuzz. Above about 8 it starts to whistle over the riff.
- FILTER 2: the harder of the two circuits, covering both filters. It clips sooner.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1.8 (42 Hz), PEAK 2.4: the high-pass clears the mud under the detune. Take it to 0 and the riff loses its definition.
- Listen for: a fuzzed, snarling note. Back both mixer levels off and it cleans up more than turning VOLUME down would.

steps.title: Bite on every note
steps.why:
A short sweep of the cutoff at the front of each note gives the riff its attack without softening the fuzz behind it.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 4.2: EG2 is envelope generator 2. This sets how far it opens the low-pass on each note.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: the bite lands instantly.
- DECAY 4.6 (220 ms), SUSTAIN 7: the sweep falls back over about a fifth of a second, and the high sustain keeps held notes loud and fuzzed.
- RELEASE 2 (140 ms): notes stop short.
- Listen for: a harder “bap” on the front of each note of a riff.

steps.title: Keep the tone moving
steps.why:
A slow triangle on the cutoff, kept small. You should not hear it as a wobble; it just stops a repeated riff sounding static.
- MG WAVE FORM 5 (triangle): MG is the modulation generator, Korg’s name for an LFO (low-frequency oscillator). A triangle moves smoothly both ways.
- FREQUENCY 3.2 (0.56 Hz): about one cycle every two seconds, slower than most riffs repeat, so each pass sounds slightly different.
- Low-pass MG/T.EXT 2.2: how far the MG moves the cutoff. Keep it low enough that you notice it only when it is gone.
- VOLUME 8: the overall output.
