- Listen for: loop a one-bar riff, then set MG/T.EXT to 0. The riff goes flatter and more mechanical.

context.vco2.pitch: The amount of fight between the two oscillators. Small values thicken; this much is deliberately rough.
context.mix.vco2: Level and distortion at once. Backing both mixer knobs off cleans the sound up more than lowering the volume does.
context.lpf.peak: The edge on the fuzz. Above about 8 it starts to whistle over the riff.
context.hpf.cutoff: Clears the mud the detuning makes. Take it to 0 and the riff loses its definition.
context.lpmod.mg: The slow drift. Keep it low enough that you notice it only when it is gone.

tweaks.hear: The fight stops and the riff becomes clean and wide instead of rough.

tweaks.try: Sweep between 3 and 7 while the riff plays
tweaks.hear: The classic filter ride, from a muffled thud to a full snarl.
All the weight goes and the riff sits in the middle, ready for a separate sub underneath.

sounds.name: Swelling Wobble Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Jon Hopkins — "Open Eye Signal"
sounds.blurb: A rolling bass whose wobble is not there at first and grows into the long notes.
sounds.how: Three cables build something the front panel cannot do. The modulation generator goes into the patch-panel VCA instead of straight to a filter, envelope 1 controls that VCA, and its output goes to the high-pass cutoff. Because envelope 1 waits before it opens, the wobble is absent for the first part of a note and then fades up — so short notes stay plain and held ones open out.

steps.title: A firm low pair
steps.why:
A sawtooth for the harmonics and a square an octave up for definition. The square stops the bass disappearing on small speakers.
- VCO1 reverse saw, SCALE 16′: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. The saw has every harmonic; 16′ is an octave below the key.
- VCO2 square, SCALE 8′: an octave above Oscillator 1, since the same footage means the same pitch on both. The square is hollow and firm.
- PITCH −0.1 (about −0.3 semitone): a slight flat offset so the two move against each other.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 8 / 5.5: the saw leads; the square is support.
- Listen for: a solid bass with a clear middle.

steps.title: Set both filters
steps.why:
The low-pass gives the bass its weight. The high-pass is the one that will be moved later, so it starts low: there is no point modulating a filter that is already out of the way.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 5.2 (687 Hz), PEAK 6: the low-pass removes what is above 687 Hz. This is the weight underneath, which stays steady while the top moves. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance.
- FILTER 2: the harder of the two circuits, covering both filters.
- High-pass CUTOFF 2.2 (55 Hz), PEAK 4.6: the high-pass trims below 55 Hz. Its resonance is what the wobble will sweep through; without it the movement is much harder to hear.
- Listen for: a full, slightly nasal bass.

steps.title: Hold the note
steps.why:
Envelope 2 opens the amplifier. The sustain is high so a note lasts long enough for the wobble to arrive, and a short attack keeps the rhythm tight.
- ATTACK 0.8 (10 ms): EG2, envelope generator 2, starts almost at once.
- DECAY 5.5 (460 ms), SUSTAIN 8: a small settle, then held notes stay full.
- RELEASE 2.4 (170 ms): notes stop cleanly.
- VOLUME 8: the overall output.
- Listen for: an even held note. Nothing moves yet.

steps.title: Modulation generator into the patch-panel VCA
steps.why:
The modulation generator goes into the spare VCA on the patch panel instead of straight to a filter. A VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) here is an amplifier for control voltages, so something else can decide how much of the wobble gets out.
- MG WAVE FORM 5 (triangle): MG is the modulation generator, Korg’s name for an LFO (low-frequency oscillator). A triangle gives a smooth up-and-down wobble.
- FREQUENCY 7.6 (6.03 Hz): about six wobbles a second. Set it against the tempo by ear.
- Cable MG OUT (triangle) → VCA IN: the MG’s first output, marked reverse saw / triangle / saw, which swings both ways, into the spare VCA.
- Listen for: no change yet; the VCA’s output goes nowhere.

steps.title: Envelope 1 opens the VCA
steps.why:
Envelope 1 now controls the spare VCA. With a delay before its attack, it holds the VCA shut for the first part of each note and then opens it, so the wobble fades in.
- Cable EG 1 OUT → CONTROL INPUT: CONTROL INPUT sets the VCA’s gain.
- DELAY TIME 5 (230 ms): EG1, envelope generator 1, waits about a quarter of a second before it starts. Notes shorter than this never wobble at all.
- ATTACK TIME 5.5 (340 ms): how gradually the wobble fades up once the delay is over.
- RELEASE TIME 3.5 (270 ms): how quickly the VCA closes after you let go.
- Listen for: still no change; the VCA output is not patched yet.

steps.title: Out to the high-pass cutoff
steps.why:
The VCA output goes to the high-pass cutoff. Short notes stay plain and long ones open out into a wobble, which is what gives the line both plain and moving notes.
- Cable VCA OUT → CUTOFF FREQ (high-pass): that socket takes envelope 2’s place at the high-pass EG2/EXT knob.
- High-pass EG2/EXT 4.4: with the cable in, this is the wobble depth, the main control of the patch.
- Listen for: play a line mixing short and long notes. The short ones are solid; on the long ones, the top starts to throb about a quarter of a second in. Change DELAY TIME to move where the wobble starts.

context.hpmod.eg2: The depth of the wobble, because the CUTOFF FREQ cable replaced envelope 2 at this knob. This is the main control of the patch.
context.eg1.delay: How long each note stays still before the wobble starts to arrive. Notes shorter than this never wobble at all, which is why the line has both plain and moving notes in it.
context.eg1.attack: How gradually the wobble fades up once the delay is over.
context.mg.freq: The speed of the wobble. Set it against the tempo by ear.
context.hpf.peak: The resonance the wobble sweeps through. Without it the movement is much harder to hear.
context.lpf.cutoff: The weight underneath, which stays steady while the top moves.

tweaks.hear: The wobble is there from the first moment. Hearing both tells you what the delay stage is for.
The wobble tightens into a buzz that arrives part way through each note.
The high-pass swings far enough to strip the bass out completely at the top of each cycle.

sounds.name: Random Squiggle Line
sounds.ref: In the style of The Chemical Brothers — the squiggling synth lines of "The Big Jump"
sounds.blurb: A held note whose filter jumps to a new setting several times a second.
sounds.how: Two cables. The modulation generator’s pulse output clocks the sample and hold, and the sample and hold — which reads noise unless you tell it otherwise — sends a new random voltage to the low-pass cutoff on every tick. High resonance makes each random setting ring at its own pitch, so one held key produces a line that sounds written.

steps.title: One bright oscillator
steps.why:
A pulse wave has plenty of harmonics for the filter to pick from, and reads clearly when the cutoff is jumping about.
- WAVE FORM pulse, PW 5: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. PW is pulse width, from a hollow square near 0 to thin and nasal towards 10. 5 sits in between.
- SCALE 8′: Korg’s octave switch in organ-pipe feet; 8′ is the pitch of the key you play.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 8 / 0: one oscillator only.
- Listen for: a plain, bright note.

steps.title: Resonant and part closed
steps.why:
The random steps will move the cutoff up and down from here. Resonance makes each setting audible as a pitch rather than just a change in brightness.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 3.4 (202 Hz): the low-pass removes what is above 202 Hz. This is the centre the steps move around.
- Low-pass PEAK 7.4: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. This is what turns random brightness into a random tune.
- FILTER 2: the harder of the two circuits, covering both filters, for more squelch.
- High-pass CUTOFF 2 (48 Hz): the high-pass trims the lowest rumble.
- Listen for: a dark, whistling note.

steps.title: Hold the note open
steps.why:
Envelope 2 opens the amplifier. Full sustain keeps the sound running, so all the movement comes from the filter.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms): EG2, envelope generator 2, reaches full at once.
- DECAY 5 (300 ms), SUSTAIN 10: at full sustain the level stays up while held.
- RELEASE 2 (140 ms): a short tail.
- VOLUME 8.5: the overall output.
- Listen for: an even, held note.

steps.title: Clock the sample and hold
steps.why:
The modulation generator’s pulse output becomes the clock for the sample and hold. Its FREQUENCY knob now sets how often a new value arrives.
- FREQUENCY 8.2 (8.33 Hz): MG is the modulation generator, Korg’s name for an LFO (low-frequency oscillator). About eight new values a second, the speed of the squiggle.
- MG WAVE FORM 5: at the centre the pulse output is an even square.
- Cable MG OUT (pulse) → CLOCK: the pulse only swings one way, a clean clock. CLOCK tells the S&H (sample and hold) when to take a reading and hold it.
- Listen for: no change yet; the sample and hold’s output is not connected.

steps.title: Random values to the cutoff
steps.why:
Random values now go to the low-pass cutoff. One held key produces a line that sounds written.
- Cable S&H OUT → CUTOFF FREQ (low-pass): with nothing in S&H IN it reads noise, so each value is random. That socket takes envelope 2’s place at the low-pass EG2/EXT knob.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 4.2: with the cable in, this sets how far each step moves the filter. Small values give a nervous flicker; large ones leap octaves.
- Listen for: a fast, bubbling run of resonant pitches over one held note. Keep portamento TIME at 0 so the steps snap; any glide smooths them into a slither.

context.mg.freq: The speed of the squiggle, because the modulation generator is the clock.
context.lpmod.eg2: How far the filter jumps on each step, since the cable replaced envelope 2 at this knob. Small values give a nervous flicker; large ones leap octaves.
context.lpf.peak: How much each step rings. This is what turns random brightness into a random tune.
context.lpf.cutoff: The centre the steps move around.
context.porta.time: At 0 the steps snap. Any glide smooths them into a slither.

tweaks.hear: A lazy random melody instead of a squiggle — you hear each step land.
The filter sings a tune of its own over the top of the note.
The filter slides between its random settings, which sounds like a drunk siren.

sounds.name: Plucked Hook Line
sounds.ref: In the style of Simian Mobile Disco — the repeated hooks of Attack Decay Sustain Release
sounds.blurb: A short, bright pluck built for one repeated phrase.
sounds.how: The whole sound is in the envelope. A square wave, a moderately resonant filter and a very short decay give a pluck that stops dead, which is what lets a fast repeated line stay readable. The high-pass keeps it clear of anything playing underneath.

steps.title: A square and its octave
steps.why:
Squares are hollow and cut through. A second one an octave up adds sparkle to the front of each pluck without making the note ambiguous.
- VCO1 pulse, PW 2: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. PW is pulse width; near 0 is a square, so 2 is close to square, just a little thinner.
- VCO2 square: a true square for Oscillator 2.
- SCALE 8′ and 4′: Korg’s octave switch in organ-pipe feet. Oscillator 2 sits an octave above Oscillator 1.
- PITCH 0.1 (about +0.2 semitone): a slight offset so the two do not lock.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 7.5 / 5: the octave on top sits lower; turn it down for a rounder, more muted hook.
- Listen for: a bright, hollow organ-like note.

steps.title: Leave room underneath
steps.why:
The high-pass keeps the hook out of the way of a bassline, and moderate resonance on the low-pass gives the pluck a ping.
- High-pass CUTOFF 3.2 (109 Hz), PEAK 2.6: the high-pass removes what is below 109 Hz, leaving room underneath for a bass part. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 6.2 (1.4 kHz), PEAK 5.4: the low-pass removes what is above 1.4 kHz. Its resonance is the ping on each note; past about 7 it starts to overpower the note itself.
- FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits, covering both filters.
- Listen for: a lighter note on low keys with a slight ring in the middle.

steps.title: Pluck it
steps.why:
The whole sound is in the envelope: a very short decay gives a pluck that stops dead, which keeps a fast repeated line readable.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 4.6: EG2 is envelope generator 2. This is the brightness flick at the front, most of what makes it a pluck rather than a blip.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: the pluck starts at once.
- DECAY 4.2 (160 ms), SUSTAIN 0: the most important control here. Each note is over in about a sixth of a second; longer and the notes run together.
- RELEASE 1.6 (110 ms), VOLUME 8.5: a short tail, and the overall output.
- Listen for: play a fast repeated phrase. Every note is distinct. Slowly lengthen DECAY and hear the hook blur.

context.eg2.decay: The length of the pluck, and the single most important control here. Longer and the notes run together.
context.lpmod.eg2: The brightness flick at the front of each note. This is most of what makes it a pluck rather than a blip.
context.hpf.cutoff: How much room is left underneath for a bass part.
context.lpf.peak: The ping on each note. Past about 7 it starts to overpower the note itself.
context.mix.vco2: The octave on top. Turn it down for a rounder, more muted hook.

tweaks.hear: The plucks bleed into each other and the hook becomes a wash.
Thinner and more nasal — it cuts harder through a busy track.
The notes hold instead of plucking, which turns the hook into a stab line.

sounds.name: Pumping Electro Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Soulwax — the Nite Versions reworkings of their own records
sounds.blurb: A hard bass that holds wide open for a moment before it clamps shut.
sounds.how: The HOLD stage on envelope 2 is doing the work. After the attack the envelope sits at full for a set time and only then starts its decay, so every note is bright and loud for a fixed moment and then drops. That plateau is what makes the line pump rather than simply pluck.

steps.title: A narrow pulse over a square
steps.why:
A narrow pulse gives the reedy upper edge the filter sweep will show off, and a square an octave below keeps it anchored.
- VCO1 pulse, PW 6.5: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. PW is pulse width; past the middle it gets thin and reedy.
- VCO2 square: hollow and solid, the weight.
- SCALE 8′ and 16′: Korg’s octave switch in organ-pipe feet. Oscillator 2 at 16′ sits an octave below Oscillator 1.
- PITCH 0: the two in tune, for a hard, solid tone.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 8 / 7.5: both in strongly.
- Listen for: a thin, nasal top over a round bottom.

steps.title: Hard filter
steps.why:
A low cutoff with plenty of resonance, on the dirtier circuit. The note only gets bright when the envelope says so.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 3.4 (202 Hz): the low-pass removes what is above 202 Hz, so at rest the note is mostly body.
- Low-pass PEAK 6.6: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, the edge on the sweep. It also thins the low end, which is why the square is there.
- FILTER 2: the grittier of the two circuits, covering both filters. FILTER 1 makes the same shape smoother and more polite.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1.4 (32 Hz): the high-pass trims only the lowest rumble.
- Listen for: a dark, slightly whistling note.

steps.title: Hold, then drop
steps.why:
HOLD is doing the work. After the attack, envelope 2 sits at full for a set time and only then decays, so each note is bright and loud for a fixed moment and then drops. That plateau is what makes the line pump.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 5.4: EG2 is envelope generator 2. This sets how far the filter opens during the hold.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms): full at once.
- HOLD TIME 3 (88 ms): how long each note stays wide open before it shuts.
- DECAY 4.4 (190 ms), SUSTAIN 1.5: how hard it clamps once the hold is over. Short is a snap; long is a sag.
- RELEASE 1.8 (120 ms): notes stop short.
- Listen for: a flat-topped “bwah” that cuts off. Turn HOLD from 0 to 5 while a line plays.

steps.title: Blunt and loud
steps.why:
No glide and plenty of level. The shape of each note is the whole point, so nothing should smear between them.
- Portamento TIME 0: each note jumps straight to pitch.
- VOLUME 8.5: the overall output.
- Listen for: straight eighth notes. Each one opens, holds and clamps the same way, which is the pumping feel.

context.eg2.hold: How long each note stays wide open before it shuts. This is the control that makes the line pump.
context.eg2.decay: How hard it clamps once the hold is over. Short is a snap; long is a sag.
context.lpmod.eg2: How far the filter opens during the hold.
context.lpf.peak: The edge on the sweep. It also thins the low end, which is why the square is there.
context.lpf.type: FILTER 2 for the grit. FILTER 1 makes the same shape sound smoother and more polite.

tweaks.hear: The plateau goes and each note becomes an ordinary pluck. This is the clearest way to hear what HOLD does.
The note stays open so long that it runs into the next one — a sustained line with a hard edge.
Fatter and less reedy, closer to a plain square bass.

sounds.name: Ring-Edged Square Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Boys Noize — hard distorted electro bass
sounds.blurb: A blunt square bass with a hard metallic edge on top of it.
sounds.how: Oscillator 2 is switched to RING, so instead of adding a second note it multiplies the two oscillators together. Set an octave apart, the tones they produce between them still belong to the note, so the result sharpens the attack and adds a metallic edge rather than turning the bass into a bell.

steps.title: A plain square
steps.why:
A plain square is the starting point for something that is about to be roughened up: hollow, solid and simple.
- WAVE FORM pulse, PW 1: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. PW is pulse width; near 0 the pulse is a square. Any higher and the bass thins out quickly.
- SCALE 16′: Korg’s octave switch in organ-pipe feet. 16′ is an octave below the key.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8: Oscillator 1 into the mixer. Oscillator 2 is still off.
- Listen for: a round, hollow bass note.

steps.title: Ring modulation on top
steps.why:
Oscillator 2 is switched to RING, so instead of adding a second note it multiplies the two oscillators together. An octave apart, the tones it makes still line up with the note, so you get a hard metallic edge rather than a clang.
- VCO2 WAVE FORM RING: replaces Oscillator 2’s output with the two oscillators multiplied.
- SCALE 8′, PITCH 0: an octave above Oscillator 1 and exactly in tune, so the edge stays with the note. Move PITCH and you get clashing metallic tones instead.
- VCO2 LEVEL 5: with RING selected this is the amount of ring modulation. At 0 it is an ordinary square bass; turn it up and the edge takes over.
- Listen for: bring VCO2 LEVEL up from 0 to 5 on a held note. A harder, buzzier edge appears on top.

steps.title: Filter it hard
steps.why:
The filter is fairly closed, on the dirtier circuit, so the metallic edge comes through as grit rather than as a separate ringing tone.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 4.4 (399 Hz): the low-pass removes what is above 399 Hz. Low keeps the edge as grit rather than clang.
- Low-pass PEAK 4.8: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a moderate boost at the cutoff.
- FILTER 2: the harder of the two circuits, covering both filters. It adds its own distortion on top of the ring modulation.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1.2 (27 Hz): the high-pass trims only sub rumble.
- Listen for: a darker, gritty bass. Open the low-pass to 7 to hear the clang come back.

steps.title: Short and hard
steps.why:
A quick decay to a middling sustain: enough body to carry a club track, short enough to stay punchy.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 4: EG2 is envelope generator 2. A moderate flick of the filter on every note.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms): the hit lands at once.
- DECAY 4.6 (220 ms), SUSTAIN 5: the flick falls back over about a fifth of a second. Envelope 2 also sets loudness, so held notes settle at about half level.
- RELEASE 1.8 (120 ms), VOLUME 8.5: short tail, and the overall output.
- Listen for: a hard, clipped front on each note, then a steady growl.

context.mix.vco2: How much ring modulation is mixed in. At 0 it is an ordinary square bass; turn it up and the edge takes over.
context.vco2.pitch: The interval feeding the ring modulator. At 0 it is a clean octave and the edge stays in tune with the note; move it and you get clashing metallic tones instead.
context.lpf.cutoff: How much of the metallic edge survives. Low keeps it as grit rather than clang.
context.lpf.type: FILTER 2 adds its own distortion on top of the ring modulation.
context.vco1.pw: Near 0 is a square. Any higher and the bass thins out quickly.

tweaks.hear: The ring modulation stops agreeing with the note and the bass turns clangy and detuned.
The metal takes over and the note underneath almost disappears.
The full ring modulation comes through — much harsher, good for a stab rather than a bassline.

sounds.name: Tight Pop Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Yellow Magic Orchestra — late-70s Korg electro-pop
sounds.blurb: A clean, rounded bass with a short bloom on every note.
sounds.how: The opposite approach to most bass patches here: nothing is driven hard. A triangle carries the weight, a square adds just enough edge to be heard, and FILTER 1 — the smoother circuit — keeps the whole thing polite. All the character is in a short, precise envelope.

steps.title: Triangle for weight, square for edge
steps.why:
Nothing is driven hard in this patch. A triangle carries the weight and a square adds just enough edge to give each note a definite shape.
- VCO1 triangle: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. A triangle has almost no harmonics, so it gives a clean, round bottom.
- VCO2 square, both SCALE 16′: Korg’s octave switch in organ-pipe feet. 16′ is an octave below the key, the same octave on both.
- PITCH 0.1 (about +0.1 semitone): barely off, for a very slow drift.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 8.5 / 4: the square is kept low. Past about 6 the tone stops being polite.
- Listen for: a soft, round note with a faint hollow edge. Mute VCO2 LEVEL to hear how plain the triangle is alone.

steps.title: The smoother filter
steps.why:
FILTER 1 with modest resonance. This patch is about restraint, and the other circuit would add a dirt that does not belong here.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 4.4 (399 Hz): the low-pass removes what is above 399 Hz. This patch lives fairly low; raise it and it turns into an ordinary buzzy bass.
- Low-pass PEAK 3.4: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a small boost at the cutoff.
- FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits, covering both filters. On FILTER 2 the patch loses its cleanness.
- High-pass CUTOFF 0 (12 Hz), PEAK 0: the high-pass is fully out of the way.
- Listen for: a warm, rounded bass with the square’s edge softened.

steps.title: A short bloom
steps.why:
A modest filter sweep and a quick decay to a middling sustain. The note opens, settles and holds: precise rather than punchy.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 3.6: EG2 is envelope generator 2. This is the small bloom at the start of each note.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: the note starts at once.
- DECAY 4.4 (190 ms), SUSTAIN 4: the bloom settles within a fifth of a second. Sustain is where the note sits after that, in brightness and loudness; it gives the line its evenness.
- RELEASE 1.8 (120 ms), VOLUME 8.5: short tail, and the overall output.
- Listen for: a small “bow” on the front of each note. Play a steady octave line and hear every note match.

steps.title: Nothing else
steps.why:
No glide and no pitch modulation. A bass part this exposed is easier to play in time with a machine than to decorate.
- Portamento TIME 0: each note jumps straight to pitch.
- Pitch MG/T.EXT 0: MG is the modulation generator, Korg’s name for an LFO (low-frequency oscillator). At 0 it does not touch pitch, so there is no vibrato.
- Listen for: nothing new; this step makes sure nothing wobbles. Push the mod wheel and vibrato appears, which is exactly what this patch avoids.

context.mix.vco2: How much edge sits on the round bottom. Past about 6 the tone stops being polite.
context.lpf.cutoff: The overall darkness. This patch lives fairly low — raise it and it turns into an ordinary buzzy bass.
context.lpmod.eg2: The small bloom at the start of each note.
context.eg2.sustain: Where the note settles after the bloom. This is what gives the line its evenness.
context.lpf.type: FILTER 1 is the point. On FILTER 2 the same patch loses its cleanness.

tweaks.hear: Far more harmonics: the bass stops being rounded and starts to buzz.
A grit arrives that this style does not want — useful for hearing what the switch does.
A held, organ-like bass instead of a plucked one.

sounds.name: Gated Machine Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Nine Inch Nails — mechanical, distorted synth bass
sounds.blurb: A held note chopped into hard pieces by a square wave.
sounds.how: One cable does it. The modulation generator’s pulse output goes to INITIAL GAIN, which adds to whatever the amplifier is already doing. Because a pulse only has two states, the sound is either on or off — no fade between them. That is a gate rather than a tremolo, and it turns a sustained note into machinery.

steps.title: Two rough sawtooths
steps.why:
Two sawtooths an octave apart and deliberately sharp, so the upper one grinds against the lower one’s harmonics. Once the gate starts chopping, a clean tone would sound thin.
- Reverse saw on both: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. Saws have every harmonic.
- SCALE 32′ and 16′: Korg’s octave switch in organ-pipe feet. Oscillator 1 two octaves below the key, Oscillator 2 one octave below.
- PITCH 0.3 (about +0.7 semitone): Oscillator 2 pushed sharp of its octave for the grind.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 8 / 7: both in strongly.
- Listen for: a heavy, rough low drone.

steps.title: Dirty filter
steps.why:
FILTER 2 with the cutoff part closed and a good deal of resonance. The high-pass stops the bottom from thumping each time the gate opens.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 4 (304 Hz): the low-pass removes what is above 304 Hz, darkening the saws.
- Low-pass PEAK 6.4: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. This is the grind inside each burst.
- FILTER 2: the harder of the two circuits, covering both filters. It distorts sooner.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1.6 (36 Hz), PEAK 3: the high-pass trims below 36 Hz so gate edges do not thump.
- Listen for: a dark, dirty growl.

steps.title: Hold the note open
steps.why:
The amplifier envelope stays up so the gate has something to chop. Without sustain there would be nothing to interrupt.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms): EG2, envelope generator 2, opens the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) at once.
- DECAY 5.5 (460 ms), SUSTAIN 8: the level must stay high. Lower it and there is nothing left to chop.
- RELEASE 2 (140 ms): notes stop short.
- VOLUME 7.5: the overall output, a little lower because the gate adds level.
- Listen for: a steady held growl.

steps.title: Chop it with the pulse output
steps.why:
The modulation generator’s pulse output goes to INITIAL GAIN, which adds to what the amplifier is already doing. A pulse has only two states, so the sound is switched rather than faded: a gate, not a tremolo.
- FREQUENCY 7.4 (5.41 Hz): MG is the modulation generator, Korg’s name for an LFO (low-frequency oscillator). About five chops a second; everything about this patch follows from this rate.
- Cable MG OUT (pulse) → INITIAL GAIN: the MG’s pulse output into the amplifier’s control.
- Listen for: the held note chopped into hard, even pieces. Turn FREQUENCY to set the chop against the tempo.

steps.title: Move the filter with it
steps.why:
A little of the same generator goes to the cutoff, so each burst is also brighter than the gaps. That is what makes it sound like a machine rather than a switch.
- Low-pass MG/T.EXT 2.6: how much the MG moves the cutoff, so how much brighter each burst is. It comes from the same generator as the gate, so the two stay locked together.
- MG WAVE FORM 5: the centre of the knob, triangle on the first output and square on the pulse output, so the gate is evenly on and off.
- Listen for: each chop now has a brighter edge. Set MG/T.EXT to 0 and the chops go flat and dull.

context.mg.freq: The rate of the gate. Everything about this patch follows from it.
context.lpmod.mg: How much brighter each burst is. The pulse is doing both jobs from one source, so they stay locked together.
context.lpf.peak: The grind inside each burst.
context.eg2.sustain: Must stay high. Lower it and there is nothing left for the gate to chop.
context.hpf.cutoff: Stops the bottom end thumping on every gate edge.

tweaks.hear: The gate passes into audio rate and stops being a rhythm — it becomes a tone of its own.
A slow, deliberate stutter you could build a bar around.
Each burst opens much brighter, which reads as a harder, more percussive machine.

sounds.name: Deep Dub Sub
sounds.ref: In the style of Basic Channel-era dub techno
sounds.blurb: A soft, almost pure low tone that you feel more than hear.
sounds.how: A triangle two octaves down with the filter closed on top of it. A triangle has hardly any harmonics to begin with, and what is left after the filter is close to a pure tone. Slow attack and release, and a little glide between notes, so nothing ever starts sharply.

steps.title: One triangle, right down
steps.why:
One triangle right down low. A triangle has hardly any harmonics to begin with, and at this depth it is nearly a sine: a tone you feel more than hear.
- VCO1 triangle, SCALE 32′: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. 32′ on Korg’s organ-pipe footage switch puts it two octaves below the key.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 9 / 0: one oscillator only, high in the mixer. Oscillator 2 is off, its switch back on reverse saw.
- Listen for: a soft, deep tone. On small speakers it may be barely there; check it on something that can reproduce low bass.

steps.title: Close the filter right down
steps.why:
Very low cutoff and almost no resonance. Anything that survives above the fundamental would give the note an edge this style does not want.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 2.6 (117 Hz): the low-pass removes what is above 117 Hz. Above about 4 you start to hear the triangle’s own harmonics and it stops being a sub.
- Low-pass PEAK 1.8: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. Keep it low; more adds a hollow tone that fights the fundamental.
- FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits, covering both filters.
- High-pass CUTOFF 0 (12 Hz), PEAK 0: the high-pass is fully out of the way.
- Listen for: the last trace of edge gone. Only a pure, round low note is left.

steps.title: No sharp edges
steps.why:
A slow-ish attack and a long release mean notes fade in and out of each other rather than being struck.
- ATTACK 2.4 (32 ms): EG2, envelope generator 2, takes the click off so each note arrives softly.
- DECAY 6 (690 ms), SUSTAIN 9, HOLD 0: a slight settle, then held notes stay nearly full.
- RELEASE 5 (850 ms): each note tails off for almost a second, overlapping the next.
- VOLUME 9: the overall output. Low notes need more level to be felt.
- Listen for: a line with no hard edges at all.

steps.title: Slide between notes
steps.why:
A little portamento joins the notes up, which is most of what makes a sub line sound dubby rather than programmed.
- Portamento TIME 2.2: the pitch slides from the previous note instead of jumping. Too much and the pitch never settles.
- Listen for: play a slow two- or three-note line. Each note bends gently into the next. Set TIME to 0 to hear it turn stiff.

context.lpf.cutoff: How pure the tone is. Above about 4 you start to hear the triangle’s own harmonics and it stops being a sub.
context.porta.time: The slide between notes. Too much and the pitch never settles.
context.eg2.attack: How softly each note arrives.
context.out.volume: Low notes need more level to be felt. Check this patch on something that can actually reproduce it.
context.lpf.peak: Keep it low. Resonance here adds a hollow tone that fights the fundamental.

tweaks.hear: The triangle’s harmonics appear and the sub becomes an ordinary bass note.
Far more to filter out: a hollow, woody tone rather than a pure one.
Long slides that arrive late — the note is still moving when the next one starts.

sounds.name: Hard EBM Sequence
sounds.ref: In the style of EBM — Front 242 and Nitzer Ebb
sounds.blurb: A short, clipped sequence line with a downward snap at the end of every note.
sounds.how: The notes are short and the filter shuts fast, so the line is all attack. Envelope 1 is sent to pitch, and because it holds its level until the key is released, each note sits slightly sharp and then drops as it ends. On a fast pattern that reads as a mechanical snap rather than a pitch bend.

steps.title: A hard pulse pair
steps.why:
A narrow pulse is thin and aggressive; the square underneath gives it enough body to survive being cut very short.
- VCO1 pulse, PW 6: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. PW is pulse width; past the middle the pulse gets thin and nasal.
- VCO2 square, both SCALE 8′: the square adds body. Same footage, same octave.
- PITCH −0.1 (about −0.2 semitone): a slight flat offset for thickness.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 8 / 6: the pulse leads.
- Listen for: a hard, reedy note.

steps.title: Bright but not open
steps.why:
The high-pass takes out anything that would blur the rhythm, and the resonant low-pass gives every note a hard front edge.
- High-pass CUTOFF 2.6 (72 Hz), PEAK 3.4: the high-pass removes what is below 72 Hz, keeping the pattern crisp. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 5 (600 Hz), PEAK 5.5: the low-pass removes what is above 600 Hz, with a resonant bark at the cutoff.
- FILTER 2: the harder of the two circuits, covering both filters.
- Listen for: a tighter, barking tone with less boom.

steps.title: Cut every note short
steps.why:
No sustain at all and a very quick decay. The gaps between notes are as much a part of this style as the notes.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 5: EG2 is envelope generator 2. This is the brightness of the front edge.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: every note starts at once.
- DECAY 4 (130 ms), SUSTAIN 0: the length of each note, about an eighth of a second. This decides whether the line is hard or flowing.
- RELEASE 1.4 (94 ms), VOLUME 8.5: a very short tail, and the overall output.
- Listen for: short, clipped notes with silence between. Play a sixteenth-note pattern.

steps.title: A snap on the way out
steps.why:
Envelope 1 is sent to pitch. It rises at once and holds while the key is down, so the pitch sits a little high for the note and drops when the key lets go. On a fast pattern that reads as a snap.
- EG1/EXT 1.4: how far envelope 1 lifts the pitch of both oscillators, and so how hard the snap is. Past about 3 it becomes an obvious bend.
- EG1 ATTACK 0 (3 ms), DELAY 0: EG1 is envelope generator 1. It reaches the top instantly with no wait.
- EG1 RELEASE 1.2 (64 ms): how fast the pitch falls away when the note ends.
- Listen for: a tiny downward flick at the end of each note. Set EG1/EXT to 3 and it turns into a clear bend.

context.fmod.eg1: How far the pitch sits above the note, and so how hard the snap is at the end of it. Past about 3 it becomes an obvious bend.
context.eg1.release: How fast the pitch falls away when the note ends.
context.eg2.decay: The length of each note. This is the control that decides whether the line is hard or flowing.
context.lpmod.eg2: The brightness of the front edge.
context.hpf.cutoff: Keeps the pattern crisp by removing the low end that would otherwise smear it.

tweaks.hear: The snap goes and the line becomes an ordinary short sequence.
The notes join up and the mechanical feel is lost.
Each note squeals as it opens — harder, closer to acid than to EBM.

sounds.name: Sliding Acid Line
sounds.ref: In the style of Chicago acid house
sounds.blurb: A squelchy line where every note slides into the next.
sounds.how: The sliding is the point. Portamento is set long enough that notes never quite arrive before the next one starts, and the filter is closed with a fair amount of resonance so each note squelches as the envelope opens it. FILTER 1 keeps it rubbery rather than screaming.

steps.title: One pulse, low
steps.why:
A single oscillator keeps the pitch slides clean. Two would slide together and sound like a chorus rather than a line.
- WAVE FORM pulse, PW 5: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. PW is pulse width, from a hollow square near 0 to thin towards 10. 5 sits in between.
- SCALE 16′: Korg’s octave switch in organ-pipe feet; 16′ is an octave below the key.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 8.5 / 0: one oscillator only.
- Listen for: a plain, buzzy bass note.

steps.title: Closed and resonant
steps.why:
A low cutoff with enough resonance to squelch. FILTER 1 is the rounder circuit, which keeps this on the rubbery side.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 3.4 (202 Hz): the low-pass removes what is above 202 Hz, so the note is dark at rest.
- Low-pass PEAK 7.2: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, the squelch. Around 7 is rubbery; above 9 the filter starts to whistle over the line.
- FILTER 1: the rounder of the two circuits, covering both filters. FILTER 2 gives a harsher squelch.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1 (24 Hz): the high-pass trims only sub rumble.
- Listen for: a dark, whistling note.

steps.title: Open and shut on every note
steps.why:
A decent sweep with a short decay: the filter opens and closes inside each note, which is the “wow” of an acid line.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 5.6: EG2 is envelope generator 2. This sets how far the filter opens on each note.
- ATTACK 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: the sweep starts at once.
- DECAY 4.2 (160 ms): how long the squelch lasts. Short is percussive; long turns each note into a sweep.
- SUSTAIN 1: the filter and the level fall almost to rest while the key is held.
- RELEASE 1.8 (120 ms): notes stop short.
- Listen for: a “wow” on every note. Ride EG2/EXT while a pattern plays.

steps.title: Slide everything
steps.why:
Enough portamento that the pitch is still travelling when the note ends. On a fast pattern that is what makes the line liquid.
- Portamento TIME 2.4: the slide between notes. At 0 this is a plain resonant bass; this is the control that makes it acid.
- VOLUME 8.5: the overall output.
- Listen for: play a fast line with big jumps. Every note bends into the next. Set TIME to 0 and back to hear the difference.

context.porta.time: The slide. At 0 this is a plain resonant bass; this is the control that makes it acid.
context.lpf.peak: The squelch. Around 7 is rubbery; above 9 the filter starts to whistle over the line.
context.lpmod.eg2: How far the filter opens on each note.
context.eg2.decay: How long the squelch lasts. Short is percussive, long turns each note into a sweep.
context.lpf.type: FILTER 1 for a round squelch, FILTER 2 for a harsher one.

tweaks.hear: Every note arrives exactly on its pitch. Much tighter, and much less like acid.

tweaks.try: Ride between 2 and 6 while the pattern runs
tweaks.hear: The standard acid performance: the line builds from a mutter to a squeal without touching anything else.
Harder and dirtier. The same line moves from Chicago towards modern techno.

sounds.name: Winding-Up Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Röyksopp — "Vision One"
sounds.blurb: A bass that sounds like it is being continuously wound up and never gets there.
sounds.how: The modulation generator is turned to its sawtooth end, where it ramps up and then snaps back to the start. Sent to the filter and, in a small amount, to pitch, it climbs repeatedly — and because the reset is instant, the ear hears the rise but not the fall, so the sound seems to keep going up. The trick is old and works every time.

steps.title: A thick low pair
steps.why:
Two sawtooths slightly apart. The climb that comes later is easier to hear on a tone that already has plenty of harmonics.
- Reverse saw on both, SCALE 16′: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator. Saws have every harmonic. 16′ on Korg’s organ-pipe footage switch is an octave below the key, the same octave on both.
- PITCH 0.2 (about +0.5 semitone): Oscillator 2 a little sharp, so the pair beats and sounds thick.
- VCO1 / VCO2 LEVEL 8 / 6.5: the first saw leads.
- Listen for: a wide, buzzy bass note.

steps.title: Start the filter low
steps.why:
The climb needs somewhere to climb from, so the filter starts low. High resonance makes the rising cutoff sing as it passes each harmonic.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 3.2 (176 Hz): the low-pass removes what is above 176 Hz. This is the bottom of each wind-up.
- Low-pass PEAK 7: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, the singing edge.
- FILTER 2: the harder of the two circuits, covering both filters.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1.4 (32 Hz): the high-pass trims only sub rumble.
- Listen for: a dark note with a whistle on top. Sweep CUTOFF up by hand to preview the climb.

steps.title: Hold the note
steps.why:
Full sustain and a longish release, so a single note lasts long enough for several turns of the climb.
- ATTACK 0.6 (8 ms): EG2, envelope generator 2, opens the amplifier almost at once.
- DECAY 6 (690 ms), SUSTAIN 10: at full sustain held notes stay at full level.
- RELEASE 4 (460 ms): about half a second of tail.
- VOLUME 8: the overall output.
- Listen for: an even held note.

steps.title: Turn the generator to sawtooth
steps.why:
The modulation generator is turned to its sawtooth end, where it ramps up and then snaps back. Sent to the filter, it climbs repeatedly, and because the reset is instant the ear hears the rise more than the fall.
- MG WAVE FORM 10 (saw): MG is the modulation generator, Korg’s name for an LFO (low-frequency oscillator). At the clockwise end it is a slow rise and instant reset. At the centre it is a triangle and the effect is lost.
- FREQUENCY 3.4 (0.63 Hz): each climb takes about a second and a half. Slow is the whole point; fast just sounds like a wobble.
- Low-pass MG/T.EXT 4.4: how far the filter climbs on each turn.
- Listen for: hold a note. The tone keeps rising, resets, rises again.

steps.title: A little of the same on pitch
steps.why:
A small amount of the same sawtooth on pitch as well. Enough to feel, not enough to sound out of tune.
- Pitch MG/T.EXT 1.2: how far the MG moves the pitch of both oscillators. Small amounts add to the illusion that it keeps going up; large ones make it a siren.
- Listen for: the note now leans slightly sharp as each climb goes on, then drops back at the reset. Set it to 0 and back to hear the effect.

context.mg.wave: At the clockwise end this is a sawtooth: a slow rise and an instant reset. At the centre it is a triangle, which rises and falls evenly and loses the effect.
context.mg.freq: How long each wind-up takes. Slow is the whole point — fast just sounds like a wobble.
context.lpmod.mg: How far the filter climbs on each turn.
context.fmod.mg: The pitch climb. Small amounts add to the illusion; large ones make it a siren.
context.lpf.peak: The resonance that sings as the cutoff passes each harmonic on the way up.

tweaks.hear: A reverse sawtooth: it now winds down instead of up, which sounds like something losing power.
The climbs come fast enough to turn into a rhythmic ratchet.
The pitch climb becomes obvious and the bass turns into a siren.

sounds.name: Lo-Fi Noise Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of Mount Kimbie — "Delta"
sounds.blurb: A bass note with a bed of hiss filtered into it, so it sounds recorded rather than generated.
sounds.how: The fourth waveform position swaps Oscillator 1 for the noise generator — but Oscillator 2 carries on as normal. That gives a pitched note and a layer of noise going through the same two filters together, which is what makes it read as a rough recording rather than a clean synth line.

steps.title: Noise in place of Oscillator 1
steps.why:
The noise generator takes Oscillator 1’s place, but Oscillator 2 carries on as normal. That gives a pitched note and a layer of hiss going through the same filters together.
- VCO1 WAVE FORM noise: VCO is voltage-controlled oscillator, but this position swaps Oscillator 1 for the noise generator.
- VCO1 LEVEL 4: now the noise level, the amount of grit.
- VCO2 reverse saw, SCALE 16′, PITCH 0: Oscillator 2 plays the note, an octave below the key, in tune.
- VCO2 LEVEL 8.5: the note itself. Keep it well above the noise or the pitch stops being clear.
- Listen for: a bright bass note with hiss round it.

steps.title: Filter the pair together
steps.why:
Both go through the same filters, which is what glues them together. The high-pass keeps the noise from piling up at the bottom, and the low-pass keeps it from hissing over the top.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1.8 (42 Hz), PEAK 2.4: the high-pass removes what is below 42 Hz. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 4.2 (348 Hz), PEAK 5: the low-pass removes what is above 348 Hz; this sets how much hiss comes through with the note.
- FILTER 2: the harder of the two circuits, covering both filters, for a slightly dirty edge.
- Listen for: the hiss turning into a soft, dark rumble inside the note, like tape.

steps.title: A soft front
steps.why:
A slight attack rather than an instant one takes the click off the front of each note, which helps the sound pass as something recorded.
- EG2/EXT (low-pass) 3.4: EG2 is envelope generator 2. A small lift of the filter on each note.
- ATTACK 1.6 (18 ms): the soft front. At 0 the note clicks, which gives the game away.
- DECAY 5 (300 ms), SUSTAIN 5: the note settles to half level and brightness while held.
- RELEASE 2.4 (170 ms), VOLUME 8.5: a short tail, and the overall output.
- Listen for: rounded note starts. Set ATTACK to 0 and hear the click come back.

steps.title: Let the tone drift
steps.why:
A very slow movement on the cutoff and a hint of glide. Too slow to hear as modulation, but it keeps repeated notes from sounding identical.
- MG WAVE FORM 5 (triangle): MG is the modulation generator, Korg’s name for an LFO (low-frequency oscillator). A triangle moves smoothly.
- FREQUENCY 2 (0.29 Hz): about one cycle every three and a half seconds.
- Low-pass MG/T.EXT 1.8: the slow drift in brightness.
- Portamento TIME 1.2: a short slide between notes, softening the changes.
- Listen for: repeat one note for a few bars. Some come out slightly brighter than others.

context.mix.vco1: The noise level, because Oscillator 1 has been swapped for the noise generator. This is the amount of grit.
context.mix.vco2: The note itself. Keep it well above the noise or the pitch stops being clear.
context.lpf.cutoff: How much hiss comes through with the note.
context.hpf.cutoff: Stops the noise piling up underneath the bass.
context.eg2.attack: The soft front. At 0 the note clicks, which gives the game away.
context.lpmod.mg: The slow drift that stops repeated notes sounding identical.

tweaks.hear: The noise takes over and the bass turns into filtered weather with a pitch behind it.
A clean, ordinary sawtooth bass. Switching between the two shows how much work the noise is doing.
The pitch sags between notes, which adds to the worn, second-hand feel.

sounds.name: Unsteady Narrow Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Thom Yorke and Atoms for Peace — AMOK
sounds.blurb: A thin, nervous lead that slides between notes and never quite sits still.
sounds.how: Two narrow pulses a hair apart give a reedy tone with a slow beat in it. The high-pass takes the body out so the line sits above a track rather than in it, and FILTER 2 adds an edge. What makes it restless is two very slow movements that have nothing to do with the notes: a fraction of a semitone of drift on the pitch, and a slow rise and fall of the low-pass. Portamento slurs every note into the next.

steps.title: Two narrow pulses
steps.why:
Both oscillators go to thin pulse waves at the same octave, with the second pulled a fraction flat. The result is reedy and narrow, with a slow beat running through it.
- WAVE FORM pulse, PW 7 on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator, the part that makes the raw tone. PW is pulse width; at 7 it leans towards the thin, nasal end. Lower it for a fuller tone.
- WAVE FORM narrow pulse on VCO 2: Oscillator 2 has no PW knob, so its narrow pulse is fixed. It matches the reedy colour of Oscillator 1.
- SCALE 8′ on both: SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet. The two switches have different ranges, but 8′ on both is the same octave.
- PITCH −0.1 (−0.2 st): Oscillator 2 a fifth of a semitone flat, so the two pulses drift in and out of step.
- VCO1 LEVEL 7.5, VCO2 LEVEL 5.5: the mixer. Oscillator 2 sits lower, as colour.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear the slow beat. Turn VCO2 LEVEL to 0 and it goes still and thinner.

steps.title: Take the body out
steps.why:
The two filters in series take weight off the bottom and brightness off the top, leaving a narrow band that sits above a track rather than in it.
- High-pass CUTOFF 3.4 (126 Hz): the high-pass filter removes everything below this point. The body of the note goes, leaving room for bass and kick. Raise it and the line thins further.
- High-pass PEAK 3: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. A little gives the bottom edge of the band a slight honk.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 5.2 (687 Hz), PEAK 5.4: the low-pass filter cuts the highs. With this much resonance the top of the band gets a nasal, vocal edge.
- Filter type FILTER 2: the harder of the two circuits, and it switches both filters. It gives the top an edge.
- Listen for: the tone going from buzzy to narrow and vocal. Flip between FILTER 1 and FILTER 2 on a held note to hear the edge come and go.

steps.title: Soft front, long tail
steps.why:
Envelope 2 shapes the loudness of every note. Here it softens the front and lets the tail hang on, so quick phrases blur slightly together.
- ATTACK TIME 2.4 (32 ms): envelope 2 (EG, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier. 32 ms is a short fade in that takes the click off the start without sounding slow.
- DECAY 5.6 (500 ms), SUSTAIN 6.5: after the peak the level eases down over half a second to about two thirds, so held notes settle a little quieter.
- RELEASE TIME 4.2 (520 ms): how long a note fades after you let go. Long enough that notes overlap where the line moves quickly; shorter makes them separate.
- VOLUME 8.5: the overall output level.
- Listen for: a soft front on each note and a tail after you let go. Play a quick run and hear the notes run into each other.

steps.title: Two slow movements
steps.why:
One slow modulation generator now moves both the pitch and the low-pass, well under a cycle a second, so the line wanders in a way that has nothing to do with the notes.
- FREQUENCY 3.2 (0.56 Hz), triangle wave: MG is Korg’s name for the LFO (low-frequency oscillator), a source of slow, repeating movement. A triangle rises and falls smoothly; at 0.56 Hz one cycle takes nearly two seconds.
- MG/T.EXT 1.5 (pitch): how far the MG moves the pitch of both oscillators. A fraction of a semitone, which sounds like an instrument drifting out of tune rather than vibrato. Past about 2 it turns into ordinary vibrato.
- MG/T.EXT 2.6 (low-pass): how far the same MG sweeps the low-pass cutoff, so the tone opens and closes under the line in step with the drift.
- Listen for: hold one long note and hear the pitch sag and lift while the tone brightens and darkens. Turn FREQUENCY up to hear it become a wobble.

steps.title: Slur the notes together
steps.why:
Portamento makes each note slide into the next instead of jumping, which stops the line sounding typed in.
- TIME 2.6: the glide time, about a third of a second here. At 0 the pitch jumps; higher and every interval becomes a slow slur.
- Listen for: play two notes a few semitones apart and hear the pitch travel between them. Set TIME to 0 and the patch turns stiff and much of its character goes.

context.fmod.mg: The drift. Keep it under about 2 — past that it turns into ordinary vibrato and the unease goes.
context.lpmod.mg: How far the tone opens and closes under the line. Both movements run from one modulation generator, so they drift in step.
context.mg.freq: The speed of the drift. Slower than the phrase is the point: the two should never line up.
context.hpf.cutoff: How much body the lead keeps. Raise it and the line thins out and sits higher above the track.
context.porta.time: The slide between notes. At 0 the patch turns stiff and much of the character goes.
context.vco2.pitch: The slow beat between the two oscillators. A hair either side of 0 is all it needs.

tweaks.hear: Long slides that arrive late — the line stops landing on the beat.
The drift becomes a seasick wobble.
Rounder and politer: the same line with the edge sanded off.
The body comes back and it stops being a lead and starts being a bass.

sounds.name: Warped Electric Keys
sounds.ref: In the style of Radiohead — the warped electronic keys of the Kid A era
sounds.blurb: Struck keys with a soft attack and a slow wow, as though the tape carrying them is stretched.
sounds.how: A triangle gives the soft, hollow tone of an electric piano, and a square an octave up adds the tine. Both are struck rather than held: instant attack, a decay of about a second, and a low sustain. The warp is a very slow modulation generator on pitch, well under a cycle a second and deep enough to hear — the sound of a tape that has been played too many times.

steps.title: Triangle with a square on top
steps.why:
A soft triangle at the root and a quiet square an octave up. Together they give the hollow body and hard tine of an electric piano.
- WAVE FORM triangle on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator, the part that makes the raw tone. A triangle is close to a pure tone, which is where the softness comes from.
- WAVE FORM square, SCALE 4′ on VCO 2: SCALE is the octave switch in organ-pipe feet. Oscillator 2’s range sits an octave above Oscillator 1’s, so 4′ against 8′ is one octave up. The square adds the hard edge.
- PITCH 0.1 (+0.3 st): nudges Oscillator 2 a little sharp so the two do not lock together.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8, VCO2 LEVEL 3.2: the mixer. The square is kept low so it adds edge without taking over.
- Listen for: turn VCO2 LEVEL up and the tone gets glassier and harder; down to 0 and it goes soft and flute-like.

steps.title: Strike, do not hold
steps.why:
Envelope 2 now gives every note the shape of something struck: it hits at once, dies back over about a second, and a little is left while the key is held.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (5 ms): envelope 2 (EG2, the envelope generator that opens the amplifier) reaches full straight away, so the note starts with a hit.
- DECAY 6.4 (970 ms), SUSTAIN 2.4: the level falls for about a second to a quarter of full. At SUSTAIN 0 the note vanishes; at 10 it stops sounding struck.
- RELEASE TIME 3.4 (320 ms): a short fade after you let go, so notes end softly rather than cutting off.
- HOLD TIME 0: no pause at full before the decay starts.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear it hit, then sink to a quiet tail. Tap short notes and they sound plucked.

steps.title: Darken it as it decays
steps.why:
Envelope 2 now sweeps the low-pass as well as the volume, so the tone dulls as the note dies, as a struck string does.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 4.6 (457 Hz): the low-pass filter keeps the lows and cuts the highs. This is the resting point, fairly dark.
- PEAK 2.6: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. A little keeps the top from going woolly.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits.
- EG2/EXT 3.4 (low-pass): how far envelope 2 lifts the cutoff on each note. The brightness arrives with the hit and falls with the decay.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1.8 (42 Hz): the high-pass filter trims only the sub-bass.
- Listen for: a bright strike and a dark tail. Turn EG2/EXT to 0 and the decay sounds unnaturally even.

steps.title: Warp the pitch
steps.why:
A slow bend on the pitch gives the wow of a stretched tape.
- FREQUENCY 2.4 (0.36 Hz), triangle wave: MG, the modulation generator, is Korg’s name for the LFO (low-frequency oscillator). A triangle at about a third of a cycle a second bends the pitch smoothly sharp and flat.
- MG/T.EXT 2.2 (pitch): the depth of the bend on both oscillators, about half a semitone. This is the whole character of the patch. Less sounds like a slight detune; more sounds seasick.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear the pitch lean flat and back, about one slow bend per note. Turn FREQUENCY up and it stops sounding like tape and becomes vibrato.

context.fmod.mg: The depth of the warp — about half a semitone here. This is the whole character of the patch.
context.mg.freq: The speed of the warp. Keep it slow: one slow bend per note or so.
context.eg2.decay: How long each key rings before it dies back to the sustain.
context.eg2.sustain: How much is left while the key is held. At 0 the note vanishes; at 10 it stops being a struck sound.
context.mix.vco2: The tine on the front of the strike. Turn it up and the keys get glassier and harder.
context.lpmod.eg2: The tone dulling as the note fades. Take it to 0 and the decay sounds unnaturally even.

tweaks.hear: One slow bend across several notes — badly aligned tape rather than a wobble.
The warp turns into a queasy, seasick pitch swing.
Short, dry plinks — closer to a toy piano.
A harder, bell-like strike on every note.

sounds.name: Wiry Detuned Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Portishead — the harsher analogue tones of Third
sounds.blurb: A hard, wiry lead with two oscillators pulled far enough apart to grind against each other.
sounds.how: Both oscillators run at almost full level into FILTER 2, which distorts as it is driven — that is where the grit comes from rather than from any effect. They are detuned by well over a semitone, so instead of a pleasant chorus you get a fast, sour beating. The high-pass takes the bottom out and a fair amount of PEAK on the low-pass gives the midrange its nasal bite.

steps.title: A saw and a square, sourly detuned
steps.why:
A saw and a square, both loud, pulled a semitone and a half apart. Too far to sound like one instrument and not far enough to sound like two, so they grind.
- WAVE FORM reverse saw on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. The reverse sawtooth is bright and buzzy, full of harmonics.
- WAVE FORM square (VCO 2), both 8′: the square is hollower. 8′ on both oscillators is the same octave on this synth.
- PITCH 0.6 (+1.5 st): Oscillator 2 a semitone and a half sharp. Pull it back under 0.2 and the lead turns sweet.
- VCO1 LEVEL 9, VCO2 LEVEL 8.5: both near the top. That much level drives the filters hard, which the next step uses.
- Listen for: a fast, sour beating on every note. Set PITCH to 0 and hear it go clean and still.

steps.title: Drive FILTER 2
steps.why:
The low-pass closes to the midrange and FILTER 2 is driven hard by the loud mixer, so the grit comes from the filter itself rather than from an effect.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 4.8 (524 Hz): the low-pass filter cuts the highs above this point. Around 500 Hz leaves a boxy midrange tone.
- PEAK 7: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. At 7 it gives the midrange a nasal bite; past 8 it starts to whistle over the note.
- Filter type FILTER 2: the more aggressive circuit. It overloads sooner than FILTER 1, and with both oscillators near full it answers with distortion.
- Listen for: flip to FILTER 1 on a held note. The patch stays loud but goes clean; back on FILTER 2 the grit returns.

steps.title: Take the bottom out
steps.why:
The high-pass takes the bottom out, which is what makes the lead wiry rather than fat.
- High-pass CUTOFF 3.8 (166 Hz): the high-pass filter removes everything below this. Low notes lose their weight, leaving hard midrange and nothing underneath. This is the difference between a lead and a bass here.
- High-pass PEAK 5: resonance on the high-pass, a boost at 166 Hz. With the low-pass resonance at the other end, the sound is squeezed into a narrow, honky band.
- Listen for: play low on the keyboard and hear how little weight there is. Turn the high-pass CUTOFF down to 0 and the body comes back.

steps.title: Play it hard
steps.why:
Envelope 2 sets how each note is played: fast in, held nearly at full and stopped quickly, so the distortion is there from the first moment.
- ATTACK TIME 0.8 (10 ms): envelope 2 (EG2) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier. Ten milliseconds is effectively instant.
- DECAY 5.5 (460 ms), SUSTAIN 8.5: a small dip after the peak, then held notes stay close to full and keep grinding.
- RELEASE TIME 2.6 (200 ms): a short tail, so notes end cleanly.
- EG2/EXT 2.4 (low-pass): envelope 2 also lifts the low-pass cutoff a little at the start of each note, for extra bite on the front.
- VOLUME 7: kept down because the driven filter is already loud.
- Listen for: a brighter snarl at the start of each note that settles within half a second.

context.vco2.pitch: The sourness. Around 0.6 is a fast grinding beat; pull it back under 0.2 and the lead turns sweet.
context.lpf.type: FILTER 2 is doing the distorting. On FILTER 1 the same patch is loud but clean.
context.lpf.peak: The nasal bite. Past 8 the resonance starts to whistle over the top of the note.
context.hpf.cutoff: How much bottom is left. This is the difference between a lead and a bass here.
context.mix.vco1: The drive into the filter. Both levels near the top is what overloads it — turn them down for the same patch, clean.
context.out.volume: Kept down because the filter is being driven hard and the output is already loud.

tweaks.hear: The grinding stops and a plain, hard saw lead is left.
The two lock into tune and the sourness becomes brightness.
Same notes, no dirt — you can hear exactly what the circuit was adding.
A honking resonance at the bottom edge, like a cheap speaker.

sounds.name: Glass Fifths Pad
sounds.ref: In the style of Aphex Twin — Selected Ambient Works-era pads
sounds.blurb: A clean, glassy pad built on open fifths, fading in and out with no edges.
sounds.how: A triangle and a square a fifth apart give a hollow, bell-like tone with very few harmonics to get in the way. The low-pass stays high with just enough PEAK to put a shine on the top, and the high-pass clears the bottom so nothing muddies the chord. Everything else is the envelope: a slow fade in, a hold at full, and a release long enough that chords overlap.

steps.title: A triangle and a fifth
steps.why:
A triangle and a square a fifth apart. Both are low in harmonics, so the tone is clean and hollow, and a fifth is open enough to sit under anything without deciding between major and minor.
- WAVE FORM triangle on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator, the raw tone source. A triangle is soft and nearly pure.
- WAVE FORM square (VCO 2), both 8′: a square is hollow and woody. 8′ on both is the same octave on this synth.
- PITCH 2.9 (+7 st): tunes Oscillator 2 up a fifth. At 0 both play the same note.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8, VCO2 LEVEL 4.6: the fifth sits under the root, so you still hear which note you played.
- Listen for: each key gives two notes, the root and the fifth above. Turn VCO2 LEVEL to 0 to hear the plain triangle.

steps.title: Shine, not bite
steps.why:
The filters barely cut here. The low-pass stays open with a little resonance for a shine on top, and the high-pass clears the bottom so nothing muddies the chord.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 7 (2.3 kHz): the low-pass filter cuts highs above this point. It stays where it started, well open, because there is little to cut.
- PEAK 3.4: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. A small amount lifts the top edge, which reads as glass. Past about 6 it whistles and the glass turns to metal.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother circuit, for a clean tone.
- High-pass CUTOFF 2.6 (72 Hz), PEAK 1.5: the high-pass filter removes the lows below about 72 Hz, with a slight bump there.
- Listen for: a faint sheen at the top of the note. Sweep the low-pass PEAK from 0 to 5 to hear the glass appear.

steps.title: Fade in, hold, fade out
steps.why:
Envelope 2 turns the sound into a pad: a slow fade in, a pause at full and a long fade out, with no edges anywhere.
- ATTACK TIME 7 (970 ms): envelope 2 (EG2) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier. Nearly a second to arrive; below about 5 it stops being a pad.
- HOLD TIME 6 (770 ms): the K-2’s extra stage keeps envelope 2 at full before the decay begins, so the note does not start sinking the moment it arrives.
- DECAY 7 (1.6 s), SUSTAIN 8.5: a slow, small drop to a high level.
- RELEASE TIME 8 (5.3 s): the fade after you let go, long enough for one chord to still be fading as the next arrives. Most of what makes a pad sound continuous.
- VOLUME 9: the overall output level, set high.
- Listen for: no edge at the start or end. Let go of a note and hear it take several seconds to die away.

steps.title: A slow shimmer
steps.why:
A very slow movement on the low-pass cutoff moves the top edge up and down. Small enough that you notice it only when it stops.
- FREQUENCY 1.6 (0.24 Hz), triangle wave: MG, the modulation generator, is Korg’s name for the LFO (low-frequency oscillator). At 0.24 Hz one cycle takes about four seconds.
- MG/T.EXT 2.2 (low-pass): how far the MG sweeps the low-pass cutoff. Keep it small; this pad is about stillness.
- Listen for: hold a note for ten seconds and hear the shine rise and fall. Turn MG/T.EXT to 0 and the pad goes static.

context.eg2.attack: How long the chord takes to arrive. Below about 5 it stops being a pad.
context.eg2.hold: Keeps the chord at full before the decay begins, so it does not start sinking the moment it arrives.
context.eg2.release: The overlap between chords. This is most of what makes a pad sound continuous.
context.vco2.pitch: The fifth. At 0 both oscillators play the same note; at 2.92 they are a fifth apart.
context.lpf.peak: The shine on the top. Past about 6 it starts to whistle and the glass turns to metal.
context.lpmod.mg: The slow shimmer. Keep it small — this pad is about stillness.

tweaks.hear: A more suspended, unresolved chord under the same notes.
The top edge sings and the pad turns metallic.
The chords arrive almost at once — an organ rather than a pad.
All the weight goes and the pad floats well above the bass.

sounds.name: Bright Melodic Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Yellow Magic Orchestra — bright melodic lead lines
sounds.blurb: A clean, carrying lead line with an octave on top and a light vibrato.
sounds.how: Two sawtooths an octave apart, both well up in the mixer, with the filter left open enough that the top octave still comes through. There is a small filter movement on each note so it has a front edge rather than just switching on, and a light vibrato so the long notes sound played. Everything about this patch is aimed at being heard over a busy arrangement.

steps.title: Saw with a saw an octave above
steps.why:
Two sawtooths an octave apart. The upper octave is what makes a lead carry over a busy arrangement.
- WAVE FORM reverse saw on both VCOs: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. The reverse sawtooth is bright and buzzy, with every harmonic.
- SCALE 8′ on VCO 1, 4′ on VCO 2: SCALE is the octave switch in organ-pipe feet. Oscillator 2’s range sits an octave above Oscillator 1’s, so 4′ puts it one octave up.
- PITCH 0.1 (+0.2 st): a slight offset so the octave is not locked, adding a little movement.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8, VCO2 LEVEL 5.4: the octave is quieter than the root, so it adds brightness without changing which note you hear.
- Listen for: raise VCO2 LEVEL and the lead cuts through more; lower it and the line sits back.

steps.title: Open, with a little edge
steps.why:
The filters stay open enough to keep the top octave, with a little resonance to sharpen the tone.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 6.4 (1.6 kHz): the low-pass filter cuts the highs. Slightly below where it started, taking off some fizz while keeping the octave.
- PEAK 3.6: Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. Enough to sharpen the tone, not enough to squeal.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the cleaner of the two circuits.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1.4 (32 Hz): the high-pass filter only trims sub-bass.
- Listen for: sweep the low-pass CUTOFF down to 4 and hear the upper octave disappear into the root. Too low and the octave you added is lost.

steps.title: A front edge on each note
steps.why:
Envelope 2 now sweeps the low-pass on each note as well as the volume, giving every note a front edge you can hear at speed.
- EG2/EXT 3.2 (low-pass): how far envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope generator) lifts the cutoff on each note. Raise it for a more percussive, plucked line.
- ATTACK TIME 0.4 (7 ms): near instant, so the edge lands on the beat.
- DECAY 5.2 (350 ms), SUSTAIN 7.5: the brightness falls back over about a third of a second and settles a little lower while the note holds.
- RELEASE TIME 2.4 (170 ms): short, so fast notes stay separate.
- VOLUME 8.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: a quick bright “tah” at the start of each note. Play a fast run with EG2/EXT at 0 and hear the notes run together.

steps.title: A little vibrato
steps.why:
A light vibrato, shallow and about five cycles a second. It only shows on the long notes, which is where a player would use it.
- FREQUENCY 7.2 (4.86 Hz), triangle wave: MG, the modulation generator, is Korg’s name for the LFO (low-frequency oscillator). Five to six cycles a second is about what a hand does.
- MG/T.EXT 1.2 (pitch): the vibrato depth on both oscillators. Keep it under about 2 or it stops sounding like a player.
- Listen for: long notes waver gently while short ones barely show it. Raise MG/T.EXT to 4 to hear it turn into a warble.

context.mix.vco2: The octave on top. This is the knob that decides whether the lead cuts through or sits back.
context.lpf.cutoff: How bright the line is. Too low and the octave you added disappears.
context.lpmod.eg2: The edge at the front of each note. Raise it for a more percussive, plucked line.
context.fmod.mg: Vibrato depth. Keep it under about 2 or it stops sounding like a player.
context.mg.freq: Vibrato speed. Five to six cycles a second is what a hand does.
context.eg2.release: Kept short so fast notes stay separate.

tweaks.hear: A hard plucked front on every note — the line turns percussive.
The octave beats against the root and the lead thickens into two instruments.
A fast, nervous flutter rather than vibrato.
Each note falls away after its attack — a plucked line instead of a sung one.

sounds.name: Tight Pop Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of Vince Clarke — Erasure-era leads
sounds.blurb: A clean, staccato pulse lead that stops dead between notes.
sounds.how: Two pulse waves, one narrow and one square, at the same octave: bright, hollow and completely dry. What makes it a pop lead is the timing rather than the tone. The envelope is short at both ends and the sustain is low, so every note has a defined front and back, and nothing runs into the note after it. No vibrato, no glide, nothing wandering.

steps.title: A narrow pulse and a square
steps.why:
A narrow pulse with a square underneath, same octave, no detune. Bright and hollow, and completely still.
- WAVE FORM pulse, PW 6.5 on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. PW is pulse width; 6.5 gives a narrow, thin and reedy pulse. Wider is fuller and rounder, narrower is thinner and more nasal.
- WAVE FORM square on VCO 2: the square gives the thin pulse a body to sit on.
- SCALE 8′ on both, PITCH 0: same octave and exactly in tune, so the two lock together and nothing beats.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8, VCO2 LEVEL 5: the mixer. Turn the square down for a thinner, more piercing lead.
- Listen for: a steady tone with no wobble. Sweep PW and hear it move between hollow and nasal.

steps.title: Bright and clean
steps.why:
The filters are set high and clean. This patch is not about the filter; it is about what the envelope does next.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 6.8 (2.0 kHz): the low-pass filter cuts the highs above about 2 kHz, taking only the harshest fizz off.
- PEAK 2.4: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. A little keeps the top lively.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits, for a clean tone.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1.6 (36 Hz): the high-pass filter trims sub-bass only.
- Listen for: very little change from the last step, which is the point. The tone should be bright but not harsh.

steps.title: Stop dead between notes
steps.why:
Envelope 2 gives every note a hard front and a clean stop. The silence between the notes is as much a part of this sound as the notes.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (5 ms): envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier. Instant, so each note starts on the beat.
- DECAY 5 (300 ms), SUSTAIN 4.5: the level drops to under half in a third of a second. Low keeps it punchy; high makes it an organ.
- RELEASE TIME 1.4 (94 ms): the full stop. Anything above about 3 and the notes smear into each other.
- HOLD TIME 0: no pause at full before the decay.
- VOLUME 8.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: staccato notes with clear gaps. Hold a note and hear it drop back after the first hit.

steps.title: A blip of filter on each note
steps.why:
The same envelope now opens the filter briefly on each note, putting a click of brightness on the front. Glide and vibrato stay off so nothing wanders.
- EG2/EXT 3 (low-pass): how far envelope 2 lifts the low-pass cutoff at the start of each note. It is what makes a short note read as a note rather than a click.
- TIME 0: portamento (glide) off. A slide would spoil the timing this patch depends on.
- MG/T.EXT 0 (pitch): no modulation generator (Korg’s LFO) on pitch, so no vibrato.
- Listen for: a brighter tick on the front of each short note. Turn EG2/EXT to 0 and short notes go flat and dull.

context.eg2.release: The full stop. Anything above about 3 and the notes smear into each other.
context.eg2.sustain: How much is left while the key is down. Low keeps it punchy; high makes it an organ.
context.lpmod.eg2: The blip of brightness on the front of each note.
context.vco1.pw: The width of the narrow pulse. Wider is fuller and rounder, narrower is thinner and more nasal.
context.porta.time: Deliberately at 0. A slide would spoil the timing this patch depends on.
context.mix.vco2: The square underneath. Turn it down for a thinner, more piercing lead.

tweaks.hear: Both oscillators are square: hollow and woody rather than reedy.
The notes blur together and the line loses its snap.
The square jumps an octave above the pulse — brighter and more brittle.
Held, organ-like notes: the same tone, a completely different feel.

sounds.name: Octave-Jumping Disco Lead
sounds.ref: In the style of early-80s Italo disco
sounds.blurb: A bright, slightly chorused lead for melodies that leap an octave at a time.
sounds.how: Two sawtooths detuned by about a third of a semitone beat slowly against each other, which is the poor man’s chorus every record of this kind used. The filter is left well open so the high notes stay bright, and a short glide takes the hard edge off each leap without turning the line into a slide.

steps.title: Two sawtooths, barely apart
steps.why:
Two sawtooths at the same octave, a fraction apart. They drift in and out of step a few times a second, which thickens the tone without any chorus unit.
- WAVE FORM reverse saw on both VCOs: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. The reverse sawtooth is bright and buzzy.
- SCALE 8′ on both: the same octave on this synth, even though the two switches have different ranges.
- PITCH 0.2 (+0.4 st): Oscillator 2 a fraction of a semitone sharp. Around 0.15 beats a few times a second; much more and it sounds out of tune.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8, VCO2 LEVEL 7.5: nearly equal, so the beating is strong.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear a steady swirl. Set VCO2 LEVEL to 0 and the tone goes flat and single.

steps.title: Keep it bright at the top
steps.why:
The low-pass is left well open. It does not follow the keyboard, so a low cutoff would make notes an octave up sound dull; kept high, the leaps stay even.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 7.2 (2.7 kHz): the low-pass filter cuts highs above this point. High enough to suit the top of the line.
- PEAK 3: Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. A little adds sparkle.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1.8 (42 Hz): the high-pass filter clears sub-bass only.
- Listen for: play an octave jump and compare the two notes; both should be about as bright. Pull the low-pass CUTOFF down to 4 and the top note goes muffled.

steps.title: Sung, not struck
steps.why:
Envelope 2 lets the notes sing: a short fade in, a high sustain so they hold their length, and a release short enough to keep the leaps separate.
- ATTACK TIME 1.6 (18 ms): envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier. A very short fade in that softens the start.
- DECAY 5.6 (500 ms), SUSTAIN 8.5: a slight settle, then each note stays near full for its length.
- RELEASE TIME 2.8 (220 ms): short enough that octave leaps stay distinct.
- EG2/EXT 1.8 (low-pass): envelope 2 lifts the cutoff a little at the start of each note, for slight brightness on the front.
- VOLUME 8: overall output level.
- Listen for: long notes staying full rather than fading, and a clean gap before each leap.

steps.title: A short glide and a little vibrato
steps.why:
A short glide rounds the front of each leap, and a light vibrato adds life to held notes.
- TIME 1.4: portamento, about a tenth of a second. The pitch slides into each note instead of jumping. Above about 3 it becomes a slide and the leaps lose their snap.
- FREQUENCY 7 (4.36 Hz), triangle wave: MG, the modulation generator, is Korg’s name for the LFO (low-frequency oscillator). Just over four cycles a second.
- MG/T.EXT 1 (pitch): a shallow pitch wobble on both oscillators, only noticeable on held notes.
- Listen for: play octave jumps and hear a quick scoop into the top note. Hold a note to hear the vibrato.

context.vco2.pitch: The thickness. Around 0.15 beats a few times a second; much more and it sounds out of tune.
context.porta.time: The round edge on each octave leap. Above about 3 it becomes a slide and the leaps lose their snap.
context.lpf.cutoff: How bright the high notes are. The filter has no keyboard tracking, so this setting has to suit the top of the line.
context.eg2.sustain: Keeps each note at full for its length, which is what makes the melody sing.
context.fmod.mg: A light vibrato on the held notes.

tweaks.hear: A fast, wobbling beat — closer to two instruments than one thick one.
Every leap becomes a long swoop up and down the octave.
A hard resonant edge on the tone, moving it from disco towards acid.
Oscillator 2 jumps an octave above and the lead gets a bright shadow on top.

sounds.name: Synth Brass Section
sounds.ref: In the style of 70s synth brass
sounds.blurb: Brass stabs that open up a fraction of a second after they start.
sounds.how: Brass is a sound that gets brighter as it gets louder. Envelope 2 drives the amplifier and the low-pass cutoff together, so an attack of about a twentieth of a second makes each chord swell into its brightest moment rather than starting there — that swell is the section leaning into the note. The decay then pulls the brightness back while the chord is still held. Two detuned sawtooths give it the body, and the high-pass keeps it from sounding like a bass.

steps.title: Two sawtooths, lightly detuned
steps.why:
Two sawtooths, lightly detuned. Saws carry every harmonic, which the filter needs to work on, and the detune suggests more than one player.
