- WAVE FORM reverse saw on both VCOs: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. The reverse sawtooth is bright and buzzy.
- SCALE 8′ on both: the same octave on this synth.
- PITCH 0.2 (+0.5 st): Oscillator 2 about half a semitone sharp. One instrument at 0, several by 0.3.
- VCO1 LEVEL 7.5, VCO2 LEVEL 7: close to equal, so the detune is clearly heard.
- Listen for: a buzzy, beating tone. Move PITCH back to 0 and the section shrinks to one player.

steps.title: Start dark
steps.why:
The low-pass closes right down so the resting tone is dull. The whole effect is the filter climbing away from here in the next step.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 3.4 (202 Hz): the low-pass filter cuts everything above about 200 Hz. The buzz goes and only a muffled body is left. Keep it dark or there is nowhere to climb from.
- PEAK 4: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. It gives the climb something to sing on. Too much and it turns into a wah.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits.
- High-pass CUTOFF 2.4 (63 Hz), PEAK 1.5: the high-pass filter clears the lowest bass so the brass does not sound like a bass line.
- Listen for: a dark, muted tone. That is intended; the next step gives it somewhere to go.

steps.title: Open the tone as it swells
steps.why:
Envelope 2 now moves the low-pass cutoff a long way as well as the volume. Each chord swells into its brightest moment, then pulls back while held. That shape is the brass.
- EG2/EXT 5.6 (low-pass): how far envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope generator) lifts the cutoff above 202 Hz. With ATTACK, this is the brass sound.
- ATTACK TIME 3.2 (58 ms): the lean into the note. At 0 it is a hard stab; too high and the section sounds like it is waking up.
- DECAY 5.8 (590 ms), SUSTAIN 6: the brightness falls back over about half a second and settles at a middle level while the note is held.
- RELEASE TIME 3 (250 ms): a short fade after you let go.
- Listen for: a “bwah” on each note: dark, bright, then mellower. Sweep ATTACK from 0 to 6 to hear the stab turn into a swell.

steps.title: Keep the stabs tight
steps.why:
Last touches that keep the stabs tight: no hold, no glide. With the 250 ms release from the step before, the stabs stop cleanly, like a section playing together.
- HOLD TIME 0: envelope 2 goes straight from the attack into the decay, so the bright peak is short.
- TIME 0: portamento off, so each stab starts on its own pitch with no slide.
- VOLUME 8: overall output level.
- Listen for: short, clean stabs. Play a rhythm and hear each one start and stop together.

context.eg2.attack: The lean into the note. At 0 it is a hard stab; too high and the section sounds like it is waking up.
context.lpmod.eg2: How far the tone opens as the chord swells. This and the attack together are the brass sound.
context.lpf.cutoff: Where the note starts before the filter climbs. Keep it dark or there is nowhere to climb from.
context.lpf.peak: The edge on the climb. Too much and it turns into a wah rather than brass.
context.vco2.pitch: The size of the section: one instrument at 0, several by 0.3.
context.eg2.sustain: How bright it settles while the chord is held.

tweaks.hear: A hard stab with no lean — closer to an organ than to brass.
The section blares. Good for one chord, tiring over a whole part.
The brightness falls away quickly: short, punchy stabs.
A harder, more aggressive section with some dirt on the loud chords.

sounds.name: Hollow Combo Organ
sounds.ref: In the style of 70s combo organ imitations
sounds.blurb: Two square waves an octave apart with no envelope movement at all — on while you hold, off when you let go.
sounds.how: An organ has no attack and no decay: it is at full the instant a key goes down and gone the instant it comes up. Setting the attack to 0, the sustain to full and the release very short gives exactly that. Both oscillators are squares an octave apart, which is how an organ builds its tone from ranks, and a light vibrato stands in for the rotating speaker.

steps.title: Two squares, an octave apart
steps.why:
Two square waves an octave apart, the way an organ stacks ranks: the same note again, higher and quieter.
- WAVE FORM pulse, PW 0 on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator, the part that makes the raw tone. With PW (pulse width) at 0 the pulse is a square, hollow and woody.
- WAVE FORM square, SCALE 4′ on VCO 2: SCALE is the octave switch in organ-pipe feet. Oscillator 2’s range is an octave above Oscillator 1’s, so 4′ against 8′ is the next rank up.
- PITCH 0.1 (+0.1 st): a hair sharp, so the two ranks are not perfectly locked.
- VCO1 LEVEL 7.5, VCO2 LEVEL 5.8: the upper rank sits lower. Turn it up for a brighter, more cutting organ.
- Listen for: turn VCO2 LEVEL to 0 and the organ loses its top; bring it back and the tone gets a brighter edge.

steps.title: No envelope at all
steps.why:
An organ has no attack and no decay: full the instant a key goes down, gone the instant it comes up. Envelope 2 is set to do nothing but switch.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (5 ms): envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier. At 0 the note is there at once.
- SUSTAIN 10, DECAY 10 (15 s): with sustain at full the decay has nothing to fall to, so its time does not matter. Drop SUSTAIN and held notes fade under your fingers.
- RELEASE TIME 1 (74 ms): the note stops almost as soon as the key comes up. Above about 3 the organ starts to sound like a pad.
- HOLD TIME 0, EG2/EXT 0 (low-pass): no hold, and envelope 2 no longer moves the filter, so the tone is the same for the whole note.
- Listen for: notes that switch on and off like a light, with a flat level in between.

steps.title: Thin it out
steps.why:
The high-pass takes the weight from underneath, which is what makes a small organ sound small. The low-pass stays high so the top rank still speaks.
- High-pass CUTOFF 3 (95 Hz), PEAK 2: the high-pass filter removes lows below about 95 Hz. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance; 2 adds a slight lift there. Low sounds like a church organ, high like a transistor combo.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 7.4 (3.1 kHz), PEAK 2: the low-pass filter cuts the highs above about 3 kHz, only taking off the harsh top. Kept high so the upper rank is not lost.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the cleaner of the two circuits.
- Listen for: low notes losing their weight. Sweep the high-pass CUTOFF from 0 to 5 to go from church to combo.

steps.title: Stand in for the rotating speaker
steps.why:
A shallow vibrato at around five and a half cycles a second stands in for the rotating speaker. On the hardware this was the only movement a combo organ had, and it stops held notes sounding dead.
- FREQUENCY 7.4 (5.41 Hz), triangle wave: MG, the modulation generator, is Korg’s name for the LFO (low-frequency oscillator). A triangle gives a smooth, even wobble.
- MG/T.EXT 1.1 (pitch): how far the MG moves the pitch of both oscillators. Shallow, so it reads as shimmer rather than wobble.
- VOLUME 7.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear the gentle waver. Turn MG/T.EXT to 0 and the organ goes flat and static.

context.eg2.sustain: Full sustain is the organ. Drop it and the chords start to fade under your fingers.
context.eg2.release: How abruptly the chord stops. Above about 3 the organ starts to sound like a pad.
context.mix.vco2: The upper rank. Turn it up for a brighter, more cutting organ.
context.hpf.cutoff: How thin the organ is. Low sounds like a church, high sounds like a transistor combo.
context.fmod.mg: The vibrato standing in for a rotating speaker.
context.lpf.cutoff: Kept high so the upper rank is not lost.

tweaks.hear: A faster shimmer, like a rotary speaker on its quick setting.
The lower rank thins into a reed — closer to a harmonium than an organ.
A full, churchy organ with all its weight underneath.
Chords hang on after you let go, which no organ does.

sounds.name: Breathy Flute
sounds.ref: In the style of 70s flute imitations
sounds.blurb: A soft triangle lead with a hiss of breath mixed in behind it.
sounds.how: A flute is a nearly pure tone with air noise on top, and the K-2 can only make one of those at a time on the front panel — the noise generator replaces Oscillator 1 rather than joining it. The patch panel solves it: a cable from the PINK noise socket into EXT SIGNAL IN puts noise into the filter chain alongside the oscillators, so the breath is filtered with the note. Pink rather than white, because white is too hissy to sound like air.

steps.title: A triangle, nearly alone
steps.why:
A single triangle, as close as an oscillator gets to the hollow, nearly pure tone of a flute. Oscillator 2 stays out of it.
- WAVE FORM triangle, SCALE 8′ on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. A triangle has almost no upper harmonics, so it sounds soft and round.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8.5: the tone’s level into the filters. Later it sets the balance between tone and air: turn it down and the patch becomes mostly breath.
- VCO2 LEVEL 0, WAVE FORM reverse saw: Oscillator 2 is muted, with its switch on a plain waveform rather than RING.
- Listen for: a pure, slightly dull tone with no buzz. Flip VCO 1 to reverse saw for a moment to hear how much less the triangle has in it.

steps.title: Blow across it
steps.why:
On the front panel the noise generator replaces Oscillator 1 rather than joining it. This cable adds noise alongside the oscillator instead, so there is air behind the note.
- PINK → EXT SIGNAL IN: carries pink noise into the filter chain, where it joins the oscillator mix at the high-pass input. Pink has less hiss on top than white and sounds closer to wind, which is why it is used for breath.
- Listen for: a hiss under every note, starting and stopping with it, because it passes through the same amplifier. Pull the cable out and the flute goes back to a plain tone.

steps.title: Filter the breath with the note
steps.why:
The noise arrives before the filters, so they shape the breath and the note together. Closing the low-pass part way turns a hiss into a breath.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 5.4 (788 Hz): the low-pass filter cuts highs above this point. Too high and the air is a hiss; too low and the flute goes muffled with it.
- PEAK 3.6: Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. It gives the breath a pitch of its own, which helps it sound like air across a hole.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother circuit.
- High-pass CUTOFF 3.4 (126 Hz), PEAK 2.4: the high-pass filter removes the lows, keeping the rumble of the noise out of the way of the note.
- Listen for: the hiss turning into a soft rush of air. Sweep the low-pass CUTOFF up and hear it turn back into hiss.

steps.title: Shape each note like a breath
steps.why:
Envelope 2 shapes each note like a breath: a moment to get going, a steady tone, and a stop when the air stops.
- ATTACK TIME 3.4 (67 ms): envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier. A soft start, as a player takes a moment to get a note speaking. Most of what makes it sound blown.
- DECAY 5.6 (500 ms), SUSTAIN 8.5: a gentle settle to a steady level.
- RELEASE TIME 2.8 (220 ms): short, as a flute stops when the air does.
- EG2/EXT 2.4 (low-pass): envelope 2 also lifts the low-pass cutoff a little as each note starts, so the breath is brighter at the front.
- VOLUME 8: overall output level.
- Listen for: a soft “fff” into each note. Set ATTACK to 0 and it starts like a keyboard rather than a flute.

steps.title: A shallow vibrato
steps.why:
A shallow vibrato for the long notes, and a hint of glide between them.
- FREQUENCY 7 (4.36 Hz), triangle wave: MG, the modulation generator, is Korg’s name for the LFO (low-frequency oscillator). Just over four cycles a second, a natural vibrato speed.
- MG/T.EXT 1.2 (pitch): shallow depth, so the vibrato only shows on the long notes, where a flute player would put it.
- TIME 0.8: a very short portamento (glide), so the pitch slurs slightly into each note.
- Listen for: long notes wavering gently, and a small scoop between notes in a quick phrase.

context.lpf.cutoff: How much of the breath comes through. Too high and it is a hiss; too low and the flute goes muffled with it.
context.hpf.cutoff: Keeps the low rumble of the noise out of the way of the note.
context.mix.vco1: The balance between tone and air. Turn it down and the patch becomes mostly breath.
context.eg2.attack: How long each note takes to speak. This is most of what makes it sound blown.
context.fmod.mg: The vibrato on the long notes.
context.lpf.peak: A little emphasis gives the breath a pitch of its own, which helps it sound like air across a hole.

tweaks.hear: The breath takes over and the flute turns into wind in a pipe.
The air becomes a hiss sitting on top of the note rather than part of it.
Every note starts instantly — it stops sounding blown and starts sounding switched on.
A piccolo: the same patch an octave up, where the breath is a bigger part of the sound.

sounds.name: Powering-Up Pad
sounds.ref: In the style of 70s science-fiction soundtrack pads
sounds.blurb: A held chord that sits still, then slowly climbs in pitch and brightness together, as though something is coming up to speed.
sounds.how: Envelope 1 has a DELAY stage, and the TOTAL socket replaces the modulation generator in every MG/T.EXT knob at once. One cable from EG 1 OUT into TOTAL therefore puts the envelope in charge of the pitch, the high-pass and the low-pass together. Because envelope 1 waits before it climbs, the chord holds steady, then everything rises at once and stays up until you let go.

steps.title: A wide, quiet chord
steps.why:
A sawtooth with a square a fifth above: plenty of harmonics for the filters to move through, and an open interval that does not commit to a key.
- WAVE FORM reverse saw on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. The reverse sawtooth is bright and full of harmonics.
- WAVE FORM square (VCO 2), both 8′: the square is hollow. 8′ on both is the same octave on this synth.
- PITCH 2.9 (+7 st): Oscillator 2 up a fifth.
- VCO1 LEVEL 7.5, VCO2 LEVEL 5.5: the fifth sits a little under the root.
- Listen for: each key sounds an open two-note chord. Set PITCH to 0 and the fifth collapses into one note.

steps.title: Start closed in
steps.why:
Both filters squeeze the sound into a narrow, distant band. That is the starting point the climb will move away from.
- High-pass CUTOFF 2.4 (63 Hz), PEAK 3.4: the high-pass filter removes the lows below this point. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance; here it puts a slight bump on the lower edge.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 3.6 (232 Hz), PEAK 4.6: the low-pass filter cuts the highs. At 232 Hz the chord is dark and far away, with a resonant edge that will sing as it moves.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits.
- Listen for: a muffled chord with most of the buzz gone. The next steps open it up.

steps.title: Hold the chord open
steps.why:
Envelope 2 holds the chord open so it is still sounding when the climb arrives, and lets it die away slowly afterwards.
- ATTACK TIME 5.5 (320 ms): envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier. A third of a second to fade in.
- SUSTAIN 10, DECAY 7 (1.6 s): full sustain, so the chord stays at full for as long as you hold it and the decay has nowhere to fall.
- RELEASE TIME 7.5 (3.9 s): a long fade after you let go, so it dies away rather than stopping.
- VOLUME 8.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: a soft start, a steady hold and a long tail.

steps.title: Set envelope 1 to wait, then climb
steps.why:
Envelope 1 is set to wait, then climb. Its only fixed route is to pitch through a knob still at 0, so nothing audible changes until the next step.
- DELAY TIME 6 (440 ms): envelope 1 (EG1, the simpler envelope generator) waits this long after a key goes down before it rises. The wait is what makes the climb land.
- ATTACK TIME 6.5 (790 ms): how long the climb takes. Short is a machine snapping on; long is something winding up.
- RELEASE TIME 7 (2.4 s): envelope 1 stays at the top while the key is held, then sinks back this slowly when you let go.
- Listen for: nothing new yet. EG1/EXT, the knob that sends envelope 1 to pitch, is still at 0.

steps.title: Put envelope 1 in charge of everything
steps.why:
One cable puts envelope 1 in charge of the pitch and both filters at once, so the held chord rises in pitch and brightness together.
- EG 1 OUT → TOTAL: carries envelope 1 into TOTAL, which replaces the modulation generator (Korg’s LFO) in every MG/T.EXT knob. Those knobs now set how far envelope 1 moves each thing.
- MG/T.EXT 2.2 (pitch): the pitch rise. Keep it small: about half a semitone is enough to unsettle a held chord.
- MG/T.EXT 3.6 (high-pass): the high-pass rises too, so the sound thins as it brightens, a lift rather than just an opening.
- MG/T.EXT 5.4 (low-pass): the largest of the three moves, and the one you hear most.
- Listen for: hold a key. Half a second of stillness, then pitch and brightness climb together over most of a second and stay up until you let go.

context.eg1.delay: How long the chord sits still before anything happens. The wait is what makes the climb land.
context.eg1.attack: How long the climb takes. Short is a machine snapping on; long is something winding up.
context.lpmod.mg: How far the low-pass opens on the climb. The largest of the three movements, and the one you hear most.
context.hpmod.mg: The high-pass rising too, so the sound thins as it brightens — a lift rather than just an opening.
context.fmod.mg: The pitch rise. Keep it small: about half a semitone is enough to unsettle a held chord.
context.lpf.cutoff: Where the chord starts before the climb.
context.eg1.release: How slowly everything sinks back when you let go.

tweaks.hear: The whole chord slides up a musical interval — more a transition than a texture.
The climb starts with the note and the pad becomes an ordinary slow sweep.
A sudden step up part way through the chord, as though something switched on.
Only the low-pass and the pitch move, so it opens up rather than lifting away.

sounds.name: Slow Swelling Fifth
sounds.ref: In the style of long-form ambient drones
sounds.blurb: One long fifth that fades up out of nothing and keeps moving very slowly while it is held.
sounds.how: A drone has to hold attention without any notes to do it, so all the interest is put into slow movement. Two sawtooths a fifth apart are detuned just enough to beat once every second or two. The envelope takes a second and a half to arrive and far longer to leave, and one very slow modulation generator moves the two filters so the band the drone lives in is never quite the same twice.

steps.title: A fifth, slightly apart
steps.why:
Two sawtooths a fifth apart, an octave down. The fifth is stable enough to sit under anything, and a small offset from a true fifth makes them beat slowly.
- WAVE FORM reverse saw on both VCOs: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. The reverse sawtooth is bright, with plenty of harmonics for the filters to work on.
- SCALE 16′ on both: SCALE is the octave switch in organ-pipe feet. 16′ is an octave below 8′, which puts the drone low; on both switches it is the same octave.
- PITCH 3 (+7.1 st): Oscillator 2 a hair above a true fifth, so the two beat once every second or two.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8, VCO2 LEVEL 6.5: the fifth sits a little under the root.
- Listen for: hold a low note and hear a slow pulse in the tone. That beating is the first of the drone’s movements.

steps.title: Find a band to sit in
steps.why:
The two filters mark out a band for the drone to live in. The high-pass keeps the very bottom from turning to mud and the low-pass takes the buzz off the top.
- High-pass CUTOFF 2.2 (55 Hz), PEAK 4: the high-pass filter removes the lows below about 55 Hz. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance; it gives the bottom edge a hump you will hear move later.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 4.6 (457 Hz), PEAK 5: the low-pass filter cuts highs above this point. With this much resonance the top edge rings slightly; raise it and the movement becomes a slow vocal sweep.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother circuit.
- Listen for: the saws turning dark and round, with a slightly nasal ring at the top.

steps.title: Fade up out of nothing
steps.why:
Envelope 2 fades the drone up out of nothing and lets it take far longer to leave.
- ATTACK TIME 7.6 (1.5 s): envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier. A second and a half to appear; any faster and it announces itself.
- SUSTAIN 10, DECAY 7.5 (2.3 s): full sustain, so the drone holds at full level for as long as the key is down.
- RELEASE TIME 9 (9.8 s): nearly ten seconds to fade after you let go, so it never quite ends.
- VOLUME 9: overall output level.
- Listen for: press a key and hear the drone rise slowly; let go and time the fade.

steps.title: Move the band, very slowly
steps.why:
One very slow modulation generator moves both filters, so the band the drone sits in is never quite the same twice.
- FREQUENCY 1.4 (0.21 Hz), triangle wave: MG, the modulation generator, is Korg’s name for the LFO (low-frequency oscillator). One cycle takes about five seconds. Keep it well under one cycle a second.
- MG/T.EXT 3.6 (low-pass): how far the MG opens and closes the top edge. This is most of the life in the drone.
- MG/T.EXT 2 (high-pass): the bottom edge moves with it, by less.
- Listen for: hold a note for twenty seconds and hear the drone brighten and darken, far too slowly to sound like an effect.

context.eg2.attack: How long the drone takes to appear. Any faster and it announces itself.
context.eg2.release: The fade out. Long enough that it is still going when you have stopped thinking about it.
context.mg.freq: The speed of the slow movement. Keep it well under one cycle a second.
context.lpmod.mg: How far the band opens and closes. This is most of the life in a drone.
context.vco2.pitch: The beating between the two oscillators. A hair either side of a true fifth is what makes it breathe.
context.lpf.peak: The edge of the band. Raise it and the movement becomes a slow vocal sweep.

tweaks.hear: Faster beating: the drone starts to sound like it is being played by two hands.
The moving band sings over the top — closer to a howl than a hum.
The movement becomes noticeable and the drone starts to sound like an effect.
A much deeper drone, where most of the sound is felt rather than heard.

sounds.name: Synthetic Choir
sounds.ref: In the style of 70s and 80s synthetic choirs
sounds.blurb: A pad with a vowel in it that opens as the chord grows, like voices coming in one after another.
sounds.how: The vowel comes from the band between the two filters, but the two edges of that band do not have to move together. A cable from EG 1 OUT into the high-pass CUTOFF FREQ socket puts envelope 1 in charge of the lower edge, while envelope 2 still drives the low-pass. Give envelope 1 a slower attack and the band widens from underneath after the chord has started, so the vowel changes as it swells.

steps.title: Two sawtooths, lightly apart
steps.why:
Two sawtooths lightly apart. Saws carry every harmonic, so the filters have something to pick a vowel out of, and the detune stands in for several singers.
- WAVE FORM reverse saw on both VCOs: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. The reverse sawtooth is bright and buzzy.
- SCALE 8′ on both: the same octave on this synth.
- PITCH 0.3 (+0.6 st): Oscillator 2 just over half a semitone sharp. At 0 it is one voice; past 0.5 the singers are out of tune with each other.
- VCO1 LEVEL 7.5, VCO2 LEVEL 7: nearly equal, so the beating is strong.
- Listen for: a thick, beating buzz. It needs the filters before it sounds like voices.

steps.title: Find the vowel
steps.why:
The two filters leave a narrow band between them, and with resonance on both edges that band is heard as a vowel, somewhere between “oh” and “aw”.
- High-pass CUTOFF 4.2 (218 Hz), PEAK 6: the high-pass filter sets the lower edge. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. Around 4 is a rounded “oh”; higher goes towards “ee”.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 5.6 (902 Hz), PEAK 5.4: the low-pass filter sets the upper edge. Bring the two edges closer for a narrower, more nasal voice.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits.
- Listen for: the buzz turning into a vowel. Move the high-pass CUTOFF slowly up and down to hear the vowel change.

steps.title: Swell the chord
steps.why:
Envelope 2 swells the chord in, holds it at full and lets it fade slowly. It also moves the upper edge of the vowel a little.
- ATTACK TIME 6.8 (840 ms): envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier. Nearly a second to arrive.
- HOLD TIME 5 (370 ms): keeps envelope 2 at full before the decay, so the chord does not begin to sink the moment it arrives.
- DECAY 7 (1.6 s), SUSTAIN 8.5: a slow, small drop to a high level.
- RELEASE TIME 7.5 (3.9 s): a long fade after you let go.
- EG2/EXT 2.6 (low-pass): envelope 2 lifts the low-pass cutoff as the note swells, so the upper edge opens with the volume.
- VOLUME 9: overall output level.
- Listen for: the voice fading in and getting slightly brighter as it arrives.

steps.title: Give the lower edge its own envelope
steps.why:
This cable gives the lower edge of the vowel its own envelope, so the two edges of the band can move on different timings.
- EG 1 OUT → CUTOFF FREQ (high-pass): carries envelope 1 (EG1) into the high-pass cutoff socket, replacing envelope 2 as the source for the high-pass EG2/EXT knob.
- EG2/EXT 4.2 (high-pass): now sets how far envelope 1 lifts the lower edge. This is what makes the vowel change.
- Listen for: envelope 1 is still on its fast default (no delay, 3 ms attack), so the lower edge jumps up at once and the voice is thinner from the start. The next step slows it down.

steps.title: Open it from underneath, late
steps.why:
Envelope 1 now waits briefly, then climbs more slowly than the chord arrives. The lower edge lifts after the chord is already sounding, so the vowel changes while it holds.
- DELAY TIME 3.5 (91 ms): envelope 1 waits about a tenth of a second before rising, so the chord holds its first vowel briefly.
- ATTACK TIME 7 (1.2 s): how slowly the lower edge rises. Slower than envelope 2’s 840 ms attack is the point.
- RELEASE TIME 7.5 (3.3 s): the edge sinks back slowly after you let go, alongside the fading chord.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear the vowel move from a round “oh” towards a thinner, brighter sound over a second or so.

context.hpf.cutoff: The lower edge of the vowel before envelope 1 moves it. Around 4 is a rounded "oh"; higher goes towards "ee".
context.hpmod.eg2: How far envelope 1 lifts that lower edge. This is what makes the vowel change.
context.eg1.attack: How slowly the vowel opens. Slower than envelope 2 is the point.
context.eg1.delay: How long the chord holds its first vowel before it starts to move.
context.lpf.cutoff: The upper edge. Bring the two edges closer together for a narrower, more nasal voice.
context.eg2.attack: How slowly the chord itself arrives.
context.vco2.pitch: How many singers. At 0 it is one voice; past 0.5 they are out of tune with each other.

tweaks.hear: The voice opens right up into an "ee" and thins as it goes.
Both edges move from the start and the vowel change disappears into the swell.
A narrow band and a much more nasal, closed-mouth voice.
The vowel softens into an ordinary pad — you can hear how much the resonance was doing.

sounds.name: Playable Filter Whistle
sounds.ref: In the style of whistling filter leads
sounds.blurb: The filter itself plays the tune: a pure whistling tone with barely any oscillator behind it.
sounds.how: With PEAK near maximum the low-pass whistles at its own cutoff, but the K-2 has no key-tracking knob for it, so that whistle normally stays on one note whatever you play. One cable from KBD CV OUT into the low-pass CUTOFF FREQ socket fixes it: the keyboard voltage now moves the cutoff, and the EG2/EXT knob sets how much. At about 3.5 the whistle follows the keys an octave for an octave and becomes a playable instrument.

steps.title: Just enough oscillator to start it
steps.why:
Just enough oscillator to set the filter ringing. A resonant filter needs something to strike it, or the first note is slow to start. It is not meant to be heard on its own.
- WAVE FORM reverse saw, SCALE 8′ on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. A saw has harmonics all the way up, so there is always something near the cutoff for the filter to ring on.
- VCO1 LEVEL 3: low. At 0 the first note can be slow to start; higher and you hear buzz under the whistle.
- VCO2 LEVEL 0, WAVE FORM reverse saw: Oscillator 2 is silent.
- Listen for: a quiet, buzzy saw. It changes completely in the next step.

steps.title: Make the filter whistle
steps.why:
With PEAK near the top the low-pass rings at its own cutoff. That ringing is now the sound source, and it is a nearly pure tone.
- PEAK 9.4: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. Near maximum the filter whistles on its own. Below about 9 the whistle stops and an ordinary filtered saw is left.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 3.8 (265 Hz): the pitch the whistle plays, middle C, which puts it in tune with the oscillator. One octave is about one unit on this knob.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits.
- High-pass CUTOFF 2.4 (63 Hz): the high-pass filter trims the low end.
- Listen for: a pure tone on every key, but on the same pitch whichever key you play. The next step fixes that.

steps.title: Let the keyboard play it
steps.why:
This cable lets the keyboard play the filter. Without it the whistle sits on one pitch, because this filter has no keyboard tracking of its own.
- KBD CV OUT → CUTOFF FREQ (low-pass): carries the keyboard control voltage (KBD CV, the pitch of the note you play) to the low-pass cutoff socket, in place of envelope 2. The low-pass EG2/EXT knob sets how far it moves the cutoff.
- Listen for: nothing changes yet, because that knob is still at 0. The next step turns it up.

steps.title: Tune the tracking
steps.why:
The EG2/EXT knob scales whatever arrives at its socket, which is now the keyboard voltage rather than envelope 2.
- EG2/EXT 3.5 (low-pass): about an octave of cutoff for an octave of keyboard, so the whistle plays in tune with the oscillator. Lower and it plays flatter intervals than the keys; higher and it plays wider ones.
- Listen for: play a scale and hear the whistle follow it. Play octaves and nudge the knob until they sound true.

steps.title: Shape the notes
steps.why:
A soft start, a moderate release and a little glide, because a whistle does not start abruptly and slurs between notes.
- ATTACK TIME 2.6 (37 ms): envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier. A short fade in, so each note is blown gently.
- DECAY 6 (690 ms), SUSTAIN 9: held notes stay almost at full.
- RELEASE TIME 3.4 (320 ms): a short tail after you let go.
- TIME 1.6: portamento, so the pitch slurs between notes like a slide whistle.
- VOLUME 9.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: play a leap and hear the whistle swoop to the new note.

context.lpf.peak: Below about 9 the whistle stops and an ordinary filtered saw is left. This is the sound source.
context.lpmod.eg2: The tracking amount. Around 3.5 is one octave for one octave; lower and the whistle plays flatter intervals than the keys, higher and it plays wider ones.
context.lpf.cutoff: The pitch the whistle plays on middle C — at 3.8 it is middle C itself, which is what puts it in tune with the oscillator. One octave is about one unit on this knob.
context.mix.vco1: How much oscillator is heard under the whistle. At 0 the first note can be slow to start.
context.porta.time: The slide between notes, which suits a whistle.
context.eg2.attack: How gently each note is blown.

tweaks.hear: The whistle moves less than the keyboard does, so the tune comes out in squashed intervals.
The sawtooth comes back and the whistle becomes a resonant lead rather than a tone of its own.
The whistle sits two octaves higher — a piercing kettle rather than a flute.
A slide whistle — the tone swoops between every note.

sounds.name: Hard Techno Kick
sounds.ref: In the style of hard techno kick drums
sounds.blurb: A short, hard kick with a click on the front and a flat, driven body.
sounds.how: The oscillator is the drum here, not the filter. A triangle an octave down gives the weight, a fast sweep of the low-pass puts the click on the front, and FILTER 2 — the dirtier of the two circuits — saturates the body rather than filtering it politely. The HOLD stage keeps the hit at full level for a moment before it collapses, which is what makes a techno kick sound solid rather than plucked.

steps.title: A triangle where a kick lives
steps.why:
A single triangle an octave down. It has a strong fundamental and little else, which is what a kick needs.
- WAVE FORM triangle, SCALE 16′ on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. SCALE is the octave switch in organ-pipe feet; 16′ is an octave below 8′, so the C below middle C lands around 65 Hz, where a kick drum sits. Lower and it disappears on small speakers.
- VCO1 LEVEL 9: loud, to drive the filter hard in the next step.
- VCO2 LEVEL 0, WAVE FORM reverse saw: Oscillator 2 stays out of it.
- Listen for: a low, soft hum while the key is held. It is not a drum yet; the envelope comes later.

steps.title: Drive it through FILTER 2
steps.why:
FILTER 2 saturates the body rather than filtering it politely. With the cutoff low and the level high, the triangle leaves the filter squared off at the edges, which is the hardness.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 3.4 (202 Hz): the low-pass filter cuts highs above about 200 Hz. It sets the pitch centre of the kick and how hard it drives; raise it and the drum gets buzzier and less solid.
- PEAK 5.8: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff.
- Filter type FILTER 2: the dirtier circuit, and where the distortion comes from. On FILTER 1 the same patch is a clean, polite kick.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1 (24 Hz), PEAK 0: the high-pass filter tightens the very bottom so kicks do not smear together at speed.
- Listen for: the hum getting thicker and slightly distorted. Flip to FILTER 1 to hear it clean up.

steps.title: Put a click on the front
steps.why:
A sweep of the low-pass at the start of each hit gives the beater click. Without it the kick is felt but not heard on a small speaker.
- EG2/EXT 4.6 (low-pass): how far envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope generator) lifts the low-pass cutoff on each note. Envelope 2 still has its default high sustain, so for now the filter opens and mostly stays open; the next step shortens it into a click.
- Listen for: a brighter front on each note. Turn the knob to 0 and the kick sounds muffled.

steps.title: Hold, then collapse
steps.why:
Envelope 2 turns the hum into a hit: full at once, held flat for a moment, then collapsing to silence.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (5 ms): envelope 2 opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier, instantly.
- HOLD TIME 1.4 (28 ms): keeps the hit at full for a moment before the decay starts, so the body is flat rather than falling away at once. This is what separates a techno kick from a plucked bass note.
- DECAY 4.6 (220 ms), SUSTAIN 0: the length of the hit. With no sustain every hit is the same length however long you hold the key.
- RELEASE TIME 1.6 (110 ms): short, for when you let go early.
- VOLUME 9.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: a solid thump with a click on top. Sweep DECAY to hear it go from a tight knock to a boom.

context.lpf.cutoff: The pitch centre of the kick and how hard it drives. Raise it and the drum gets buzzier and less solid.
context.lpf.type: FILTER 2 is where the distortion comes from. On FILTER 1 the same patch is a clean, polite kick.
context.lpmod.eg2: The click on the front. Turn it off and the kick sounds muffled.
context.eg2.hold: How long the body stays at full level before it falls. This is what separates a techno kick from a plucked bass note.
context.eg2.decay: The length of the hit. Long enough to boom, short enough to leave room for the next one.
context.hpf.cutoff: Tightens the very bottom so the kicks do not smear into each other at speed.

tweaks.hear: A longer, flatter hit that starts to sound like a distorted bass note.
The distortion backs off and the same kick turns clean and round — house rather than techno.
The filter starts to ring at the cutoff, adding a tone on top of the thump.
An octave up: the kick becomes a floor tom.

sounds.name: Industrial Metal Hit
sounds.ref: In the style of Skinny Puppy and late-80s industrial percussion
sounds.blurb: A hard, tuneless clang, like something heavy being struck.
sounds.how: The RING position on Oscillator 2’s waveform switch multiplies the two oscillators together instead of adding them. What comes out is the sum and difference of their frequencies, which do not line up as harmonics, so the ear hears metal rather than a note. The high-pass takes the body away so it reads as a strike, and FILTER 2 adds the dirt.

steps.title: A narrow pulse into the ring modulator
steps.why:
Oscillator 2’s RING position multiplies the two oscillators together instead of adding them. What comes out is the sum and difference of their frequencies, which do not line up as harmonics, so the ear hears metal.
- WAVE FORM pulse, PW 8 on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. A narrow pulse has far more harmonics than a triangle, and every one gets multiplied, so the clang is dense rather than hollow.
- WAVE FORM RING, SCALE 4′ on VCO 2: RING replaces Oscillator 2’s output with the two multiplied. 4′ puts Oscillator 2 an octave above Oscillator 1.
- VCO1 LEVEL 3, VCO2 LEVEL 9: mostly ring tone, with a little plain pulse. Oscillator 1 feeds the ring too, so its level knob is not the whole story.
- Listen for: at an octave the result still sounds fairly like a note. The next step detunes it.

steps.title: Tune it to nothing in particular
steps.why:
Octaves and fifths sound like notes. An interval that is neither puts the sum and difference tones between the harmonics, which is what makes it sound like struck metal.
- PITCH 3.4 (+8.2 st): Oscillator 2 just over eight semitones sharp. Every position is a different piece of metal, and none of them is a note.
- Listen for: the tone turning clangy and bell-like. Sweep PITCH slowly while holding a key and hear the metal change.

steps.title: Take the body out and dirty it
steps.why:
The high-pass removes the weight that would make this a bass note, and FILTER 2 saturates the clang so it sounds hit rather than played.
- High-pass CUTOFF 4.4 (251 Hz), PEAK 4: the high-pass filter removes the lows below about 250 Hz; PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. This sets how heavy the object is: low sounds like a girder, high like a sheet of tin.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 8 (4.6 kHz), PEAK 3.6: the low-pass filter opens above where it started, keeping the bright top of the clang.
- Filter type FILTER 2: the dirtier circuit. FILTER 1 gives the same hit clean, which sounds far more polite.
- Listen for: the clang losing its bottom and gaining grit. Sweep the high-pass CUTOFF to change the size of the object.

steps.title: Strike it
steps.why:
Envelope 2 turns the tone into a strike: all the energy at the front, then gone.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (5 ms), HOLD 1 (21 ms): envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier, instantly and holds it at full for about 20 ms.
- DECAY 4.2 (160 ms), SUSTAIN 0: how long it rings. Short is a hammer on an anvil; long is a bin lid.
- RELEASE TIME 2 (140 ms): a short tail if you let go early.
- EG2/EXT 3 (low-pass): a short filter sweep that makes the first few milliseconds brighter than the rest.
- VOLUME 8.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: a hard clank that dies away fast. Sweep DECAY from 2 to 7 to hear it go from anvil to bin lid.

context.vco2.pitch: Which piece of metal you are hitting. Every position is a different one, and none of them is a note.
context.mix.vco1: How much plain oscillator survives alongside the clang. At 0 the hit has no pitch at all.
context.hpf.cutoff: How heavy the object is. Low sounds like a girder, high like a sheet of tin.
context.eg2.decay: How long it rings. Short is a hammer on an anvil; long is a bin lid.
context.lpf.type: FILTER 2 is doing the damage. FILTER 1 gives the same hit clean, which sounds far more polite.

tweaks.hear: The hit changes metal at every position — pipe, plate, bell, scaffolding.
A long ringing clang instead of a dead hit.
The weight comes back and the clang turns into an explosion.
A squarer wave into the ring modulator: fewer, clearer clang tones and a more bell-like hit.

sounds.name: Closed Hi-Hat
sounds.ref: In the style of synth-made closed hi-hats
sounds.blurb: A short tick of bright noise, tight enough to play in sixteenths.
sounds.how: The fourth position on Oscillator 1’s waveform switch swaps the oscillator for the noise generator. A hi-hat is noise with everything below a couple of kilohertz taken away, cut off before it can become a hiss. The whole sound is over in about forty milliseconds, and the high-pass does the rest.

steps.title: Noise instead of an oscillator
steps.why:
The fourth position on Oscillator 1’s waveform switch is not a wave: it swaps the oscillator for the noise generator. A hi-hat is built from noise, so that is the only source needed.
- WAVE FORM noise on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. On this position the oscillator is disconnected and noise takes its place. Most synths give noise its own mixer channel; here it costs you an oscillator.
- VCO1 LEVEL 9: with the switch on noise, this knob is now the noise level.
- VCO2 LEVEL 0: Oscillator 2 is muted, so there is no pitch in it.
- Listen for: a steady hiss while the key is held, a little softened by the low-pass, which is still at its starting point of 2.3 kHz.

steps.title: Take everything below the top away
steps.why:
A hi-hat lives above about two kilohertz. The high-pass does nearly all the work; the low-pass only takes the very top edge off so it is not painful.
- High-pass CUTOFF 7.6 (2.3 kHz): the high-pass filter removes everything below this point. The main control on the patch: below about 6 it turns into a snare.
- High-pass PEAK 2.4: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. A little gives the hat a pitch of its own, which helps it sit in a busy pattern.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 9.4 (12 kHz), PEAK 1.5: the low-pass filter opens nearly all the way. Bring it down to make the hat duller and further away.
- Filter type FILTER 2: the more aggressive of the two circuits. It switches both filters.
- Listen for: the hiss thinning to a bright, tinny sizzle.

steps.title: Make it a tick
steps.why:
Envelope 2 cuts the sizzle down to a tick, short enough to play in sixteenths.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (5 ms): envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier, instantly.
- HOLD TIME 0: no pause at full before the decay.
- DECAY 2.6 (42 ms), SUSTAIN 0: the whole sound is over in about forty milliseconds, however long you hold the key. Past about 4 it is no longer a closed hat.
- RELEASE TIME 1.2 (83 ms): short, so letting go early leaves no tail.
- VOLUME 8.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: a crisp “tss” on each key. Play fast repeated notes and sweep DECAY between 2 and 5 to hear closed turn towards half-open.

context.hpf.cutoff: How thin the hat is. This is the main control: below about 6 it turns into a snare.
context.eg2.decay: The length of the tick. Past about 4 it is no longer a closed hat.
context.lpf.cutoff: The top edge. Bring it down to make the hat sound duller and further away.
context.hpf.peak: A little resonance gives the hat a pitch of its own, which helps it sit in a busy pattern.
context.mix.vco1: The noise level, because the waveform switch is on noise.

tweaks.hear: A pedal hat: half open, still tight enough to play fast.
Fatter and wetter, closer to a shaker than a hat.
The noise takes on a pitch and the hat turns metallic and cheap, like an early drum machine.

sounds.name: Open Hat and Cymbal
sounds.ref: In the style of synth-made open hats and cymbals
sounds.blurb: A long wash of bright noise with a metallic ring in it.
sounds.how: The same noise as a closed hat, held open for a second instead of forty milliseconds. What makes it a cymbal rather than a hiss is resonance on the high-pass: it picks out a band and rings it, and sweeping that band down as the sound decays gives the shimmer of a cymbal dying away.

steps.title: Noise, wide open
steps.why:
The same starting point as any synth cymbal: noise and nothing else.
- WAVE FORM noise on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. The fourth position swaps the oscillator for the noise generator.
- VCO1 LEVEL 9: with the switch on noise, this knob is the noise level.
- VCO2 LEVEL 0: Oscillator 2 is muted, so there is no pitch.
- Listen for: a steady hiss while the key is held.

steps.title: Ring a band of it
steps.why:
Resonance on the high-pass picks out one band of the noise and rings it. That is the difference between a cymbal and a hiss.
- High-pass CUTOFF 6.6 (1.1 kHz): the high-pass filter removes everything below about 1 kHz. This is where the ring sits; lower is a bigger, heavier cymbal.
- High-pass PEAK 7.2: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. High enough to ring, which is the metal in the tone. At 0 you have a wash of noise and nothing more.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 9.4 (12 kHz), PEAK 2.8: the low-pass filter is almost fully open. Bring it down for an older, duller cymbal.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits.
- Listen for: a pitched, whistling ring inside the hiss. Turn the high-pass PEAK down to 0 and it goes back to plain noise.

steps.title: Let it ring out
steps.why:
Envelope 2 lets the wash ring out on its own. With no sustain it fades away whether you hold the key or not.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier, instantly, with no pause at full.
- DECAY 6.4 (970 ms), SUSTAIN 0: about a second to die away. Around 6 is an open hat; higher becomes a crash.
- RELEASE TIME 3.4 (320 ms): if you let go early the sound fades over a third of a second instead of cutting off.
- VOLUME 8.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: a hit that dies away over about a second. Hold the key down and it still fades on its own.

steps.title: Let the shimmer fall
steps.why:
Envelope 2 now sweeps the high-pass as well, so the ringing band starts higher and drops as the sound dies. That fall is what the ear reads as a cymbal rather than a burst of noise.
- EG2/EXT 3.6 (high-pass): how far envelope 2 lifts the high-pass cutoff on each hit. The ring starts high and bright and slides down with the decay.
- Listen for: a shimmer that falls in pitch as it fades. Turn the knob to 0 and the ring stays on one pitch.

context.eg2.decay: How long the cymbal rings. Around 6 is an open hat; higher becomes a crash.
context.hpf.peak: The metallic ring. With it at 0 you have a wash of noise and nothing more.
context.hpf.cutoff: Where the ring sits. Lower is a bigger, heavier cymbal.
context.hpmod.eg2: The shimmer: how far the ringing band falls as the sound decays.
context.lpf.cutoff: The top of the wash. Bring it down for an older, duller cymbal.

tweaks.hear: A crash cymbal with a tail several seconds long.
The metal goes and a plain wash of noise is left — useful as a riser, useless as a cymbal.
The band falls a long way, giving a sweeping, almost gong-like decay.

sounds.name: Chopped Handclap
sounds.ref: In the style of early drum-machine handclaps
sounds.blurb: Several bursts of noise in quick succession, followed by a short tail.
sounds.how: A handclap is not one sound but several hands landing a few milliseconds apart. Three cables build that here: white noise goes into the spare VCA on the patch panel, the modulation generator’s pulse output opens and shuts that VCA about twenty times a second, and the result goes back into the filter chain. The main envelope shapes the whole thing, so the chopping only lasts as long as the hit.

steps.title: Nothing from the oscillators
steps.why:
The whole sound will come in through the patch panel, so both oscillators come out of the mixer. A clap has no pitch in it.
- VCO1 LEVEL 0, VCO2 LEVEL 0: the mixer sends nothing from the VCOs (voltage-controlled oscillators) to the filters.
- WAVE FORM triangle / reverse saw: plain waveforms, so neither switch is on noise or RING. They are silent anyway.
- Listen for: silence. The next three steps build the clap out of cables.

steps.title: Noise into the spare VCA
steps.why:
The patch panel has a spare VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) of its own, doing nothing. White noise goes into it.
- WHITE → VCA IN: carries white noise, every frequency at once, bright and hissy, into the spare VCA. Whatever reaches its CONTROL INPUT decides how much gets through.
- Listen for: still silence. Nothing is opening the spare VCA yet, and its output goes nowhere.

steps.title: Chop it with the modulation generator
steps.why:
The modulation generator’s pulse output now switches the spare VCA fully on and fully off, chopping the noise into bursts.
- MG OUT (pulse) → CONTROL INPUT: MG is the modulation generator, Korg’s name for the LFO (low-frequency oscillator). Its pulse output has only two values, so the VCA is either open or shut.
- FREQUENCY 10 (22 Hz): the top of the range. The bursts arrive roughly forty milliseconds apart, the spacing of hands in a clap. Slower and you hear separate hits.
- WAVE FORM 5 (triangle): at the centre of the knob the pulse output is a square, so the VCA is open and shut for equal times.
- Listen for: nothing yet. The chopped noise reaches the filters in the next step.

steps.title: Send the bursts to the filters
steps.why:
EXT SIGNAL IN joins the oscillator mix at the input of the filter chain, so the chopped noise is now heard, shaped by the same two filters as anything else.
- VCA OUT → EXT SIGNAL IN: carries the chopped noise from the spare VCA into the filters, then through the main amplifier and envelope 2.
- Listen for: a fast, rattling burst of noise for as long as the key is held. Envelope 2 is still at its default high sustain, so it keeps going; the last step turns it into a single clap.

steps.title: Shape the hit
steps.why:
A clap sits in the upper middle. The high-pass takes the weight out, and resonance on the low-pass gives it a body so it is not just hiss.
- High-pass CUTOFF 5 (379 Hz), PEAK 3.4: the high-pass filter removes the lows; PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. Low sounds like a slap on a table; high sounds like fingertips.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 7.6 (3.5 kHz), PEAK 4.8: the low-pass filter trims the harsh top, and its resonance gives the clap a body so it reads as hands rather than static.
- Filter type FILTER 2: the more aggressive of the two circuits.
- Listen for: the rattle moving from hiss towards a papery, mid-range crackle.

steps.title: Bursts, then tail
steps.why:
Envelope 2 cuts the rattle down to one clap: two or three bursts, then a short tail.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier, instantly.
- DECAY 4.4 (190 ms), SUSTAIN 0: how many bursts get through before the amplifier closes. This sets the size of the clap.
- RELEASE TIME 3.2 (280 ms): the tail after the last burst. It is what makes the clap sound like it happened in a room.
- VOLUME 9: overall output level.
- Listen for: a clap with a slight flutter at the front. Sweep DECAY and hear more or fewer bursts get through.

context.mg.freq: The spacing of the hands. Slower and you hear separate hits; faster than this the synth cannot go.
context.eg2.decay: How many bursts get through before the amplifier closes. This is what sets the size of the clap.
context.eg2.release: The tail after the last burst. A long release is what makes a clap sound like it happened in a room.
context.hpf.cutoff: How thin the clap is. Low sounds like a slap on a table; high sounds like fingertips.
context.lpf.peak: Gives the clap a body so it reads as hands rather than static.

tweaks.hear: The hands separate into two or three distinct hits — more of a stadium clap.
A long reverberant tail, as though the clap were in a hall.
One burst only: a short noise tick rather than a clap.
Brighter and sharper, closer to a rim hit than a clap.

sounds.name: Falling Tom
sounds.ref: In the style of electronic toms
sounds.blurb: A round drum whose pitch falls away as it decays.
sounds.how: Every electronic tom is the same trick: a soft wave, a short envelope and a pitch that falls. Envelope 1 is the one wired to oscillator pitch, so the EG1/EXT knob sets how far the drum drops and RELEASE TIME sets how long it takes. Play up and down the keyboard and each tom is tuned differently, which is how a whole rack of them comes from one patch.

steps.title: A soft, round wave
steps.why:
A triangle an octave down. It has almost no harmonics, which is what a drum skin sounds like; a sawtooth here would buzz.
- WAVE FORM triangle on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. The triangle is soft and round.
- SCALE 16′ on VCO 1: SCALE is the octave switch in organ-pipe feet; 16′ is an octave below 8′. 32′ gives floor toms, 8′ gives high rack toms.
- VCO1 LEVEL 9, VCO2 LEVEL 0: Oscillator 1 only. Oscillator 2 is muted, on a plain waveform.
- Listen for: a low, soft hum. Each key will become a differently tuned tom, which is how a whole rack comes from one patch.

steps.title: Keep it warm
steps.why:
The low-pass takes the edge off the attack, and a little resonance near the cutoff gives the skin its body.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 4.6 (457 Hz): the low-pass filter cuts highs above this point. Raise it and the tom gets harder and more synthetic.
- PEAK 4.2: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. It adds a slight ring around 450 Hz.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother circuit, for a warm tone.
- High-pass CUTOFF 0.8 (21 Hz), PEAK 0: the high-pass filter is almost fully open, so the low end is kept.
- Listen for: the hum getting rounder and warmer.

steps.title: Set envelope 1 to fall
steps.why:
Envelope 1 is the one wired to oscillator pitch. Here it jumps to the top the moment a key goes down and slides back once the key is released.
- DELAY TIME 0: envelope 1 (EG1, the simpler envelope generator) starts at once, with no wait.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (3 ms): the pitch is at the top the instant the key goes down.
- RELEASE TIME 3.4 (250 ms): how long the pitch takes to fall back once you let go. Quick is a tight tom; slow is a syndrum. The phrase plays very short notes, so the fall is most of what you hear.
- Listen for: nothing yet. The EG1/EXT depth knob is still at 0, so the envelope is not moving the pitch.

steps.title: Choose how far it drops
steps.why:
The EG1/EXT knob under the VCO mixer is the depth: how far envelope 1 bends the pitch of both oscillators.
- EG1/EXT 4.2: around 4 gives the few semitones a real tom falls; much more and it turns into a zap. This knob is the difference between a drum and a sound effect.
- Listen for: play short notes and hear each one start high and drop as you let go. Hold a key and the pitch stays up until you release it.

steps.title: Short and round
steps.why:
Envelope 2 makes it a drum: an instant hit, a decay of a few hundred milliseconds and no sustain.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0.8 (18 ms): envelope 2 (EG2) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier, instantly and holds it at full for a moment.
- DECAY 5 (300 ms), SUSTAIN 0: the length of the hit. Longer turns the tom into a timpani.
- RELEASE TIME 3.4 (320 ms): carries the tail past the end of the very short notes in the phrase, which is where the pitch fall happens.
- VOLUME 9: overall output level.
- Listen for: a round “doom” that bends down as it fades. Play a quick run down the keyboard for a tom fill.

context.fmod.eg1: How far the tom falls. This is the difference between a drum and a sound effect.
context.eg1.release: How long the fall takes. Quick is a tight tom; slow is a syndrum.
context.lpf.cutoff: How muffled the skin is. Raise it and the tom gets harder and more synthetic.
context.eg2.decay: The length of the hit. Longer turns the tom into a timpani.
context.vco1.scale: The range of the drum. 32′ gives floor toms, 8′ gives high rack toms.

tweaks.hear: A long dive: the disco syndrum of the late seventies.
The fall happens almost instantly, leaving a hard click at the front of the drum.
The filter rings along with the drum, adding a second tone that makes it sound electronic rather than acoustic.

sounds.name: Rimshot Click
sounds.ref: In the style of electronic rimshots and clicks
sounds.blurb: A dry wooden click, ten milliseconds long.
sounds.how: The narrow pulse on Oscillator 2 is the thinnest wave the K-2 has: almost no fundamental, all upper harmonics. Put it through a resonant band and cut it off after about ten milliseconds and there is no time to hear a pitch — only the ring of the filter, which the ear reads as wood. This is the shortest useful envelope on the instrument.

steps.title: The narrow pulse
steps.why:
Oscillator 2’s third position is a narrow pulse, thinner than anything Oscillator 1 offers. It is nearly all upper harmonics, which is what a click needs.
- WAVE FORM narrow pulse, SCALE 4′: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. 4′ puts Oscillator 2 an octave above Oscillator 1’s 8′.
- PITCH 1.2 (+2.9 st): retunes the source under the filter. It matters less than the filter does, because the sound is over before the pitch registers.
- VCO1 LEVEL 0, VCO2 LEVEL 9: Oscillator 2 only. Oscillator 1 is muted, on triangle.
- Listen for: a thin, buzzy, nasal tone while the key is held.

steps.title: Ring a narrow band
steps.why:
The two filters squeeze in on each other and resonate at both edges. With a sound this short, that ring is most of what you hear, and it gives the click its woody pitch.
- High-pass CUTOFF 5.4 (500 Hz), PEAK 5.6: the high-pass filter removes the lows below 500 Hz; PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. Raise the cutoff and the last of the body goes.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 7 (2.3 kHz): the low-pass filter sets the top edge and the pitch of the click. Higher is a rimshot, lower is a woodblock.
- Low-pass PEAK 7.4: the wood. With it down there is nothing but a faint tick.
- Filter type FILTER 2: the more aggressive circuit, harder at high resonance.
- Listen for: the buzz turning into a narrow, ringing band.

steps.title: Ten milliseconds
steps.why:
Envelope 2 cuts each note to about ten milliseconds: too short to hear a pitch, only the ring of the filter, which the ear reads as wood.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier, instantly.
- DECAY 1.3 (13 ms), SUSTAIN 0: about as short as it usefully goes. Anything above about 2 and it stops being a click and becomes a blip.
- RELEASE TIME 1.4 (94 ms): just long enough for the filter to stop ringing.
- VOLUME 9.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: a dry “tok”. Sweep the low-pass CUTOFF between 5 and 8 to move from woodblock to rimshot.

context.lpf.peak: The wood. This is the sound: with the resonance down there is nothing but a faint tick.
context.lpf.cutoff: The pitch of the click. Higher is a rimshot, lower is a woodblock.
context.hpf.cutoff: How dry it is. Raising it takes the last of the body away.
context.eg2.decay: Anything above about 2 and it stops being a click and becomes a blip.
context.vco2.pitch: Retunes the source under the filter. It matters less than the cutoff, because the sound is over before the pitch registers.

tweaks.hear: A lower, hollower knock — a woodblock or a claves hit.
The click becomes a short pitched blip, closer to a bleep than a drum.
The filter rings on after the hit, turning the click into a plucked, almost marimba-like tone.

sounds.name: Gunshot
sounds.ref: In the style of film and game gunshots
sounds.blurb: A hard crack with a low thump behind it.
sounds.how: A gunshot is a crack and a thump arriving together. The noise generator supplies both, and the trick is the filter: envelope 2 throws the cutoff wide open for the first few milliseconds and drops it several octaves as it falls, so the sound starts as a bright crack and ends as a low thud. FILTER 2 saturates the front of it, which is what stops it sounding like a polite burst of static.

steps.title: Noise, loud
steps.why:
The noise generator has every frequency in it at once, which is why it can be both the crack and the thump.
- WAVE FORM noise on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. The fourth position swaps the oscillator for the noise generator.
- VCO1 LEVEL 9.5: with the switch on noise, this is the noise level, near full.
- VCO2 LEVEL 0: Oscillator 2 muted, so there is no pitch.
- Listen for: a steady hiss while the key is held.

steps.title: Start low and dirty
steps.why:
The cutoff rests low, so that is where the sound ends up. FILTER 2 and a fair amount of PEAK give the report its body.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 2.6 (117 Hz): the low-pass filter cuts everything above about 120 Hz, leaving a low rumble. Low is a rifle; raise it and it becomes a pistol.
- PEAK 6.4: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. It gives the report its body. Too much and it whistles instead of banging.
- Filter type FILTER 2: the dirtier circuit. It saturates the front of the shot, which stops it sounding like a polite burst of static.
- High-pass CUTOFF 0.6 (18 Hz), PEAK 0: the high-pass filter is effectively open, so no low end is lost.
- Listen for: the hiss becoming a dark, rumbling roar.

steps.title: Throw the filter open and drop it
steps.why:
A large amount of envelope 2 on the cutoff throws the filter wide open for the first few milliseconds and drops it several octaves as it falls, closing within about a tenth of a second. The crack and the thump are the same sound at two ends of that sweep.
- EG2/EXT 8 (low-pass): how far envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope generator) lifts the cutoff. Turn it down and you are left with a dull thud.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0.6 (15 ms): instant, and held at full for a moment so the crack has some length.
- DECAY 5.4 (420 ms), SUSTAIN 0: how fast the sweep falls, and so how fast the shot is over. Envelope 2 also runs the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier), so the volume falls with it.
- Listen for: a bright crack sliding down into a low thud.

steps.title: Cut it dead
steps.why:
A short release so nothing hangs around after the shot. Anything longer and it turns into an explosion.
- RELEASE TIME 2.6 (200 ms): the fade after you let go. Any length here becomes the echo after the shot.
- VOLUME 9.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: tap the key briefly and the tail stops quickly. Raise RELEASE to 6 and the shot becomes a distant blast.

context.lpmod.eg2: The distance between the crack and the thump. Turn it down and you are left with a dull thud.
context.lpf.cutoff: Where the shot ends up. Low is a rifle; raise it and it becomes a pistol.
context.eg2.decay: How fast the sweep falls, and so how fast the shot is over.
context.lpf.peak: The body of the report. Too much and it whistles instead of banging.
context.eg2.release: Any length here becomes the echo after the shot.

tweaks.hear: A long rolling tail: a shot in a canyon rather than a room.
The crack disappears and only the thump is left — a distant shot.
The sweep slows right down into an explosion or a rocket launch.

sounds.name: Two-Tone Klaxon
sounds.ref: In the style of alarm and klaxon effects
sounds.blurb: A hard two-note alarm that switches back and forth on its own.
sounds.how: The modulation generator has two outputs. The one wired to the front panel sweeps smoothly, which gives a wailing siren; the pulse output on the patch panel only has two values, which gives a klaxon that jumps between two notes. One cable takes that pulse to the FREQ socket, where it stands in for envelope 1 at the EG1/EXT knob — so that knob now sets the interval between the two notes.

steps.title: A hard, carrying tone
steps.why:
A narrow pulse and a square, slightly apart. The pulse cuts through anything, which is what an alarm is for, and the offset makes it sound like a real horn rather than a test tone.
- WAVE FORM pulse, PW 7 on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. PW is pulse width; 7 is towards the thin, nasal end.
- WAVE FORM square (VCO 2), both 8′: the square adds body. 8′ on both is the same octave on this synth.
- PITCH 0.2 (+0.4 st): Oscillator 2 slightly sharp. A real klaxon is never quite in tune with itself.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8, VCO2 LEVEL 6: the pulse leads.
- Listen for: a hard, buzzy tone with a fast beat running through it.

steps.title: Leave it bright
steps.why:
Alarms are meant to be heard. The low-pass stays high and the high-pass takes out the bottom, so it sounds like a horn rather than a bass note.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 8 (4.6 kHz), PEAK 3.2: the low-pass filter opens above where it started, keeping the bright top. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance; a little adds an edge without making it louder.
- Filter type FILTER 2: the more aggressive of the two circuits.
- High-pass CUTOFF 3.4 (126 Hz), PEAK 2.6: the high-pass filter removes the lows. Raise it and the horn sounds thinner and more urgent.
- Listen for: the tone getting brighter and more pinched.

steps.title: Hold the note open
steps.why:
Envelope 2 holds the note fully open, so the alarm runs for as long as the key is held and the switching can do all the work.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (5 ms): envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier, instantly.
- SUSTAIN 10, DECAY 6 (690 ms): full sustain, so the level never drops while you hold.
- RELEASE TIME 1.6 (110 ms): stops quickly when you let go.
- VOLUME 7.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: a flat, constant tone for as long as you hold the key.

steps.title: Patch the pulse output to FREQ
steps.why:
The modulation generator’s pulse output now drives the pitch. Because the pulse has only two values, the pitch has only two values: a klaxon rather than a siren.
- MG OUT (pulse) → FREQ: MG is Korg’s name for the LFO (low-frequency oscillator). FREQ takes envelope 1’s place at the EG1/EXT knob, so the pulse now moves the pitch of both oscillators.
- EG1/EXT 3.2: the interval between the two notes. Small values give a European two-tone horn; large ones give a fire alarm.
- FREQUENCY 5.6 (2.05 Hz): how fast it switches. Around two cycles a second is a road vehicle; faster is an alarm clock.
- Listen for: hold a key and hear it flip between two notes, up and down about twice a second. Pull the cable and it goes back to one steady tone.

context.fmod.eg1: The interval between the two notes, now that the pulse output is arriving at this knob. Small values give a European two-tone horn; large ones give a fire alarm.
context.mg.freq: How fast it switches. Around two cycles a second is a road vehicle; faster is an alarm clock.
context.hpf.cutoff: How thin and urgent the horn sounds.
context.vco2.pitch: The beating between the two oscillators. A real klaxon is never quite in tune with itself.
context.lpf.peak: Adds an edge to the tone without making it louder.

tweaks.hear: A wide leap between the two notes: an American emergency siren rather than a European one.
Fast switching that stops sounding like two notes and starts sounding like one rough tone.

tweaks.try: Raise to 2 with the cable still in
tweaks.hear: The smooth output joins in as well, so the klaxon wails between its jumps.

sounds.name: Computer Room Chatter
sounds.ref: In the style of 70s computer-room chatter
sounds.blurb: Hold one key and the synth chatters away on its own, a new note on every tick.
sounds.how: Three cables and it plays itself. The modulation generator’s pulse output clocks the sample and hold, so a new random voltage arrives on every tick, and that voltage goes to the pitch of both oscillators. The same pulse also goes to INITIAL GAIN, which opens the amplifier in time with the clock — so instead of one long sliding tone you get separate bleeps, each at its own pitch.

steps.title: One clean oscillator
steps.why:
One clean oscillator. The interest is in the pattern, not the tone, so nothing else is needed.
- WAVE FORM pulse, PW 5 on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. PW (pulse width) at 5 gives a clear, hollow pulse that reads well at speed.
- SCALE 8′, VCO1 LEVEL 8: the middle octave, at a healthy level into the filters.
- VCO2 LEVEL 0: Oscillator 2 is muted.
- TIME 0: portamento (glide) off. At 0 the notes jump; any glide and the bleeps smear into a burble.
- Listen for: a plain, steady tone while the key is held.

steps.title: Bright, with a ping
steps.why:
The filter stays fairly open so each bleep is legible, with enough resonance that the front of each one pings.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 7 (2.3 kHz): the low-pass filter stays where it started. Lower it and the machine sounds further away.
- PEAK 5.4: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. It sets how much each bleep pings as it arrives.
- Filter type FILTER 2: the more aggressive of the two circuits.
- High-pass CUTOFF 3.2 (109 Hz), PEAK 2: the high-pass filter takes out the low end so the chatter sounds small.
- Listen for: a nasal ring on top of the tone. It shows more once the notes start changing.

steps.title: Clock the sample and hold
steps.why:
The modulation generator’s pulse output now clocks the sample and hold (S&H), the circuit that takes a reading of a voltage on each tick and holds it until the next.
- MG OUT (pulse) → CLOCK: MG is Korg’s name for the LFO (low-frequency oscillator). Its pulse output never goes below zero, which makes it a clean clock.
- FREQUENCY 8.2 (8.33 Hz): about eight ticks a second, the speed of the chatter. Later it sets the gating too, so the two can never drift apart.
- WAVE FORM 5 (triangle): at the centre of the knob the pulse output is an even square.
- Listen for: nothing new yet. The S&H is ticking, but its output is not connected to anything.

steps.title: Send the steps to pitch
steps.why:
With nothing patched to its input the sample and hold reads noise, so every tick lands on a random voltage. Sent to pitch, that is a different note every tick.
- S&H OUT → VCO 1+2 CV IN: carries the stepped random voltage to the pitch input of both oscillators (CV means control voltage). Here it adds to whatever note you play.
- Listen for: hold a key and the pitch jumps about eight times a second. The amplifier stays open between steps, so for now it is one continuous, stepping tone.

steps.title: Chop the amplifier with the same clock
steps.why:
The same clock now opens the amplifier, so each step becomes its own bleep instead of part of one continuous tone.
- MG OUT (pulse) → INITIAL GAIN: INITIAL GAIN adds to envelope 2 at the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier). The pulse opens it on each tick and shuts it in between.
- ATTACK 0, DECAY 3 (60 ms), SUSTAIN 0: envelope 2 (EG2) now closes straight after the key press, so the pulse is the only thing opening the amplifier. SUSTAIN has to be 0; any sustain and the bleeps join into one sliding tone.
- RELEASE TIME 1.5 (100 ms): a short tail after you let go.
- VOLUME 7.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: separate bleeps, each at its own pitch, with gaps between. Hold one key and let it chatter.

context.mg.freq: The speed of the chatter. It sets the clock and the gating at once, so the two can never drift apart.
context.lpf.peak: How much each bleep pings as it arrives.
context.lpf.cutoff: How bright the chatter is. Lower it and the machine sounds further away.
context.porta.time: At 0 the notes jump. Any glide and the bleeps smear into a burble.
context.eg2.sustain: It has to be at 0. Any sustain and the amplifier stays open between ticks, which joins the bleeps into one sliding tone.

tweaks.hear: A deliberate, thinking-machine pace instead of a chatter.
Each bleep slides into the next: a burbling, drunken version of the same pattern.
The whole thing jumps an octave and turns into a bird or a modem.
The filter rings on each bleep, and the pitch of the ring changes with the step.

sounds.name: Dripping Water
sounds.ref: In the style of dripping-water effects
sounds.blurb: Isolated plinks, each at a slightly different pitch.
sounds.how: A drip is a single pinged tone that dies almost at once, and no two drips are quite the same pitch. Wind PEAK up until the low-pass rings on its own and it becomes the sound source; a slowly clocked sample and hold, patched to the low-pass CUTOFF FREQ socket, then moves where it rings between one drip and the next. Every key press catches whatever voltage the sample and hold happens to be holding.

steps.title: Just enough to strike it
steps.why:
A resonant filter needs something to start it ringing. A whisper of triangle is enough; any more and you hear the oscillator instead of the drip.
- WAVE FORM triangle, SCALE 4′ on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. SCALE is the octave switch in organ-pipe feet; 4′ is the top of Oscillator 1’s range, an octave above 8′.
- VCO1 LEVEL 3: how hard the filter is struck. Turn it up and you hear the oscillator as well as the ring.
- VCO2 LEVEL 0, WAVE FORM reverse saw: Oscillator 2 is muted.
- Listen for: a quiet, high, soft tone. It is only the striker; the drip comes from the filter.

steps.title: Make the filter ring
steps.why:
With PEAK near the top the low-pass rings at its cutoff. That pure ringing tone, cut short, is a drip.
- Low-pass PEAK 9.6: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff. Near maximum the filter rings on its own and becomes the sound source. Below about 9 the ringing stops and the drips disappear.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 6.4 (1.6 kHz): the pitch the drips sit around.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits.
- High-pass CUTOFF 3.6 (144 Hz), PEAK 1.5: the high-pass filter clears the low end so the drips stay small.
- Listen for: a high, whistling tone over the triangle while the key is held.

steps.title: Plink
steps.why:
Envelope 2 cuts the whistle short. The whole drip is over before you can hear it as a note.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier, instantly.
- DECAY 4.2 (160 ms), SUSTAIN 0: the length of each drip. Longer and it becomes a plucked note rather than water.
- RELEASE TIME 2.4 (170 ms): a short tail if you let go early.
- VOLUME 9.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: a “plink” on each key. The ring sits at the same pitch whichever key you play; the next two steps vary it.

steps.title: Clock the sample and hold slowly
steps.why:
A slow clock for the sample and hold (S&H), the circuit that takes a reading of a voltage on each tick and holds it until the next. The held voltage changes about twice a second, so consecutive drips usually differ but sometimes repeat, which is what real dripping does.
- MG OUT (pulse) → CLOCK: MG, the modulation generator, is Korg’s name for the LFO (low-frequency oscillator). Its pulse output is the clock.
- FREQUENCY 5.4 (1.84 Hz): how often the held voltage changes. Not how often a drip falls; that is up to you and the keyboard.
- WAVE FORM 5 (triangle): at the centre of the knob the pulse output is an even square.
- Listen for: nothing new yet. The S&H is ticking, but its output goes nowhere until the next step.

steps.title: Move the ring between drips
steps.why:
The sample and hold now moves the cutoff, and so the pitch of the ring, between one drip and the next.
- S&H OUT → CUTOFF FREQ (low-pass): carries the stepped voltage to the low-pass cutoff socket, where it takes envelope 2’s place at the EG2/EXT knob. With nothing at its input the S&H reads noise, so each step is random.
- EG2/EXT 3.2 (low-pass): how far the S&H moves the ringing pitch. A little sounds like a tap; a lot sounds like a cave.
- Listen for: tap the key every so often and each plink lands on whatever pitch the S&H is holding. Play quickly and you catch the same pitch twice.

context.lpf.peak: Below about 9 the filter stops ringing and the drips disappear. This is the sound source.
context.lpmod.eg2: How much the pitch varies from drip to drip. A little sounds like a tap; a lot sounds like a cave.
context.lpf.cutoff: The pitch the drips sit around.
context.eg2.decay: The length of each drip. Longer and it becomes a plucked note rather than water.
context.mix.vco1: How hard the filter is struck. Turn it up and you hear the oscillator as well as the ring.
context.mg.freq: How often the pitch changes, which is not the same as how often a drip falls — that is up to you and the keyboard.

tweaks.hear: The drips scatter across several octaves: less like a tap, more like a cave system.
Each drip rings on like a tuned bar — closer to a glass harmonica than water.
The strike comes through as a click on the front of every drip.
The weight comes back underneath and the drips turn into heavy blobs.

sounds.name: Engine Rumble
sounds.ref: In the style of engine and machinery effects
sounds.blurb: A low mechanical chug with loose rattle over the top.
sounds.how: Two things make an engine: a regular thump, and a rattle that is not regular at all. The thump comes from the modulation generator shaking the pitch at about twelve cycles a second — too fast to hear as separate notes, slow enough to hear as a chug. The rattle comes from noise patched in through the side, which never lines up with the chug. FILTER 2 keeps the whole thing dirty.

steps.title: A low triangle
steps.why:
A low triangle for the chug, with a quieter sawtooth above it, tuned flat. Low and soft, so the chug is felt rather than heard as a note.
- WAVE FORM triangle, SCALE 32′ on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. SCALE is the octave switch in organ-pipe feet; 32′ is the lowest, two octaves below 8′. A sawtooth in its place would sound like a synth rather than a machine.
- WAVE FORM reverse saw, SCALE 16′: Oscillator 2’s range sits an octave above Oscillator 1’s, so 16′ here is one octave above the triangle.
- PITCH −0.4 (−1 st): Oscillator 2 a semitone flat. It beats against the first and stops the rumble sounding electronic.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8, VCO2 LEVEL 4: the triangle leads; the saw adds grit.
- Listen for: a deep, slightly sour hum.

steps.title: Shake the pitch at chug speed
steps.why:
The modulation generator shakes the pitch at about twelve cycles a second. At that speed the ear stops hearing separate wobbles and starts hearing a rhythm: the chug.
- FREQUENCY 8.8 (12 Hz): MG, the modulation generator, is Korg’s name for the LFO (low-frequency oscillator). This is the engine speed. Below about 7 you hear separate wobbles; above 9 it turns into a tone.
- WAVE FORM 0 (reverse saw): a ramp with a sudden jump in it, which gives an uneven, knocking chug. At 5 the triangle makes it smooth and electric.
- MG/T.EXT 2.4 (pitch): how hard it chugs. Keep it small: this is a machine turning over, not a siren. Past about 4 it sounds like it is breaking.
- Listen for: hold a key and hear the hum turn into a fast, regular putter.

steps.title: Add the rattle
steps.why:
Pink noise comes in through the side and joins the oscillators at the input of the filter chain. It has nothing to do with the chug, which is exactly why it sounds like loose metal.
- PINK → EXT SIGNAL IN: carries pink noise, softer on top than white, into the filters alongside the oscillators.
