- Listen for: a rushing hiss over the chug. The low-pass is still fairly open, so for now there is too much of it; the next step buries it.

steps.title: Keep it dark and dirty
steps.why:
The low-pass sits low so most of the noise is buried and only the rumble comes through. FILTER 2 saturates as the chug peaks, which adds the knock.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 3.4 (202 Hz): the low-pass filter cuts everything above about 200 Hz. It decides how much of the rattle survives; raising it brings the machine closer.
- PEAK 5: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff, which gives the rumble a hollow edge.
- Filter type FILTER 2: the dirtier circuit, which saturates on the peaks of the chug.
- High-pass CUTOFF 0 (12 Hz), PEAK 0: the high-pass filter fully open, keeping all the low end.
- Listen for: the hiss dropping to a low rattle under a dark, knocking chug.

steps.title: Run it continuously
steps.why:
Envelope 2 lets the engine run: full sustain, so it idles for as long as the key is down rather than starting again with each press.
- ATTACK TIME 3 (50 ms): envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier. A short fade in so the engine does not click on.
- SUSTAIN 10, DECAY 6 (690 ms): full sustain, so the level never drops while you hold.
- RELEASE TIME 4.4 (590 ms): the engine winds down over about half a second when you let go.
- VOLUME 8.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: hold a key for a steady idle. Turn the MG FREQUENCY knob while holding to rev it up and down.

context.mg.freq: The engine speed. Below about 7 you hear separate wobbles; above 9 it turns into a tone.
context.fmod.mg: How hard it chugs. Past about 4 the machine starts to sound like it is breaking.
context.mg.wave: At 0 the modulation is a reverse sawtooth, which gives an uneven, knocking chug. At 5 the triangle makes it smooth and electric.
context.lpf.cutoff: How much of the rattle survives. Raising it brings the machine closer.
context.vco2.pitch: The second oscillator, tuned flat, beats against the first and stops the rumble sounding electronic.

tweaks.hear: A big slow diesel instead of a running motor.
The engine starts to misfire and tear itself apart.
The rattle comes forward and the machine sounds like it is in the room.
A smooth turbine rather than a knocking piston engine.

sounds.name: Tape Stop
sounds.ref: In the style of tape and turntable spin-down effects
sounds.blurb: A note that slows to a halt as it fades, like power being cut to a tape machine.
sounds.how: The instrument listens to itself. Its own output goes into the external signal processor, whose envelope follower produces a voltage that rises and falls with how loud the synth currently is. That voltage is patched to the FREQ socket, where it stands in for envelope 1 at the EG1/EXT knob — so as the note fades, the pitch falls with it. Nothing on the front panel alone can bend the pitch downwards over a held note.

steps.title: Something worth slowing down
steps.why:
Two sawtooths slightly apart, so the beating between them slows along with the pitch and the effect is easier to hear.
- WAVE FORM reverse saw on both VCOs: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. A bright, buzzy tone with plenty in it to hear.
- SCALE 8′ on both: the same octave on this synth.
- PITCH 0.3 (+0.6 st): Oscillator 2 just over half a semitone sharp, for a clear, fast beat.
- VCO1 LEVEL 7.5, VCO2 LEVEL 6.5: close to equal.
- Listen for: a thick, beating saw tone.

steps.title: Warm, not bright
steps.why:
A medium cutoff, because the top end disappearing as the pitch falls is part of what makes it sound mechanical.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 5.8 (1.0 kHz): the low-pass filter cuts the highs above about 1 kHz. It does not move with the pitch, so as the note slows its harmonics slide below the cutoff and it gets duller.
- PEAK 3.6: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother circuit.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1 (24 Hz), PEAK 0: the high-pass filter barely touches the low end.
- Listen for: a warmer, rounder saw.

steps.title: Set the note fading
steps.why:
A decay to no sustain drives the whole effect: the loudness falling is what the envelope follower will read, and so what pulls the pitch down.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (5 ms): envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier, instantly.
- HOLD TIME 1.6 (32 ms): a moment at full speed before the slow-down starts, so you hear what is being stopped.
- DECAY 6.6 (1.1 s), SUSTAIN 0: the note fades to silence over about a second. This is how long the machine takes to stop: short is a power cut, long is a hand on the platter.
- RELEASE TIME 3 (250 ms): a short tail if you let go early.
- VOLUME 8.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: each note fading away over a second even when held. The pitch does not move yet.

steps.title: Feed the output to the signal processor
steps.why:
The synth’s own output goes into the external signal processor, a section that turns an outside sound into voltages the synth can use. Its envelope follower makes a voltage that rises and falls with how loud the synth is.
- SIGNAL OUT → SIGNAL IN: carries the main output round into the processor’s input.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 6: the preamp gain, or how hard the output drives the follower. Too low and the pitch will barely move; too high and it stays up until the note has almost gone.
- Listen for: no change yet. The follower’s voltage is not patched anywhere until the next step.

steps.title: Let the loudness set the pitch
steps.why:
The loudness now sets the pitch. As the note fades, the voltage from the follower falls, and the pitch falls with it.
- ENV OUT → FREQ: carries the envelope follower’s voltage to FREQ, which takes envelope 1’s place at the EG1/EXT knob.
- EG1/EXT 5.2: the depth of the slow-down, or how far the pitch falls between full level and silence. The main control of the effect.
- Listen for: hold a note and hear it sag in pitch and dull in tone as it fades, like power being cut to a tape machine. Change DECAY for a faster or slower stop.

context.fmod.eg1: How far the pitch falls as the note dies. This is the main control of the effect.
context.eg2.decay: How long the machine takes to stop. Short is a power cut; long is a hand on the platter.
context.esp.level: How hard the output drives the follower. Too low and the pitch barely moves; too high and it stays up until the note has almost gone.
context.eg2.hold: A moment at full speed before the slow-down starts, so you hear what is being stopped.
context.lpf.cutoff: The tone. It does not move with the pitch, which is why the sound also gets duller as it slows.

tweaks.hear: A very slow wind-down, several seconds long.
The pitch drops more than an octave: less tape machine, more sinking ship.
The follower barely reacts and the note simply fades at pitch, which shows how much of the effect is the cable.
New notes slide in as well as out, so the machine never quite settles.

sounds.name: Tuning the Radio
sounds.ref: In the style of radio-tuning and static effects
sounds.blurb: Static with squeals and half-heard stations drifting through it.
sounds.how: Two sounds at once: a station, which is the oscillators, and static, which is noise patched in through the side. What sells it is the sample and hold, clocked fast and sent to the high-pass CUTOFF FREQ socket, so the band the noise passes through jumps about several times a second — the chattering, whistling sound of a dial being turned between stations.

steps.title: A weak station
steps.why:
The station: kept quiet and slightly out of tune with itself, so it sounds received rather than played.
- WAVE FORM pulse, PW 6 on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. PW (pulse width) at 6 leans slightly towards thin and nasal.
- WAVE FORM reverse saw (VCO 2), both 8′: a buzzy saw at the same octave.
- PITCH 0.3 (+0.7 st): Oscillator 2 over half a semitone sharp, so the two clash slightly.
- VCO1 LEVEL 4, VCO2 LEVEL 3: low. They set how strong the station is against the static; turn them up and the radio comes into tune.
- Listen for: a quiet, sour, buzzing tone.

steps.title: Static through the side door
steps.why:
White noise comes in through the side as static. It joins the oscillators at the filter chain, so both are shaped by the same two filters, which buries the station in the static rather than sitting it on top.
- WHITE → EXT SIGNAL IN: carries white noise, every frequency at once, into the filters with the oscillators.
- Listen for: loud hiss over the quiet station.

steps.title: A narrow, whistling band
steps.why:
Resonance on both filters leaves a narrow band with a whistle at each edge. A radio between stations is mostly band-limited noise with a carrier whistle in it.
- High-pass CUTOFF 5 (379 Hz), PEAK 7.4: the high-pass filter sets the lower edge; PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. This whistle is the carrier tone you hear as a radio passes a station.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 7.2 (2.7 kHz), PEAK 6.4: the low-pass filter sets the upper edge. Lower it for an old valve set, raise it for a cheap transistor radio.
- Filter type FILTER 2: the more aggressive circuit, harder at high resonance.
- Listen for: the hiss narrowing into a thin, whistling band.

steps.title: Jump the band about
steps.why:
The sample and hold (S&H), clocked fast, now throws the lower edge of the band around. That is the sound of a dial being swept between stations.
- MG OUT (pulse) → CLOCK: MG, the modulation generator, is Korg’s name for the LFO (low-frequency oscillator). Its pulse tells the S&H when to take a new reading; with nothing at its input it reads noise.
- S&H OUT → CUTOFF FREQ (high-pass): the random steps go to the high-pass cutoff socket, taking envelope 2’s place at that section’s EG2/EXT knob.
- FREQUENCY 8.6 (10 Hz), WAVE FORM 5: ten jumps a second. Slow it right down and you hear each position as a separate squeal.
- EG2/EXT 4.6 (high-pass): how wildly the dial swings.
- Listen for: the whistle chattering to a new pitch ten times a second.

steps.title: Hold it
steps.why:
Envelope 2 holds the radio on while a key is down, so the chattering does the work.
- ATTACK TIME 1.5 (16 ms): envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier, with a very short fade in.
- SUSTAIN 10, DECAY 6 (690 ms): full sustain, so the level never drops while you hold.
- RELEASE TIME 3 (250 ms): a short fade when you let go.
- VOLUME 8.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: a steady wash of chattering static. Raise VCO1 LEVEL while holding and the station comes up through it.

context.hpmod.eg2: How wildly the dial swings, now that the sample and hold is arriving at this knob.
context.mg.freq: How fast the dial is being turned. Slow it right down and you hear each position as a separate squeal.
context.hpf.peak: The whistle. This is the carrier tone you hear as a radio passes a station.
context.mix.vco1: How strong the station is against the static. Turn it up and the radio comes into tune.
context.lpf.cutoff: The top of the band. Lower it for an old valve set, raise it for a cheap transistor radio.

tweaks.hear: The dial turns slowly and each position holds long enough to sound like a station.
The station comes through clearly and the static becomes background — tuned in at last.
The band barely moves: interference on one station rather than a sweep across the dial.
The whistles go and it becomes plain static.

sounds.name: Short Pop Pluck
sounds.ref: In the style of early-80s synth-pop plucked lines
sounds.blurb: A short, woody pluck that stops dead, for lines that need to stay out of the way.
sounds.how: Everything here is in the envelope. Envelope 2 opens the amplifier and the low-pass together, with no sustain and a decay of about a tenth of a second, so the note is over before you have let the key go. The high-pass takes the body out so the pluck reads as wood rather than as a bass note, and FILTER 1 keeps it rounded. A touch of PEAK gives each pluck a pitch of its own on the front.

steps.title: A saw and a square an octave up
steps.why:
A sawtooth with a square an octave above. The saw gives the filter something to work on, and the square puts the click in the top, which the ear hears as the pluck.
- WAVE FORM reverse saw on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. Bright and buzzy, with every harmonic.
- WAVE FORM square, SCALE 4′ on VCO 2: SCALE is the octave switch in organ-pipe feet. Oscillator 2’s range sits an octave above Oscillator 1’s, so 4′ is one octave up.
- PITCH 0.1 (+0.1 st): a hair sharp, just enough to stop the two locking.
- VCO1 LEVEL 7, VCO2 LEVEL 5: the octave sits a little lower.
- Listen for: a bright, organ-like tone for now. The pluck comes from the envelope.

steps.title: Take the weight out
steps.why:
The high-pass takes the low end out so the pluck is light. The low-pass sits part way down with some PEAK, which gives the front of each note a short ringing edge.
- High-pass CUTOFF 3 (95 Hz), PEAK 2.5: the high-pass filter removes the lows below about 95 Hz. At 0 the sound gains a body and turns into a bass. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 4.6 (457 Hz), PEAK 4.8: the low-pass filter cuts the highs, leaving a woody, muted tone. The resonance is the short ring on the front; too much and every pluck becomes a blip.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother circuit, which keeps it rounded.
- Listen for: the tone going dark and hollow.

steps.title: Open and shut
steps.why:
Envelope 2 now sweeps the low-pass open and shut on each note, arriving and going in about a tenth of a second. That fast shut is the whole sound.
- EG2/EXT 4.6 (low-pass): how far envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope generator) lifts the cutoff. It sets how bright the front of each pluck is.
- ATTACK TIME 0 (5 ms), HOLD 0: the envelope reaches full at once, so the brightness lands on the beat.
- DECAY 4 (130 ms), SUSTAIN 0: the length of the pluck, and the most important control here. Past about 5 it becomes a short note. Envelope 2 also runs the VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier), so the note dies on its own.
- Listen for: a woody “tok” on each key. Sweep DECAY from 3 to 6 to hear pluck turn into note.

steps.title: Stop it dead
steps.why:
No sustain means the note ends on its own decay however long the key is held. A very short release stops one pluck running into the next, and glide stays off.
- RELEASE TIME 1.4 (94 ms): if you let go before the decay finishes, the note stops almost at once.
- TIME 0: portamento off, so each pluck starts on its own pitch.
- VOLUME 8.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: play a quick line and hear each note sit apart, leaving space around it.

context.eg2.decay: The length of the pluck, and the single most important control here. Past about 5 it stops being a pluck and becomes a short note.
context.eg2.sustain: At 0 the note dies whatever the key does. Raise it and the pluck grows a tail.
context.lpmod.eg2: How bright the front of each pluck is. This is the attack you hear.
context.hpf.cutoff: How light the pluck is. At 0 it gains a body and turns into a bass.
context.lpf.peak: The short ring on the front of each note. Too much and every pluck becomes a blip.

tweaks.hear: The plucks lengthen and start to overlap into a line.
Each note holds on after the pluck — the same attack on a sustained sound.
A hard blip on the front of every note, closer to a marimba.
The click moves an octave higher: a brighter, more brittle pluck.

sounds.name: Bowed String Line
sounds.ref: In the style of 70s solo string imitations
sounds.blurb: A single bowed string line, with the bow arriving before the tone does.
sounds.how: A string player does two things a synth has to be told to do: the note arrives gradually as the bow takes hold, and it is never quite steady. The first is envelope 2 with a slow attack on both the amplifier and the low-pass, so the note gets louder and brighter together. The second is a small amount of modulation on the pitch, slow enough to read as a player rather than as an effect. Two sawtooths a hair apart give the body.

steps.title: Two sawtooths, barely apart
steps.why:
Two sawtooths, barely apart. Sawtooths hold every harmonic, as a bowed string does, and a small offset gives a slow beat that fills the tone out without sounding like two instruments.
- WAVE FORM reverse saw on both VCOs: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. Bright and buzzy, like a bow on a string.
- SCALE 8′ on both: the same octave on this synth.
- PITCH 0.1 (+0.2 st): Oscillator 2 a fraction of a semitone sharp. A quarter of a semitone is plenty.
- VCO1 LEVEL 7, VCO2 LEVEL 6.5: nearly equal.
- Listen for: a buzzy tone with a slow swirl in it.

steps.title: Thin it from below
steps.why:
A little high-pass takes out weight a solo string does not have, and the low-pass with some PEAK leaves a resonant peak in the middle, where a string body would put one.
- High-pass CUTOFF 2.4 (63 Hz), PEAK 3.4: the high-pass filter removes the lows below about 63 Hz. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost at the cutoff.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 5.4 (788 Hz), PEAK 4.4: the low-pass filter cuts the highs, and the resonance puts a peak near 800 Hz for a woody, nasal body.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother circuit.
- Listen for: the buzz softening into a reedy, woody tone.

steps.title: The bow takes hold
steps.why:
The bow takes hold: the note arrives and brightens together over about a third of a second, rather than switching on.
- ATTACK TIME 5.5 (320 ms): envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier. This is the bow, and what separates a string from an organ; at 0 the patch loses the whole idea.
- EG2/EXT 3.2 (low-pass): the same envelope opens the low-pass, so the tone brightens as the note arrives. Keep it in step with the attack.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 6 (690 ms), SUSTAIN 8: a slight settle after the peak, then a steady level while bowing.
- RELEASE TIME 4.6 (660 ms): the note dies away over about two thirds of a second after you let go.
- Listen for: each note swelling in and getting brighter as it arrives.

steps.title: Never quite steady
steps.why:
A slow triangle on the pitch, kept small, so the note is never quite steady, as with a real player.
- FREQUENCY 5.2 (1.65 Hz), triangle wave: MG, the modulation generator, is Korg’s name for the LFO (low-frequency oscillator). At 1.65 Hz this is slower than a player’s vibrato, which is around 5 to 6 Hz; turn FREQUENCY up to about 7.4 for that.
- MG/T.EXT 1.2 (pitch): the depth, which decides whether it sounds human or seasick. Under about 2 it sounds played; over it, mechanical.
- Listen for: a gentle waver in pitch on long notes.

steps.title: Join the notes up
steps.why:
A short portamento is the finger sliding along the string between notes.
- TIME 1.8: the glide time. Small amounts only: too much and it stops being a string and becomes a theremin.
- VOLUME 8.5: overall output level.
- Listen for: play a slow melody and hear each note slur into the next.

context.eg2.attack: The bow. This is what separates a string from an organ; at 0 the patch loses the whole idea.
context.lpmod.eg2: How much the tone brightens as the note arrives. Keep it in step with the attack.
context.fmod.mg: Vibrato depth. Under about 2 it sounds played; over it, mechanical.
context.mg.freq: The vibrato rate. 5 to 6 Hz is what a player does.
context.vco2.pitch: The slow beat that gives the tone its body. A quarter of a semitone is plenty.
context.porta.time: The slide between notes. Small amounts only.

tweaks.hear: A much slower bow — the line turns into a section swelling rather than one player.
A wide, operatic vibrato.
The body comes back and it moves from violin towards cello.
A stronger resonance in the middle: more nasal, closer to a viola.

sounds.name: Dark Pad that Drifts Sharp
sounds.ref: In the style of Boards of Canada — "Olson"
sounds.blurb: A dull, warm pad with a soft rush of noise behind it, whose pitch creeps very slightly sharp while a note is held.
sounds.how: A triangle and a quiet sawtooth go through a low-pass filter with almost no PEAK, which keeps the tone round. The drift is envelope 1 on the pitch of both oscillators, through the EG1/EXT knob. DELAY TIME makes it wait about a second, the attack then takes several seconds, and the depth is about a sixth of a semitone, so a held note ends up a touch sharp of where it started, like a tape machine that does not quite hold its speed. A cable from the PINK noise socket into EXT SIGNAL IN adds the noise, and because it joins before the filters it is darkened along with the note.

steps.title: A triangle with a quiet sawtooth beside it
steps.why:
The triangle is the softest wave on the panel and carries the note. A little sawtooth at the same octave adds grain, and a tiny PITCH offset makes the pair beat about once a second.
- WAVE FORM triangle on VCO 1: VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator. Soft and round, nearly pure.
- WAVE FORM reverse saw (VCO 2), both 8′: the saw adds buzz. 8′ on both is the same octave on this synth.
- PITCH 0 (+0.1 st): a few cents sharp. More and it starts to sound out of tune.
- VCO1 LEVEL 9, VCO2 LEVEL 3.5: mostly triangle; VCO2 LEVEL sets how much sawtooth grain sits on top.
- Listen for: a soft tone with a slow pulse in it.

steps.title: Keep the filter low and flat
steps.why:
The low-pass sits at about 800 Hz with PEAK nearly off, so nothing rings and the sawtooth loses its buzz. A touch of high-pass takes out the lowest rumble and nothing else.
- Low-pass CUTOFF 5.4 (788 Hz): the low-pass filter cuts the highs. It sets how dark the pad is, and later how loud the noise is, since the noise goes through the same filter.
- PEAK 1: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. Nearly off, so the tone stays round and flat.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the smoother circuit.
- High-pass CUTOFF 1.5 (34 Hz), PEAK 0: the high-pass filter clears only the sub-bass.
- Listen for: a dull, warm tone with no edge.

steps.title: Fade in, fade out
steps.why:
An attack of about a second and a release of about four turn it into a pad. A small amount of envelope 2 on the low-pass makes each note brighten slightly as it arrives.
- ATTACK TIME 7 (970 ms): envelope 2 (EG2, envelope generator) opens the VCA, the voltage-controlled amplifier. About a second to fade in.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 7 (1.6 s), SUSTAIN 8: a slow settle to a steady level.
- RELEASE TIME 7.5 (3.9 s): the fade after you let go, long enough for one note to overlap the start of the next.
- EG2/EXT 2 (low-pass): a little brightness that rises with the fade in.
- VOLUME 7: overall output level.
- Listen for: notes that swell in and hang on long after you let go.

steps.title: Set envelope 1 to arrive late and slowly
steps.why:
Envelope 1 is set to arrive late and slowly. Nothing changes yet, because its depth knob is still at 0.
- DELAY TIME 7.4 (1.1 s): envelope 1 (EG1, the simpler envelope generator) stays at zero for about a second after the key goes down. Notes shorter than this will not drift at all.
- ATTACK TIME 8.5 (4.4 s): the rise then takes over four seconds. The slower it is, the harder it is to notice as a movement.
- RELEASE TIME 7 (2.4 s): how slowly it falls back after you let go.
- Listen for: nothing new. EG1/EXT is still at 0.

steps.title: A very small amount of it on the pitch
steps.why:
EG1/EXT under the VCO mixer sends envelope 1 to the pitch of both oscillators, so a held note creeps slightly sharp, like a tape machine that does not quite hold its speed.
- EG1/EXT 0.8: the whole rise is about a sixth of a semitone: too small to hear as a slide, but enough that a long note does not sit dead still. Past about 2 it becomes an obvious upward slide.
- Listen for: the drift is meant to be hard to hear. Turn EG1/EXT up to 3, hold a note for six seconds and hear it rise, then set it back to 0.8.

steps.title: Noise, through the filters
steps.why:
PINK is the duller of the two noise sockets. Into EXT SIGNAL IN it joins the oscillators before the high-pass filter, so both filters and the amplifier treat it as part of the note.
- PINK → EXT SIGNAL IN: carries pink noise into the filter chain. The low-pass darkens it, and it fades in and out with everything else.
- Listen for: a soft rush behind each note, like tape hiss. Lower the low-pass CUTOFF and the noise gets quieter along with the tone.

context.fmod.eg1: The size of the drift. At 0.8 a held note ends about a sixth of a semitone sharp. Past about 2 it becomes an obvious upward slide.
context.eg1.delay: How long a note stays at its true pitch before the drift begins. Notes shorter than this do not drift at all.
context.eg1.attack: How long the drift takes once it starts. The slower it is, the harder it is to notice as a movement.
context.lpf.cutoff: How dark the pad is, and how loud the noise is, since the noise goes through the same filter.
context.vco2.pitch: The slow beat between the two oscillators. A few cents is enough; more and it starts to sound out of tune.
context.mix.vco2: How much sawtooth grain there is on top of the triangle.
context.eg2.release: The fade after you let go. It is long enough for one note to overlap the start of the next.

tweaks.try: Turn to 0, hold a note, then set it back to 0.8
tweaks.hear: At 0 a long note sits completely still. At 0.8 it leans sharp after a second or two.
The pad brightens and the noise comes forward as a hiss, because both go through the same filter.
The drift starts with the note, so even short notes move.
Only the triangle is left: a plainer, flute-like pad.

sounds.name: Two Filter Tones
sounds.ref: In the style of Biosphere — "Poa Alpina"
sounds.blurb: Two soft, nearly pure tones a fifth apart with no oscillator behind them: a wavering low one that stays put and a steady upper one that follows the keys.
sounds.how: Both filters are used as sound sources. The low-pass has PEAK high enough to whistle on its own, which gives a steady, sine-like tone at its cutoff. The high-pass has PEAK just short of that point, so it only rings when something excites it; a little noise from Oscillator 1’s fourth waveform position keeps it ringing, and because noise is uneven the tone wavers in level. One cable from KBD CV OUT to the low-pass CUTOFF FREQ socket makes the upper tone follow the keys while the lower one holds.

steps.title: Noise instead of an oscillator
steps.why:
Neither tone in this sound comes from an oscillator. Oscillator 1 is turned into a noise source, and noise is what will set the high-pass filter ringing in the next step.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) noise: the fourth position is not a wave. It disconnects Oscillator 1 and puts the noise generator in its place, so from now on VCO1 LEVEL is the noise level.
- VCO1 LEVEL 4, VCO2 LEVEL 0: a modest amount of noise and nothing from Oscillator 2. VCO stands for voltage-controlled oscillator. Kept low, the noise is a trigger for the filter rather than hiss you are meant to hear; more noise would drive the high-pass harder and make the low tone louder and rougher.
- Listen for: play any key and you get plain hiss. The key makes no difference to it yet.

steps.title: Ring the high-pass for the low tone
steps.why:
The high-pass filter (HPF: it removes everything below its cutoff) is set so it almost rings by itself. Fed with noise, it picks out one narrow band and you hear that band as a soft, wavering low note.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 3.2 · 109 Hz: this is the pitch of the low tone. Turn it up and the tone rises; it does not follow the keyboard.
- PEAK (HPF) 9.2: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost right at the cutoff. At 9.2 the filter only rings while the noise excites it, which is why the tone swells and fades. Below about 8.5 it sinks back into filtered hiss; above about 9.2 it whistles on its own, louder and harder.
- Filter type FILTER 1: the gentler of the two circuits. The switch governs both filters.
- Listen for: a hollow, breathy hum around 110 Hz inside the hiss. Nudge PEAK down and hear it dissolve into noise.

steps.title: Let the low-pass whistle for the upper tone
steps.why:
The low-pass filter (LPF: it removes everything above its cutoff) is pushed past the point where it whistles on its own. That whistle is the upper tone, a nearly pure sine a fifth above the low one.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 3.1 · 165 Hz: the pitch of the upper tone when you play middle C. Tune it against the low tone by ear, going by the readout: the two CUTOFF knobs are not scaled alike, so the numbers round the knobs do not line up.
- PEAK (LPF) 9.6: has to stay above about 9 or the upper tone stops, because nothing else is producing it. At this height the low-pass also lets very little else through, which is why the hiss disappears.
- Listen for: the hiss goes and two clean tones are left. Sweep the low-pass CUTOFF slowly and hear the interval go sour and sweet again as it passes the fifth.

steps.title: Open slowly and stay open
steps.why:
Envelope generator 2 (EG2) opens the amplifier on every note, so its shape decides how the drone comes in and goes away. Here it fades in slowly and hangs on.
- ATTACK (EG2) 7 · 970 ms: nearly a second to reach full, so there is no click or bump at the start. Shorter makes the tones start abruptly.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 7 · 1.6 s, SUSTAIN 10: with sustain at full, the decay has nothing to fall to. The level stays at the top for as long as a key is down.
- RELEASE (EG2) 8.5 · 7.2 s: a long fade after you let go.
- VOLUME 9: the tones are quiet by nature, so the output comes up.
- Listen for: play the next key before letting go of the last. The envelope does not start again, so the drone carries on unbroken.

steps.title: Make the upper tone follow the keys
steps.why:
A cable makes the upper tone follow the keyboard, while the low tone stays put. This is what turns two fixed tones into something you can play.
- Cable KBD CV OUT → CUTOFF FREQ (low-pass): KBD CV is the keyboard’s control voltage, the voltage that tells the synth which note is down. Patched into the low-pass CUTOFF FREQ socket, it takes envelope 2’s place at the low-pass EG2/EXT knob.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 3.5: now sets how closely the whistle tracks the keys. About 3.5 gives an octave for an octave; less compresses the intervals, and at 0 it ignores the keyboard.
- TIME 4: portamento, so the upper tone slides between notes rather than jumping. The low tone is not affected.
- Listen for: play a slow line. The upper tone glides over a fixed drone at 110 Hz, like a melody over a pedal note.

steps.title: A very slow drift on the low tone
steps.why:
The modulation generator (MG, Korg’s name for the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator used to move other controls) drifts the low tone very slightly, so the two tones do not sit perfectly still against each other.
- WAVE FORM (MG) 5 · triangle: a smooth, even up-and-down movement with no jumps.
- FREQUENCY 0.6 · 0.14 Hz: one cycle about every seven seconds. Faster turns the drift into an obvious wobble.
- MG/T.EXT (HPF mod) 0.4: moves the high-pass cutoff by roughly a tenth of a semitone either way. Keep it very small; much more and the fifth goes sour.
- Listen for: hold a note for ten seconds or so. The low tone goes very slightly in and out of tune with the upper one, giving a slow beating between them.

context.hpf.peak: At 9.2 the high-pass rings only while the noise excites it, which is what makes the low tone waver. Below about 8.5 the pitch fades into filtered hiss. Above about 9.2 it whistles by itself, much louder and harder, and drowns the upper tone.
context.hpf.cutoff: The pitch of the low tone. It does not follow the keyboard.
context.lpf.peak: Has to stay above about 9 or the upper tone stops. It is the only thing producing it.
context.lpf.cutoff: The pitch of the upper tone when you play middle C. Tune it against the low tone by ear.
context.lpmod.eg2: With the KBD CV cable in place this knob sets how closely the upper tone follows the keys. About 3.5 gives an octave for an octave; at 0 it ignores the keyboard.
context.mix.vco1: The noise level, which here means how hard the high-pass is driven. More noise gives a louder and rougher low tone.
context.porta.time: How slowly the upper tone slides between notes. The low tone is not affected.
context.hpmod.mg: The slow drift of the low tone. Keep it very small or the fifth goes sour.

tweaks.try: Hold middle C and raise slowly from 3.1 to about 3.5
tweaks.hear: The upper tone climbs from a fifth to an octave above the low one. Most positions in between sound out of tune with it.
The low tone loses its pitch and drops back to a faint band of noise under the upper tone.
The low tone gets louder and less even as the filter is driven harder.
The upper tone jumps between notes instead of sliding.

sounds.name: Soft Bell Keys
sounds.ref: In the style of Brian Eno — "1/1"
sounds.blurb: Softly struck notes with a faint bell tone inside them, for slow, widely spaced playing.
sounds.how: The ring modulator is usually the harsh part of this synth. Here it is kept quiet and tuned so that it lands on harmonics. Oscillator 2 sits an octave and a fifth above Oscillator 1, which is three times its frequency, and the sums and differences of the two then fall on whole multiples of the note instead of between them. A triangle carries the note and the ring output adds a small bell tone on top. The low-pass closes as each note dies away, so the bell is heard at the start and the tail is nearly pure.

steps.title: A triangle for the note
steps.why:
A triangle wave carries the note. It is close to a pure tone, soft and round, and it will also be one of the two signals the ring modulator multiplies in the next step.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) Triangle: few harmonics, so it sounds gentle and a little hollow. The reverse sawtooth it replaces is bright and buzzy.
- SCALE (osc 1) 8′: SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, marked in organ-pipe feet. 8′ is normal pitch; 16′ would be an octave lower.
- VCO1 LEVEL 6.5: how much of Oscillator 1 (VCO, voltage-controlled oscillator) goes into the filters. It has to stay up, because the ring modulator needs Oscillator 1 as an input.
- Listen for: a soft, flute-like tone with no edge.

steps.title: Turn Oscillator 2 into the ring modulator, quietly
steps.why:
Oscillator 2 is switched to its RING position, which replaces it with the two oscillators multiplied together. Ring modulation produces the sum and difference of their frequencies, the clangy, metallic part of a bell.
- WAVE FORM (osc 2) RING: from now on Oscillator 2’s mixer channel carries the ring output rather than Oscillator 2 itself. Because Oscillator 1 is one input, turning VCO1 LEVEL down changes the ring tone too.
- VCO2 LEVEL 6.5: how much bell is in the note. Even at 6.5 it sits well behind the triangle, because most of what the ring modulator produces is above the low-pass cutoff once the filter is set.
- Listen for: a clangy, out-of-tune edge on every note. The next step tunes it.

steps.title: Tune it an octave and a fifth up
steps.why:
Oscillator 2 is tuned an octave and a fifth above Oscillator 1, three times its frequency. At that ratio the ring modulator’s sums and differences land on harmonics of the note, so the bell tone sounds in tune.
- SCALE (osc 2) 4′: an octave above Oscillator 1. Oscillator 2’s range sits an octave higher than Oscillator 1’s, so 8′ on both would be the same octave.
- PITCH 2.9 · +7 st: adds the fifth. Small moves either side make the bell tone turn over faster; large moves make it clang. PITCH is never exact, so the bell also turns over slowly.
- Listen for: the clang from the last step becomes a clear bell tone. Move PITCH a little off and back to hear it go from in tune to metallic.

steps.title: A low-pass that closes with the note
steps.why:
The low-pass filter (LPF: it removes everything above its cutoff) closes as each note dies away. The bell tone sits above the resting cutoff, so it is heard at the start and fades before the note does.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 4.6 · 457 Hz: where the tail of the note ends up. Lower is darker, more like a muffled electric piano.
- PEAK (LPF) 1, FILTER 1: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. A touch gives the tail some definition without ringing.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 5.6: envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope generator) lifts the cutoff by about two and a half octaves at the start of each note. More makes the attack brighter.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 1.5 · 34 Hz, PEAK 0: the high-pass sits below the note and only clears out sub-bass.
- Listen for: the bell comes through on the strike, then only the round triangle is left.

steps.title: Struck softly, left to ring
steps.why:
Envelope 2 opens the amplifier on every note. This is the shape of something struck: a soft edge, then a long ring with no held level.
- ATTACK (EG2) 1.2 · 13 ms: takes the click off the front. At 0 each note has a harder edge.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 8 · 3.4 s, SUSTAIN 0: with no sustain, every note dies away by itself over a few seconds, however long the key is held. DECAY sets how long a held note rings.
- RELEASE (EG2) 7 · 2.9 s: long enough that letting go early does not cut the note off.
- VOLUME 9.5: soft tones need the level up.
- Listen for: play slowly, with space between notes. Each one rings out, and the bell tone fades well before the note ends.

context.vco2.pitch: The interval that decides whether the ring modulator sounds in tune. 2.92 is a fifth. Small moves either side make the bell tone turn over faster; large moves make it clang.
context.mix.vco2: How much bell there is in the note. With RING selected this knob is the ring modulator’s level.
context.mix.vco1: The plain triangle. It has to stay up, because the ring modulator needs Oscillator 1 as one of its inputs.
context.lpmod.eg2: How much brighter the start of a note is than its tail. This is what lets the bell tone fade before the note does.
context.lpf.cutoff: Where the tail of the note ends up. Lower is darker and more like a muffled electric piano.
context.eg2.decay: How long a held note rings.
context.eg2.attack: Takes the click off the start. At 0 each note has a harder edge.

tweaks.try: Turn to 0, then back up to 6.5
tweaks.hear: At 0 it is a plain soft triangle. Bringing it up adds the bell tone at the start of each note.
The ring modulator’s tones fall between the harmonics and the note turns into a small, out-of-tune bell.
The bell tone drops an octave and thickens the note instead of sitting above it.
Shorter notes, closer to a music box.

sounds.name: Soft Nylon Pluck
sounds.ref: In the style of Air — "Alone in Kyoto"
sounds.blurb: A rounded pluck with no thump on the front: each note starts thin and fills out as it fades.
sounds.how: Envelope 2 has a depth knob on each filter, and this sound uses both. On the low-pass it does the usual thing: it opens the filter at the start of the note and closes it as the note dies. On the high-pass the same envelope pushes the cutoff up at the start, which takes the low end out of the first moment of the note, and then lets it fall back so the body returns. Each note begins as a narrow band in the middle and ends low and dark.

steps.title: One sawtooth
steps.why:
One sawtooth is the raw material for the pluck. It has the full set of harmonics a plucked string has, which the filters will shape.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) Reverse saw: bright and buzzy, with every harmonic present. It is also the init setting.
- SCALE (osc 1) 8′: normal pitch. SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, marked in organ-pipe feet.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8, VCO2 LEVEL 0: one VCO (voltage-controlled oscillator) only. Two would beat against each other and blur a short note.
- Listen for: a plain, buzzy tone that does not change over time. The next steps give it a shape.

steps.title: Pluck the low-pass
steps.why:
The low-pass filter (LPF: it removes everything above its cutoff) is closed down and set to open at the start of each note. That quick bright-to-dark movement is what the ear hears as a pluck.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 4.4 · 399 Hz: how dark the tail is. Higher gives a brighter, harder note; lower a more muffled one.
- PEAK (LPF) 2, FILTER 1: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. A little gives the pluck definition without making it ring.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 4.4: envelope 2 (EG2) lifts the cutoff by about an octave and a half at the start of each note. More makes the attack brighter.
- Listen for: notes now start brighter than they sustain. The decay is still slow, so the pluck is not sharp yet.

steps.title: Shape the note
steps.why:
Envelope 2 now gets a pluck shape. It drives the amplifier and the low-pass together, so both the level and the brightness fall away.
- ATTACK (EG2) 0.6 · 8 ms: nearly instant, so the note starts on the beat.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 6.6 · 1.1 s, SUSTAIN 0: every note dies away by itself in about a second, however long the key is held. DECAY is the length of the pluck and also how fast the filter closes.
- RELEASE (EG2) 6 · 1.6 s: a little longer than the decay, so short key presses still ring on.
- Listen for: a proper plucked note, bright at the start and darker as it fades. Hold a key and it still dies away.

steps.title: Lift the high-pass at the start
steps.why:
The high-pass filter (HPF: it removes everything below its cutoff) is pushed up at the start of each note by the same envelope. That takes the thump off the front, so notes start thin and fill out as they fade.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 2.4 · 63 Hz: where it comes to rest once the note has decayed. Keep it low or the tail loses its body too.
- PEAK (HPF) 1: barely any resonance, so the rising cutoff does not whistle.
- EG2/EXT (HPF mod) 7: lifts the high-pass by more than three octaves at the start of each note, then lets it fall back. At 0 the pluck has a thump on the front.
- Listen for: turn EG2/EXT (HPF) down to 0 and back to 7. The difference is the low thump at the start of the note, gone at 7.

steps.title: Set the level
steps.why:
With the low end held back at the start, each note carries less energy than a plain pluck, so the output comes up to make up the difference.
- VOLUME 10: full output.
- TIME 0: portamento off, so each note starts on its own pitch instead of sliding from the last. Right for a plucked string.
- Listen for: play a slow, spaced-out figure. Each note should sound rounded, with no thump, and sit at a similar level to the other sounds you use.

context.hpmod.eg2: How much low end is held back from the start of each note. At 0 the pluck has a thump on the front; at 7 it starts thin and fills out.
context.hpf.cutoff: Where the high-pass comes to rest once the note has decayed. Keep it low or the tail loses its body as well.
context.lpmod.eg2: How bright the start of the pluck is.
context.lpf.cutoff: How dark the tail is. This and the low-pass EG2/EXT knob set the whole tone of the pluck.
context.eg2.decay: The length of the pluck. It also sets how fast both filters move, because the same envelope drives them.
context.eg2.release: How long a note rings after a short key press.

tweaks.hear: At 0 every note starts with a low thump. At 7 the thump is gone and the low end arrives a moment later.
A duller pluck, closer to a finger on a bass string.
A short, dry pluck, more like a muted string.
Almost no harmonics for the filters to work on: a soft, round blip.

sounds.name: Waves on a Shore
sounds.ref: In the style of Jean-Michel Jarre — "Oxygène, Pt. 6"
sounds.blurb: Each key press is one wave: a low rush that builds, brightens as it breaks and draws back over several seconds.
sounds.how: Noise through both filters, with envelope 2 doing three jobs at once. It fades the noise in and out at the amplifier. It opens the low-pass, so the hiss gets brighter as the wave builds. And it raises the high-pass, so the low rumble thins out at the top of the wave and comes back as the water draws away. There is no PEAK on either filter, so nothing whistles. A very slow modulation generator moves the low-pass a little, so no two waves come out the same.

steps.title: Noise instead of an oscillator
steps.why:
Noise replaces the oscillator. Waves have no pitch, so noise is the right raw material; the filters and envelope will shape it into surf.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) noise: the fourth position swaps Oscillator 1 for the noise generator, so VCO1 LEVEL becomes the noise level.
- VCO1 LEVEL 10, VCO2 LEVEL 0: full noise, nothing from Oscillator 2 (VCO means voltage-controlled oscillator).
- Listen for: bright hiss. Which key you press makes no difference, because noise has no pitch and neither filter follows the keyboard.

steps.title: Start dark, with no PEAK
steps.why:
Both filters are set to leave a low rush with no resonance. The low-pass (LPF) cuts the highs and the high-pass (HPF) cuts the lowest rumble.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 4.8 · 524 Hz: how dark the water is between waves. The envelope will open it from here.
- PEAK (LPF) 0.5 and PEAK (HPF) 0: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. Keep both near 0; resonance puts a pitch into the noise and it starts to sound like wind, and water does not whistle.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 3 · 95 Hz: trims the deepest rumble so the rush does not turn to mud.
- FILTER 1: the gentler filter circuit.
- Listen for: the bright hiss becomes a soft, low rush.

steps.title: A slow rise and a slower fall
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope generator) opens the amplifier, so its shape is the shape of each wave: a slow build, a settle and a long draw-back.
- ATTACK (EG2) 7.4 · 1.3 s: how long a wave takes to build. Shorter sounds like a breaker; longer, a slow swell.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 7 · 1.6 s, SUSTAIN 4: after the peak the level settles to under half if you keep holding the key.
- RELEASE (EG2) 7.6 · 4.2 s: how long the water draws back after you let go. This is most of what you hear.
- VOLUME 10: full output.
- Listen for: hold a key for a couple of seconds, then let go. The release is the water drawing back.

steps.title: Brighter as it builds
steps.why:
The low-pass is opened by the envelope, so the wave gets brighter as it builds and duller as it fades, as surf does when it breaks.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 6: opens the filter by nearly three octaves at the top of the envelope. At 0 the wave only gets louder, not brighter; higher makes the break hiss more.
- Listen for: a hiss at the peak of each wave that goes dull again as it fades. Turn the knob to 0 and back to compare.

steps.title: Thinner at the top
steps.why:
The same envelope raises the high-pass at the same moment. The low rumble drops out at the top of the wave and returns as it falls, which is the heavy-then-light movement of water breaking.
- EG2/EXT (HPF mod) 5: raises the high-pass by nearly two octaves at the envelope peak. At 0 the wave stays heavy all the way through; more thins the top of the wave further.
- Listen for: the low end thins out just as the wave hisses brightest, then comes back underneath as the water draws away.

steps.title: No two waves the same
steps.why:
The modulation generator (MG, Korg’s name for the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator that moves other controls) nudges the low-pass very slowly, so each wave catches the filter at a different point.
- WAVE FORM (MG) 5 · triangle: a smooth, even rise and fall.
- FREQUENCY 0.6 · 0.14 Hz: one cycle about every seven seconds, slower than the waves themselves.
- MG/T.EXT (LPF mod) 2.4: moves the low-pass by about a third of an octave either way. More makes the difference between waves obvious.
- Listen for: play a wave every few seconds. Some come out brighter than others, so the sea never repeats exactly.

context.eg2.attack: How long a wave takes to build. Shorter and it sounds like a breaker; longer and it is a slow swell.
context.eg2.release: How long the water takes to draw back after you let go. This is most of what you hear.
context.eg2.sustain: The level a wave settles to if you keep holding the key.
context.lpmod.eg2: How much the wave brightens at its top.
context.hpmod.eg2: How much low rumble is removed at the top of the wave. At 0 the wave stays heavy all the way through.
context.lpf.cutoff: How dark the water is between waves.
context.lpf.peak: Keep it near 0. Resonance puts a pitch into the noise and it starts to sound like wind.
context.lpmod.mg: The difference between one wave and the next.

tweaks.hear: The waves keep their low rumble at the top and sound bigger and nearer.
Each wave arrives quickly, like a breaker hitting the beach.
A pitch appears in the hiss and the sea turns into wind.
A heavier, more distant sea.

sounds.name: Rain on a Window
sounds.ref: In the style of Burial — "Archangel"
sounds.blurb: A quiet, uneven patter of noise that fades in while you hold a key and fades out when you let go.
sounds.how: Rain is a great many small bursts of noise, none as loud as the last. The sample and hold supplies the unevenness. Clocked about 17 times a second, it takes a new random reading on every tick, and that reading goes to INITIAL GAIN, where it opens the amplifier by a different amount each time. The readings go below zero as often as above it, and a low one shuts the amplifier, so a good share of the ticks are gaps. On the way the readings pass through the patch-panel VCA, with envelope 1 on its CONTROL INPUT, so the patter fades in and out with the key instead of running all the time.

steps.title: Noise instead of an oscillator
steps.why:
Noise is the raw material for rain. Oscillator 1 is swapped for the noise generator; the patch panel will later break that noise into uneven bursts.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) noise: the fourth position is not a wave. It disconnects Oscillator 1 (a VCO, voltage-controlled oscillator) and puts the noise generator in its place, so VCO1 LEVEL becomes the noise level.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8, VCO2 LEVEL 0: plenty of noise and nothing from Oscillator 2.
- Listen for: a plain, bright hiss. The key you press makes no difference to it.

steps.title: Keep only the middle and top
steps.why:
Rain on glass has no low end, so the filters keep only the middle and top of the noise.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 5.4 · 500 Hz: the high-pass filter (HPF) removes everything below its cutoff. At 500 Hz the rumble goes; lower it and the rain sounds heavier and nearer.
- PEAK (HPF) 3: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. A little puts a slight pitch on each burst, which later reads as the tick of a drop landing.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 7.6 · 3.5 kHz, PEAK 1: the low-pass filter (LPF) removes everything above its cutoff. Here it takes the harshest hiss off the top; higher is brighter rain.
- FILTER 1: the gentler of the two filter circuits.
- Listen for: the hiss thins out into a lighter, mid-range spray.

steps.title: A faint hiss to start from
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope, which opens the amplifier on every note) is set to fade in slowly to a low level. On its own that is a faint, steady hiss for the random voltage to push around.
- ATTACK (EG2) 7 · 970 ms: about a second to fade in.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 5 · 300 ms, SUSTAIN 2: the level settles low. Once the random voltage arrives in the last step it pushes the amplifier above and below this level, so SUSTAIN ends up deciding how many ticks are silent. Higher gives denser, more even rain; at 0 about half are gaps.
- RELEASE (EG2) 7 · 2.9 s: a slow fade after you let go.
- VOLUME 9: output up, as the sound is quiet.
- Listen for: hold a key and a soft hiss fades in and stays.

steps.title: Clock the sample and hold quickly
steps.why:
The sample and hold (S&H) takes a reading of its input each time it is clocked and holds it until the next one. With nothing in its S&H IN socket it reads noise, so every tick is a new random voltage.
- Cable MG OUT (pulse) → CLOCK: the modulation generator (MG, Korg’s name for the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator) sends its pulse output to CLOCK, telling the sample and hold when to take a reading.
- FREQUENCY 9.5 · 17 Hz: about 17 readings a second, which becomes the number of drops a second. Slower and the drops turn into separate, longer bursts.
- WAVE FORM (MG) 5 · triangle: at the middle position the pulse output is a square, an even on-off clock.
- Listen for: nothing changes yet. The random voltage is not going anywhere audible.

steps.title: Send the readings through the patch-panel VCA
steps.why:
The random readings are routed through the spare VCA on the patch panel. VCA stands for voltage-controlled amplifier: something that sets how much of a signal gets through.
- Cable S&H OUT → VCA IN: the stepped random voltage goes into the VCA’s input. It is there so that something else, envelope 1 in the next step, can decide how much of it gets out.
- Listen for: still no change. The VCA’s output is not patched anywhere yet.

steps.title: Envelope 1 opens the VCA while a key is held
steps.why:
Envelope 1 (EG1) opens the patch-panel VCA while a key is held, so the patter fades in and out with the key instead of running all the time.
- Cable EG 1 OUT → CONTROL INPUT: envelope 1’s voltage sets the VCA’s gain, so the random voltage gets through in proportion.
- DELAY TIME 0: envelope 1 starts rising the moment a key goes down.
- ATTACK (EG1) 7 · 1.2 s: how quickly the patter builds up. Shorter makes the rain start at once.
- RELEASE (EG1) 7.5 · 3.3 s: how long the patter takes to die away after you let go.
- Listen for: nothing new until the last cable goes in.

steps.title: Out to INITIAL GAIN
steps.why:
The last cable sends the random voltage to the amplifier, where it chops the hiss into drops.
- Cable VCA OUT → INITIAL GAIN: INITIAL GAIN adds a voltage to envelope 2 at the main amplifier. Each reading above zero opens it further until the next tick, which is one burst of noise. Each reading below zero takes away from envelope 2, and when the total falls below zero the amplifier shuts, which leaves a gap.
- Listen for: hold a key. An uneven patter builds over about a second and dies away over a few seconds when you let go. Turn FREQUENCY down to hear the drops separate; raise SUSTAIN LEVEL and the gaps fill in.

context.mg.freq: How many drops a second, because the modulation generator clocks the sample and hold. Slower and the drops become separate, longer bursts.
context.eg2.sustain: The level the random voltage pushes up and down from. Higher and fewer ticks fall silent, so the rain is denser and more even; at 0 about half of them are gaps.
context.hpf.cutoff: How much low end is removed. Lower it and the rain sounds heavier and nearer.
context.hpf.peak: Puts a slight pitch on each burst, which reads as the tick of a drop landing.
context.lpf.cutoff: How bright the rain is.
context.eg1.attack: How quickly the patter builds up after the key goes down.
context.eg1.release: How long the patter takes to die away after you let go.

tweaks.hear: Fewer, longer bursts: heavy drops from a gutter rather than fine rain.
Most of the gaps fill in and the patter becomes a steady, uneven hiss: heavier rain.
The low end comes back and the rain sounds heavier, as if on a roof.
Each burst takes on a pitch and the rain starts to sound like it is landing in water.

sounds.name: Overtone Steps
sounds.ref: In the style of Cluster & Eno — "Ho Renomo"
sounds.blurb: One held low note whose overtones are picked out one after another, climbing in slow, even steps.
sounds.how: A sawtooth contains a whole series of overtones above the note you play, and a resonant low-pass brings out whichever one sits at its cutoff. Move the cutoff in steps and you hear those overtones one at a time, as a slow arpeggio. The steps come from the sample and hold reading envelope 1 instead of noise. Envelope 1 rises smoothly over several seconds, the modulation generator’s pulse output tells the sample and hold when to take a reading, and the staircase that results goes to the low-pass CUTOFF FREQ socket.

steps.title: One low sawtooth
steps.why:
One low sawtooth is the source. A sawtooth contains the whole series of overtones above the note, and the lower the note, the closer together they sit and the more of them the filter can step through.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) Reverse saw: every harmonic present, which is what gives the filter something to pick out.
- SCALE (osc 1) 8′: SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, marked in organ-pipe feet. Play low on the keyboard for the most steps.
- VCO1 LEVEL 6, VCO2 LEVEL 0: one VCO (voltage-controlled oscillator) only. A second one would put its own overtones in between and muddy the steps.
- Listen for: a bright, buzzy low note.

steps.title: A resonant low-pass, starting low
steps.why:
A resonant low-pass filter (LPF: it removes everything above its cutoff) is set to pick out one overtone at a time.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 3 · 154 Hz: where the staircase starts, near the second overtone of a low C.
- PEAK (LPF) 7.8: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. At 7.8 it lifts one overtone clear of the rest without whistling by itself. Below about 5 the steps are only changes in brightness; above about 9 the filter sings its own pitch and stops following the overtones.
- FILTER 1: the smoother of the two circuits at high PEAK.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 2.8 · 83 Hz, PEAK 0: the high-pass (HPF) trims the fundamental so the overtones are easier to hear. At 0 the low note is as loud as the overtone.
- Listen for: a dark note with one ringing, whistly partial.

steps.title: Hold the note
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope that opens the amplifier) holds the note for as long as the filter moves.
- ATTACK (EG2) 5 · 220 ms: a short fade in rather than a hard start.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 6 · 690 ms, SUSTAIN 10: full sustain, so the decay has nothing to fall to and the note stays at full level while the key is down.
- RELEASE (EG2) 7.5 · 3.9 s: the note keeps sounding as the steps come back down after you let go.
- VOLUME 7: resonance this high makes the filter loud, so the volume stays moderate.
- Listen for: a steady, sustained note that fades out slowly on release.

steps.title: A slow ramp from envelope 1
steps.why:
Envelope 1 (EG1) is set up as a slow ramp. It will be sampled into steps, but nothing is listening to it yet.
- DELAY TIME 0: the ramp starts as soon as the key goes down.
- ATTACK (EG1) 8.8 · 5.7 s: about six seconds to climb. This is how long the staircase takes; with the step speed it sets how many steps there are and how big each one is.
- RELEASE (EG1) 8 · 4.6 s: about four seconds to come back down after you let go.
- EG1/EXT 0: keeps envelope 1 off the oscillator pitch, so the note itself does not bend.
- Listen for: no change yet.

steps.title: Sample the ramp
steps.why:
The sample and hold (S&H) reads the ramp at regular ticks and holds each reading, turning a smooth rise into a staircase.
- Cable EG 1 OUT → S&H IN: replaces the noise the sample and hold normally reads, so the readings climb in order instead of jumping at random.
- Cable MG OUT (pulse) → CLOCK: the modulation generator (MG, Korg’s name for the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator) tells the sample and hold when to read.
- FREQUENCY 6 · 2.54 Hz: about two and a half steps a second. Faster gives more, smaller steps.
- WAVE FORM (MG) 5 · triangle: the pulse output is an even square at this position.
- Listen for: still no change. The staircase is not patched anywhere yet.

steps.title: Staircase to the low-pass
steps.why:
The staircase goes to the low-pass cutoff, so the filter climbs through the overtones one at a time, like a slow arpeggio played by one note.
- Cable S&H OUT → CUTOFF FREQ (low-pass): takes envelope 2’s place at the low-pass EG2/EXT knob.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 6: now sets how high the staircase reaches, about three octaves at 6. Less keeps the climb in the lower overtones.
- Listen for: hold a low note. Distinct overtones ring out in turn, climbing over about six seconds, then step back down after you let go. Change FREQUENCY to hear the steps get shorter or longer.

context.mg.freq: The speed of the steps, because the modulation generator clocks the sample and hold.
context.eg1.attack: How long the climb takes. Together with the step speed it decides how many steps there are and how big each one is.
context.eg1.release: How long the steps take to come back down after you let go.
context.lpmod.eg2: How high the staircase reaches, because the CUTOFF FREQ cable replaced envelope 2 at this knob.
context.lpf.peak: How clearly each overtone stands out. Below about 5 the steps are only changes in brightness; above about 9 the filter whistles by itself and stops following the overtones.
context.lpf.cutoff: Where the staircase starts.
context.hpf.cutoff: How much of the fundamental is left under the overtones. Raise it and the low note recedes; at 0 it is as loud as the overtone being picked out.
context.out.volume: Resonance this high makes the filter loud, so the volume comes down to keep it soft.

tweaks.hear: About one step a second, each overtone held long enough to hear as a note.
The separate overtones merge into a filter that opens in small jumps.
The climb takes just over a second: a quick run up the overtones and then a held top.

tweaks.try: Switch to pulse and set PW to 0
tweaks.hear: A square-ish wave has only every other overtone, so the steps are wider apart and some land on nothing.

sounds.name: Muted Cello with Late Vibrato
sounds.ref: In the style of Goldfrapp — "Pilots"
sounds.blurb: A dark, low string line where long notes start plain and the vibrato arrives about a second in.
sounds.how: String players rarely start a note with vibrato: they add it once the note has settled. The front panel cannot do that, because the MG/T.EXT knob applies the modulation generator all the time. Three cables fix it. The modulation generator goes through the patch-panel VCA, envelope 1 opens that VCA after its DELAY TIME, and the VCA’s output goes to TOTAL, where it takes the modulation generator’s place at the MG/T.EXT knobs. Short notes get no vibrato at all and long ones have it fade in.

steps.title: Two low sawtooths, barely apart
steps.why:
Two sawtooths in the same low octave, a few cents apart, give the width of a bowed string. The slight detune makes them beat slowly against each other.
- WAVE FORM (both) Reverse saw: bright and full of harmonics, like a bowed string before the body colours it.
- SCALE 16′ on both: SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet. Oscillator 2’s range sits an octave higher, so its 16′ is its lowest setting; here both land in the cello register.
- PITCH 0.1 · +0.1 st: a few cents sharp on Oscillator 2. Wider turns the slow beat into a fast chorus.
- VCO1 LEVEL 7, VCO2 LEVEL 6: both oscillators (VCOs, voltage-controlled oscillators) in, the second a little lower.
- Listen for: a slow, even swirl on a held note.

steps.title: Dark, as if muted
steps.why:
The filters make the string dark and muted.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 4.6 · 457 Hz: the low-pass filter (LPF) cuts everything above its cutoff. About 450 Hz is much lower than for an open string. Raise it for a brighter, open cello.
- PEAK (LPF) 3.5: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. A little adds a bump where the body of the instrument would resonate.
- FILTER 1: the gentler filter circuit.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 2 · 48 Hz, PEAK 2: the high-pass filter (HPF) trims the lowest end, so low notes do not boom.
- Listen for: the buzz goes and a woody, muffled tone is left.

steps.title: A slow bow
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope) opens the amplifier and, through its depth knob, the low-pass too, so each note swells like a bow taking hold of the string.
- ATTACK (EG2) 5.8 · 400 ms: the bow taking hold. Shorter gives a firmer start.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 6.5 · 1.1 s, SUSTAIN 8: a little ease-off after the swell, then a steady held level.
- RELEASE (EG2) 5.5 · 1.2 s: notes die away rather than stopping.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 3: the same envelope opens the low-pass a little, so notes get brighter as they get louder.
- TIME 1.5: a short portamento slide, like a finger shifting position.
- VOLUME 8.
- Listen for: each note grows into its full tone rather than starting at it.

steps.title: Modulation generator into the patch-panel VCA
steps.why:
The modulation generator (MG, Korg’s name for the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator) will make the vibrato. It is sent into the patch-panel VCA rather than straight to pitch, so that something else can decide when it arrives.
- WAVE FORM (MG) 5 · triangle: a smooth up-and-down, right for vibrato.
- FREQUENCY 7.4 · 5.41 Hz: vibrato rate. 5 to 6 Hz is what a player does.
- Cable MG OUT (triangle) → VCA IN: the spare VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) on the patch panel sets how much of the wobble gets through.
- Listen for: no change yet. The VCA’s output is not patched anywhere.

steps.title: Envelope 1 opens the VCA, late
steps.why:
Envelope 1 (EG1) opens the VCA late, so the vibrato only gets through once a note has been held.
- Cable EG 1 OUT → CONTROL INPUT: envelope 1’s voltage sets how far the VCA is open.
- DELAY TIME 6.6 · 640 ms: how long each note stays plain before the vibrato starts to arrive. Notes shorter than this get none.
- ATTACK (EG1) 6.6 · 860 ms: the vibrato then fades up over most of a second. Shorter makes it switch on abruptly.
- RELEASE (EG1) 3 · 200 ms: it goes away quickly after you let go.
- Listen for: still no change until the last cable.

steps.title: VCA out to TOTAL
steps.why:
The VCA output goes to TOTAL, and the vibrato now reaches the pitch.
- Cable VCA OUT → TOTAL: a cable in TOTAL replaces the modulation generator at every MG/T.EXT knob. Only the pitch one is turned up, so the delayed vibrato reaches the oscillators and nothing else.
- MG/T.EXT (pitch) 1.4: vibrato depth. Under about 2 it sounds played; more becomes a wobble.
- Listen for: play short notes and long ones. Short notes stay plain; on long ones the pitch starts to waver about a second in, as a cellist adds vibrato once the note has settled.

context.eg1.delay: How long each note stays plain before the vibrato starts to arrive. Notes shorter than this get none.
context.eg1.attack: How gradually the vibrato fades up once the delay is over.
context.fmod.mg: Vibrato depth, fed from the TOTAL socket rather than straight from the modulation generator. Under about 2 it sounds played.
context.mg.freq: Vibrato rate. 5 to 6 Hz is what a player does.
context.lpf.cutoff: How muted the string is. Raise it for an open, brighter cello.
context.eg2.attack: The bow taking hold. Shorter for a firmer start to each note.
context.vco2.pitch: The slow beat between the two oscillators that gives the tone its width.

tweaks.hear: The vibrato starts with the note. Compare it with the delayed version on the long notes.
A wide vibrato, still arriving late.
The mute comes off and the tone opens up.
The same delayed wobble now moves the high-pass too, because TOTAL feeds every MG/T.EXT knob.

sounds.name: Saxophone Solo Line
sounds.ref: In the style of a solo tenor saxophone
sounds.blurb: A reedy solo voice with grit in the body, where the vibrato only arrives once a note has been held.
sounds.how: A sawtooth and a narrow pulse a few cents apart give the two-tone rasp of a reed. Both mixer levels are high and FILTER 2 is selected, so the filter input is driven into distortion — that is the grit. The high-pass takes the weight out from below and the low-pass leaves a resonant peak around the middle of the range, which is where a saxophone body resonates. Three cables handle the vibrato: the modulation generator goes through the patch-panel VCA, envelope 1 opens that VCA half a second after each note starts, and the VCA output goes to TOTAL, where it takes the modulation generator’s place at the MG/T.EXT knobs. Short notes stay plain; long ones start to waver.

steps.title: Sawtooth against a narrow pulse
steps.why:
A sawtooth and a narrow pulse a few cents apart give the two-tone rasp of a reed.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) Reverse saw: the full set of harmonics, the body of the tone.
- WAVE FORM (osc 2) npulse: a narrow pulse, thin and reedy, adds the edge on top.
- SCALE 8′ on both: SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet. Oscillator 2’s range sits an octave higher, but 8′ means the same octave on both.
- PITCH 0.1 · +0.2 st: a few cents apart, so they beat slowly and do not sound like one oscillator. Past about 0.3 it turns into two instruments.
- VCO1 LEVEL 7.5, VCO2 LEVEL 5: both VCOs (voltage-controlled oscillators) well up, which matters for the grit in the next step.
- Listen for: a buzzy, slightly nasal tone with a slow shimmer.

steps.title: Drive the filters and squeeze a band out
steps.why:
The filters squeeze the tone into a band and FILTER 2 roughs it up.
- FILTER 2: the more aggressive circuit, governing both filters. It distorts sooner, and with both mixer levels this high the filter input is driven into grit.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 4.1 · 204 Hz, PEAK 3: the high-pass filter (HPF) takes the weight out from below, so the line sits like a solo instrument rather than a pad.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 6.3 · 1.5 kHz: the low-pass (LPF) sets the top of the band. Towards 5 gives a soft subtone; past 7 a hard, honking top.
- PEAK (LPF) 5: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. Around 5 it gives a reedy band roughly where a sax body resonates; past 7 it whistles.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 1.8: envelope 2 brightens the start of each note a little.
- Listen for: a honky, gritty mid-range tone.

steps.title: Let each note speak, then hold
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope that opens the amplifier) shapes each note like a breath through a reed.
- ATTACK (EG2) 2.4 · 32 ms: a reed takes about thirty milliseconds to speak. At 0 it starts like a switch.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 5 · 300 ms, SUSTAIN 9.5: near-full sustain keeps the line going while the key is down.
- RELEASE (EG2) 2.2 · 150 ms: the note stops soon after the key comes up, like a player stopping the breath.
- TIME 1.1: a short portamento slide, so slurred phrases join up instead of stepping.
- VOLUME 7.
- Listen for: play legato. Notes speak softly at the front and glide into each other.

steps.title: Modulation generator into the patch-panel VCA
steps.why:
The modulation generator (MG, Korg’s name for the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator) will provide vibrato. It goes into the patch-panel VCA first, so that something else can decide how much of it gets through, and when.
- WAVE FORM (MG) 5 · triangle: a smooth up-and-down, right for vibrato.
- FREQUENCY 7.3 · 5.13 Hz: about 5 Hz is a player’s vibrato rate.
- Cable MG OUT (triangle) → VCA IN: into the spare VCA (voltage-controlled amplifier) on the patch panel, not straight to pitch.
- Listen for: no change yet.

steps.title: Envelope 1 opens the VCA, late
steps.why:
Envelope 1 (EG1) opens the VCA half a second into each note.
- Cable EG 1 OUT → CONTROL INPUT: envelope 1’s voltage sets how much of the vibrato gets through the VCA.
- DELAY TIME 6.2 · 500 ms: how long a note stays plain before the vibrato starts to come in. Notes shorter than this get none.
- ATTACK (EG1) 6 · 520 ms: it then fades up over the next half second.
- RELEASE (EG1) 3 · 200 ms: gone quickly once you let go.
- Listen for: still nothing until the VCA output is patched.

steps.title: VCA out to TOTAL
steps.why:
The VCA output goes to TOTAL, and the late vibrato reaches the pitch.
- Cable VCA OUT → TOTAL: a cable in TOTAL puts the VCA output in the modulation generator’s place at every MG/T.EXT knob. Only the pitch one is up, so nothing else moves.
- MG/T.EXT (pitch) 1.6: vibrato depth. Under about 2 sounds played. The mod wheel turns this knob further, so pushing it part-way through a note deepens the vibrato.
- Listen for: short notes stay plain; long ones start to waver after about half a second, the way a player leans into a held note.

context.lpf.type: FILTER 2 is where the grit comes from: it distorts sooner, and both mixer levels are high enough to make it do so.
context.lpf.cutoff: The top of the band and the main tone control. Down towards 5 gives a soft, low-register subtone; up past 7 gives a hard, honking top.
context.lpf.peak: The emphasis that stands in for the body resonance. Around 5 is reedy; past 7 it starts to whistle instead.
context.hpf.cutoff: Takes the weight out from below so the line sits like a solo instrument rather than a synth pad.
context.eg2.attack: How long each note takes to speak. Around thirty milliseconds reads as a reed; at 0 it reads as a switch.
context.vco2.pitch: The beat between the two oscillators. Very small offsets thicken the tone; past about 0.3 it turns into two instruments.
context.eg1.delay: How long a note stays plain before the vibrato starts to come in. Notes shorter than this get none at all.
context.fmod.mg: Vibrato depth, fed from TOTAL rather than straight from the modulation generator. Under about 2 it sounds played. The mod wheel turns this knob further, so the vibrato comes in when you push the wheel part-way through a note.
context.porta.time: A short slide between notes, so a slurred phrase joins up instead of stepping.

tweaks.hear: The vibrato starts with every note, including the short ones. Put it back and compare the long notes.

tweaks.try: Move between 5 and 7.5 as the line plays
tweaks.hear: From a soft low-register tone to a hard, bright top — this is the knob to ride by hand.
The narrow pulse goes and the reedy edge with it. What is left is an ordinary sawtooth lead.
The grit backs off and the tone turns polite — closer to a soft alto than a driven tenor.

sounds.name: Open Trumpet Line
sounds.ref: In the style of a solo open trumpet
sounds.blurb: A bright sawtooth line where every note opens up over its first fraction of a second, the way a lip takes hold.
sounds.how: A trumpet does not start bright. The lip takes a moment to settle and the tone opens as it does, so the whole patch is one sawtooth with envelope 2 opening the low-pass at the same time as it raises the loudness. The attack is set at about sixty milliseconds, which is long enough to hear the tone bloom rather than snap. The high-pass takes out the low weight a sawtooth has and a trumpet does not. No cables.

steps.title: One sawtooth, with a second behind it
steps.why:
A sawtooth is the raw material for brass: it has every harmonic, which the filter needs to work with. A second sawtooth a few cents away fills the tone out without changing the note.
- WAVE FORM Reverse saw on both: bright and buzzy.
- SCALE 8′ on both: SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet. 8′ is the same octave on both oscillators.
- PITCH 0.1 · +0.1 st: Oscillator 2 a few cents sharp, so the two beat slowly and the tone gets thicker.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8, VCO2 LEVEL 4: the first VCO (voltage-controlled oscillator) leads and the second sits behind it as body. Bring VCO2 up and the detune becomes more obvious.
- Listen for: a full, slightly moving buzz.

steps.title: Take the weight out and close the top
steps.why:
The filters take out the weight a sawtooth has and a trumpet has not, and close the top so the note has somewhere to open to.
- FILTER 1: the gentler of the two circuits; the switch covers both filters.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 3.2 · 109 Hz, PEAK 2: the high-pass filter (HPF) removes everything below its cutoff. At about 110 Hz it takes out the bottom a brass instrument does not have.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 5.6 · 902 Hz: the low-pass filter (LPF) removes everything above. Fairly closed, so the envelope can open it. This is also where the note rests, and the main control of how loud the line reads.
- PEAK (LPF) 4.2: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. A little emphasis gives the note an edge as it opens.
- Listen for: a darker, leaner tone with less low end.

steps.title: Bloom it open on every note
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope) raises the loudness and the low-pass cutoff together over about sixty milliseconds. That bloom is the whole sound: the note arrives dull and brightens as the lip takes hold.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 4.2: the size of the bloom. At 0 every note starts at full brightness and the brass goes; past about 6 it turns into a filter sweep.
- ATTACK (EG2) 3.2 · 58 ms: long enough to hear the tone bloom rather than snap. At 0 the note is simply switched on.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 3.2 · 70 ms, SUSTAIN 8.5: a quick settle to near full, so held notes keep their strength.
- RELEASE (EG2) 2 · 140 ms: short, so the line stops when the playing does.
- Listen for: each note opens up just after you press the key. Set the EG2/EXT knob to 0 to hear the difference.

steps.title: Join the notes up
steps.why:
The last touches join the notes and add a little life to the pitch.
- TIME 1: portamento, a slide of about fifty milliseconds between notes. Enough to join a slurred phrase without a swoop.
- WAVE FORM (MG) 5 · triangle, FREQUENCY 7.4 · 5.41 Hz: the modulation generator (MG, Korg’s name for the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator) moving smoothly at about five cycles a second, a player’s vibrato rate.
- MG/T.EXT (pitch) 0.9: a small waver on the pitch. Keep it under about 1.5 or it stops sounding like a player. The mod wheel turns this knob further, so you can push vibrato in part-way through a note.
- VOLUME 7.5.
- Listen for: play a legato phrase; the notes glide briefly and long ones carry a faint waver.

context.lpmod.eg2: The size of the bloom. At 0 every note starts at full brightness and the brass character goes; past about 6 it turns into a filter sweep instead.
context.eg2.attack: How long the bloom takes. Sixty milliseconds is a lip taking hold; at 0 the note is simply switched on.
context.lpf.cutoff: Where the note rests once it has opened. This is the main control of how loud the line reads.
context.lpf.peak: A little emphasis at the top of the bloom gives the note an edge as it opens.
context.hpf.cutoff: Takes out the low end a sawtooth has and a trumpet has not.
context.eg2.sustain: Near full, so a held note keeps going at strength rather than fading under the player.
context.fmod.mg: A small waver on the pitch. Keep it under about 1.5 or it stops sounding like a player. The mod wheel turns this knob further, so the vibrato comes in when you push the wheel part-way through a note.

tweaks.try: Move between 2 and 6 while the line plays
tweaks.hear: From a flat, even tone to a strong swell on the front of every note.
The bloom goes and the line sounds switched on rather than played.
A harder, more piercing trumpet, closer to a lead line than a solo.
The body drains away and what is left is a thin, distant, muted trumpet.

sounds.name: Hollow Clarinet
sounds.ref: In the style of a solo clarinet in its low register
sounds.blurb: A dark, woody solo voice built from one square wave and almost nothing else.
sounds.how: A clarinet is a pipe stopped at one end, so it makes mostly odd harmonics — and that is exactly what a square wave is. One oscillator at close to fifty per cent pulse width, a low-pass sitting at about 840 Hz, and no filter envelope worth speaking of. Almost everything else is switched off. The work is all in leaving things alone: no second oscillator, no resonance to speak of, and a filter that does not move.

steps.title: One square wave, on its own
steps.why:
A clarinet is a pipe stopped at one end, so it makes mostly odd harmonics, which is exactly what a square wave is. One oscillator does the whole job.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) Pulse, PW 0.8: PW is pulse width. At 0 the wave is an exact square, the most hollow; nudged to 0.8 it is just off symmetrical, which stops it sounding like a test tone. Past about 3 the even harmonics come in and it turns nasal, more oboe than clarinet.
- SCALE (osc 1) 8′: SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8.5, VCO2 LEVEL 0: one VCO (voltage-controlled oscillator) only. Oscillator 2’s wave is set to Square, but its level is at 0 so it is not heard.
- Listen for: a hollow, woody buzz.

steps.title: Dark, and barely resonant
steps.why:
The low-pass filter (LPF: it removes everything above its cutoff) keeps the upper odd harmonics down, which is what makes the low register woody rather than buzzy.
- FILTER 1: the gentler circuit.
