- CUTOFF (LPF) 5.5 · 843 Hz: how woody or buzzy. Around 5.5 is the low register; raise it towards 7 for the brighter upper register.
- PEAK (LPF) 2.2: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. Only a trace: a clarinet has no strong resonance to imitate, and more makes it read as a synth straight away.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 2.2 · 55 Hz, PEAK 0: the high-pass filter (HPF) only clears out sub-bass.
- Listen for: the buzz rounds off into a dark, reedy tone.

steps.title: Leave the filter alone
steps.why:
Almost every synth patch sweeps the filter on each note; a clarinet does not change colour as it speaks. So envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope) is used for loudness only.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 0.6: kept almost at 0 on purpose. More and each note brightens as it starts, which no clarinet does.
- ATTACK (EG2) 2.8 · 43 ms: about forty milliseconds, how long a reed takes to start. At 0 notes click on.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 5 · 300 ms, SUSTAIN 9.5: near-full sustain, so held notes keep their strength.
- RELEASE (EG2) 2 · 140 ms: stops soon after the key comes up, like a breath ending.
- Listen for: notes start softly with no change in tone. Turn EG2/EXT up to 5 to hear how synth-like a filter sweep makes it.

steps.title: Join the notes and steady the pitch
steps.why:
A short slide and a very small waver finish the line.
- TIME 1: portamento, so slurred notes join up.
- WAVE FORM (MG) 5 · triangle, FREQUENCY 7.2 · 4.86 Hz: the modulation generator (MG, Korg’s name for the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator) moving smoothly at about five cycles a second.
- MG/T.EXT (pitch) 0.8: vibrato depth, kept very small. Clarinet players use far less vibrato than most wind players; raise it and it starts to sound like a flute. The mod wheel turns this knob further, so you can add vibrato part-way through a note.
- VOLUME 8.
- Listen for: a steady pitch with only a trace of movement on long notes.

context.vco1.pw: The whole tone lives here. At 0 the wave is an exact square and the sound is at its most hollow; past about 3 the even harmonics come in and it turns nasal, which is an oboe rather than a clarinet.
context.lpf.cutoff: How woody or how buzzy. Around 5.5 is the low register; raise it towards 7 for the brighter upper one.
context.lpmod.eg2: Kept almost at 0 on purpose. Any real amount here makes each note change colour as it starts, which no clarinet does.
context.lpf.peak: A trace only. Wind it up and the pipe turns into a resonant filter, which reads as a synth straight away.
context.eg2.attack: About forty milliseconds, which is how long a reed takes to start.
context.eg2.sustain: Near full, so a held note keeps its strength.
context.fmod.mg: A small waver. Raise it and the clarinet starts to sound like a flute instead. The mod wheel turns this knob further, so the vibrato comes in when you push the wheel part-way through a note.

tweaks.hear: The hollow, odd-harmonic tone thins out and turns nasal as the even harmonics arrive.
The bright upper register of the instrument, about an octave up in character.
Each note now opens as it starts. It sounds like a synth again — which is why it is at 0.6.
Down an octave into bass clarinet territory, where the hollow tone is at its strongest.

sounds.name: Nasal Oboe
sounds.ref: In the style of a solo oboe
sounds.blurb: A thin, nasal double-reed line, carved out by closing both filters in on each other.
sounds.how: This is the patch that needs the high-pass and the low-pass together. A narrow pulse gives the raw buzz, then the high-pass at about 500 Hz with PEAK up strips the fundamental away and boosts what is left, while the low-pass closes in from 2.5 kHz. What survives is a narrow, emphasised band with almost no bottom — which is what makes a double reed sound nasal. Two oscillators a few cents apart stand in for the two blades of the reed beating against each other. No cables.

steps.title: Two narrow pulses, a few cents apart
steps.why:
Two narrow pulses give the thin, buzzy raw material. The second one, just off pitch, stands in for the two blades of a double reed, which never vibrate exactly together.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) Pulse, PW 8.6: PW is pulse width. Near 10 the pulse is thin and buzzy; wind it back towards 0 and the tone hollows out into a clarinet.
- WAVE FORM (osc 2) npulse: Oscillator 2’s narrow pulse.
- SCALE 8′ on both: SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet; 8′ is the same octave on both.
- PITCH 0.1 · +0.1 st: a few cents apart, so the two beat slowly.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8, VCO2 LEVEL 3.5: the second VCO (voltage-controlled oscillator) sits well behind the first.
- Listen for: a thin, buzzy tone with a slow shimmer.

steps.title: Strip the bottom away with PEAK up
steps.why:
The high-pass filter (HPF: it removes everything below its cutoff) is set above the fundamental of most notes, so the note is heard through its harmonics rather than its root. This is the step that makes it nasal.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 5.4 · 500 Hz: the bottom of the band and the main control of how nasal it is. Drop it to 3 and the fundamental comes back: the oboe turns into an ordinary reedy lead.
- PEAK (HPF) 6.2: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance, a boost right at the cutoff. Well up, it gives the honk, and it is the knob that separates a double reed from a clarinet.
- Listen for: the low end disappears and a pinched, honky tone is left.

steps.title: Close in from above
steps.why:
The low-pass filter (LPF) closes in from above. With both filters used together there is a narrow band left, with an emphasis at each end: a formant peak no single filter can make.
- FILTER 1: the gentler circuit; the switch covers both filters.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 7.1 · 2.5 kHz: the top of the band, taking the top off the buzz. Bring it down towards 6 and the two cutoffs squeeze together, thinner still.
- PEAK (LPF) 4.2: a moderate emphasis at the top edge of the band.
- Listen for: the fizz on top goes, and the tone sounds nasal rather than buzzy. Sweep the low-pass CUTOFF down slowly to hear the band narrow.

steps.title: A soft front to each note
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope that opens the amplifier) gives each note a soft front. The filter envelope stays small, because the nasal colour should not change as the note speaks.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 1.4: only a slight brightening at the start.
- ATTACK (EG2) 2.4 · 32 ms: about thirty milliseconds, how long a double reed takes to speak.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 4.5 · 200 ms, SUSTAIN 9.5: near-full sustain holds the line at strength.
- RELEASE (EG2) 2 · 140 ms: stops soon after the key comes up.
- Listen for: notes start softly but not slowly, with the tone the same from start to end.

steps.title: Join the notes and add a small waver
steps.why:
A short slide slurs the phrase, and a quick, shallow vibrato finishes it.
- TIME 0.9: portamento, so slurred notes join.
- WAVE FORM (MG) 5 · triangle, FREQUENCY 7.4 · 5.41 Hz: the modulation generator (MG, Korg’s name for the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator) at about five cycles a second. Oboe vibrato is quick.
- MG/T.EXT (pitch) 1: depth barely off zero. The mod wheel turns this knob further, so you can bring vibrato in part-way through a note.
- VOLUME 9: set high because the high-pass has thrown away most of the energy in the sound.
- Listen for: a small, quick waver on long notes.

context.hpf.cutoff: The bottom of the band, and the main control of how nasal this is. Drop it to 3 and the fundamental comes back and the oboe turns into an ordinary reedy lead.
context.hpf.peak: The emphasis that makes the honk. This is the single knob that separates a double reed from a clarinet.
context.lpf.cutoff: The top of the band. Bring it down towards 6 and the two cutoffs squeeze together, which is thinner still.
context.vco1.pw: How narrow the pulse is. Near 10 it is thin and buzzy; wind it back towards 0 and the tone hollows out into a clarinet.
context.vco2.pitch: The slow beat between the two oscillators, standing in for the two blades of the reed.
context.eg2.attack: About thirty milliseconds, which is how long a double reed takes to speak.
context.fmod.mg: A quick, shallow waver, barely off zero. The mod wheel turns this knob further, so the vibrato comes in when you push the wheel part-way through a note.
context.out.volume: Set high because the high-pass has thrown away most of the energy in the sound.

tweaks.try: Sweep between 2 and 6 while a long note rings
tweaks.hear: The body drains out and the tone goes from reedy to thin and pinched. This is the whole range between a bassoon and an oboe.

tweaks.try: Leave it where it is and push the mod wheel a quarter of the way up on the long final note
tweaks.hear: Vibrato arrives part-way through the note instead of being there from the start.
The honk goes. Without the emphasis it is just a thin sound, not a nasal one.

tweaks.try: Set to 16, with the high-pass down at 3
tweaks.hear: A bassoon: the same reed an octave down, dark, with the fundamental left in.
The two cutoffs close on each other and the band narrows to something almost vocal.

sounds.name: Recorder with a Chiff
sounds.ref: In the style of a solo treble recorder
sounds.blurb: A hollow wooden line with a short puff of air at the front of every note.
sounds.how: A recorder is nearly a pure tone with a burst of breath as the airstream catches. The triangle covers the tone and a cable from the WHITE noise socket into EXT SIGNAL IN puts air into the filter chain alongside it, where both are shaped together. The burst is the interesting part: envelope 2 is set with almost no sustain and pointed at the high-pass cutoff, so the high-pass jumps up for about forty milliseconds and drops back — thin and airy at the front, hollow and woody after. With envelope 2’s sustain that low it cannot hold the amplifier open, so a second cable takes EG 1 OUT to INITIAL GAIN to do that job instead.

steps.title: A triangle, high up
steps.why:
A triangle has almost no harmonics, as close as an oscillator gets to the hollow tone of a wooden pipe.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) Triangle: soft and hollow, where the default reverse saw is bright and buzzy.
- SCALE (osc 1) 8′: SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet. Play high on the keyboard for a treble recorder.
- VCO1 LEVEL 7: the balance between tone and air once the noise cable is in; turn it down and the patch becomes mostly breath.
- VCO2 LEVEL 0, WAVE FORM (osc 2) Reverse saw: the second VCO (voltage-controlled oscillator) stays out of it.
- Listen for: a plain, flute-like tone.

steps.title: Put air into the filter chain
steps.why:
A cable adds air. The noise position on the waveform switch would replace the oscillator; the cable adds noise alongside it instead.
- Cable WHITE → EXT SIGNAL IN: white noise, every frequency at once, goes into the filter chain at the high-pass input. The air is filtered together with the note rather than sitting on top of it. It comes in at a fixed level, so VCO1 LEVEL is how you balance the two.
- Listen for: a loud hiss joins the note. The filters in the next step tame it into breath.

steps.title: Hollow it out between the two filters
steps.why:
Both filters close in to leave a narrow band, which makes the tone read as a pipe rather than an oscillator.
- FILTER 1: the gentler circuit; the switch covers both filters.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 6 · 1.2 kHz, PEAK 3.5: the low-pass filter (LPF) removes everything above its cutoff and keeps the hiss down to a breath. Too high and it is a hiss; too low and the wooden tone goes with it. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 3 · 95 Hz, PEAK 2.5: the high-pass filter (HPF) sets the bottom of the band. This is where it rests between chiffs, which sets how much body the note has.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 0.8: only a trace of filter movement.
- Listen for: the hiss becomes a soft, breathy layer under a woody tone.

steps.title: Point envelope 2 at the high-pass instead
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope) is turned into a short burst and pointed at the high-pass cutoff. That burst is the chiff, the puff of air as the airstream catches.
- EG2/EXT (HPF mod) 6: the size of the chiff. The high-pass jumps to about 550 Hz and falls back to about 100 Hz. At 0 the puff of air goes.
- ATTACK (EG2) 2 · 24 ms: a fast rise.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 2.6 · 42 ms: about forty milliseconds, a tongued note. Past about 4 it turns into a slow filter sweep.
- SUSTAIN 1: almost none, so envelope 2 is a transient and nothing else. It also opens the amplifier, so notes now die almost at once; the next step fixes that.
- RELEASE (EG2) 1.6 · 110 ms.
- Listen for: a thin, breathy blip on each key.

steps.title: Hold the amplifier open with envelope 1
steps.why:
With envelope 2 sustaining at 1 the note would die as soon as it started. Envelope 1 (EG1) takes over the job of holding the amplifier open.
- Cable EG 1 OUT → INITIAL GAIN: INITIAL GAIN adds a voltage to the amplifier on top of envelope 2. Envelope 1 holds at full for as long as a key is down, so envelope 2 is free to be a pure transient.
- DELAY TIME 0, ATTACK (EG1) 2.2 · 20 ms: the body arrives just behind the chiff. This is now the attack you hear.
- RELEASE (EG1) 2 · 110 ms: short, because a recorder stops when the air does.
- VOLUME 5.5: low, because both envelopes add to the amplifier at the start of a note.
- Listen for: each note starts thin and breathy, then the hollow body comes in and holds.

steps.title: Join the notes
steps.why:
A short slide and a trace of vibrato finish the line.
- TIME 0.7: portamento, so slurred notes join up.
- WAVE FORM (MG) 5 · triangle, FREQUENCY 7.5 · 5.71 Hz: the modulation generator (MG, Korg’s name for the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator) moving smoothly at about five and a half cycles a second.
- MG/T.EXT (pitch) 0.9: a trace of vibrato, almost nothing on its own. The mod wheel turns this knob further, so you can push it in on long notes.
- Listen for: play a phrase with some long notes; the chiff on every note, and a slight waver on the held ones.

context.hpmod.eg2: The size of the chiff — how far the high-pass jumps at the front of each note. At 0 the breath and the note start together and the puff of air goes.
context.eg2.decay: How long the chiff lasts. Around forty milliseconds is a tongued note; raise it past 4 and it turns into a slow filter sweep.
context.eg2.sustain: Kept near 0 so envelope 2 is a transient and nothing else. This is only possible because envelope 1 is holding the amplifier open through INITIAL GAIN.
context.eg1.attack: How quickly the body of the note arrives behind the chiff. This is now the attack you hear.
context.eg1.release: How the note stops. Short, because a recorder stops when the air does.
context.mix.vco1: The balance between tone and air, because the noise comes in through a cable at a fixed level. Turn it down and the patch becomes mostly breath.
context.lpf.cutoff: How much of the air comes through. Too high and it is a hiss; too low and the wooden tone goes with it.
context.hpf.cutoff: Where the high-pass rests between chiffs, which sets how much body the note has.
context.out.volume: Set low because envelope 1 and envelope 2 both add to the amplifier at the start of a note.
context.fmod.mg: A trace of vibrato, almost nothing on its own. The mod wheel turns this knob further, so the vibrato comes in when you push the wheel part-way through a note.

tweaks.hear: Without it the notes simply start; with it there is a puff of air on the front of each one.
The chiff stretches into a slow opening sweep and the recorder turns into a synth pad.
The air takes over and the line turns into wind across the top of a bottle.
A descant recorder, an octave up, where the breath is a bigger part of the sound.

sounds.name: Deep Double Knock
sounds.ref: A dull knock at the bottom of the range with a second, softer knock just behind it
sounds.blurb: A short low knock at the bottom of the range, answered a fifth of a second later by a quieter one.
sounds.how: There is no oscillator in this sound. PEAK on the high-pass filter is wound up until the filter almost rings on its own, and a burst of noise is all it takes to set it going at its cutoff — around fifty hertz. Envelope 1 is cabled to INITIAL GAIN, and because envelope 1 has a DELAY stage it opens the amplifier a second time about two hundred milliseconds after the first knock, so one key gives two.

steps.title: Noise instead of an oscillator
steps.why:
There is no oscillator in this sound. Oscillator 1 is swapped for noise, which is the hammer that will strike the high-pass filter and set it ringing.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) noise: the fourth position disconnects Oscillator 1 (a VCO, voltage-controlled oscillator) and puts the noise generator in its place.
- VCO1 LEVEL 9.5: how hard the filter is struck. Turn it down and the ring is weaker, because there is less to set it going.
- VCO2 LEVEL 0: nothing from Oscillator 2.
- Listen for: plain hiss for now. Almost all of it will be thrown away by the filters.

steps.title: Make the high-pass ring at fifty hertz
steps.why:
The high-pass filter (HPF: it removes everything below its cutoff) is pushed to the edge of oscillating, so the noise sets it ringing at its cutoff. That ring is the knock.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 2 · 48 Hz: the pitch of the knock, about fifty hertz, down in sub-bass territory. Every step up moves it higher; past about 4 it stops feeling like a sub.
- PEAK (HPF) 9.2: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. Here it is the whole sound. Below about 8 the ring goes and there is nothing left but a faint puff of noise.
- Listen for: a low hum under the hiss, more felt than heard on small speakers.

steps.title: Close the low-pass over the top
steps.why:
The noise is still broadband. The low-pass filter (LPF: it removes everything above its cutoff) closes over the top and throws nearly all of it away.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 2.3 · 96 Hz: the lid on the noise. Raise it and the hiss comes back over the top of the knock.
- PEAK (LPF) 5: a little emphasis just above the ring, which thickens the knock. Past about 8 the low-pass starts ringing too and adds a second tone.
- FILTER 1: the gentler circuit; the switch covers both filters.
- Listen for: the hiss disappears and only the deep ring is left.

steps.title: One short hit
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope that opens the amplifier) is cut down to one short hit.
- ATTACK (EG2) 0 · 5 ms: instant, so the knock has a hard front.
- HOLD 0.8 · 18 ms: HOLD keeps envelope 2 at full for a moment before the decay starts, giving the hit a little more body.
- DECAY 3.6 · 97 ms, SUSTAIN 0: the length of the first knock. With no sustain it dies away by itself, and the ring dies with the amplifier rather than after it.
- RELEASE (EG2) 1.6 · 110 ms.
- VOLUME 10: the ring is quiet, so the output goes to full.
- Listen for: a single dull thud on each key.

steps.title: Cable envelope 1 to the amplifier and delay it
steps.why:
Envelope 1 (EG1) is cabled to the amplifier and delayed, so it opens the amplifier a second time a fifth of a second after the first knock. One key gives two knocks.
- Cable EG 1 OUT → INITIAL GAIN: INITIAL GAIN adds to whatever envelope 2 is doing, so envelope 1 can open the amplifier on its own.
- DELAY TIME 5 · 230 ms: the gap between the two knocks. At 0 they land together and the trick disappears.
- ATTACK (EG1) 0 · 3 ms: the second knock starts sharply too.
- RELEASE (EG1) 2 · 110 ms: the length of the second knock once you let go. Keep it shorter than the first.
- Listen for: tap a key briefly. A thud, then a softer one just behind it. Change DELAY TIME to move the second knock.

context.hpf.peak: The whole sound. Below about 8 the ring goes and there is nothing left but a faint puff of noise.
context.hpf.cutoff: The pitch of the knock. Every step up the knob moves it higher; past about 4 it stops feeling like a sub.
context.lpf.cutoff: The lid on the noise. Raise it and the hiss comes back over the top of the knock.
context.mix.vco1: How hard the filter is struck. Turn it down and the ring is weaker, because there is less to set it going.
context.lpf.peak: A little emphasis just above the ring, which thickens the knock. Past about 8 the low-pass starts ringing too and adds a second tone.
context.eg1.delay: The gap between the two knocks. At 0 they land together and the trick disappears.
context.eg1.release: The length of the second knock, which should stay shorter than the first.
context.eg2.decay: The length of the first knock.

tweaks.hear: The second knock walks away from the first, from a flam to a separate beat.
The knock climbs out of the sub range and turns hollow and woody.
The filter tips into oscillating properly and the knock grows a long humming tail.
The hammer is softer, so the knock is quieter and rounder with less grit on the front of it.

sounds.name: Stepped Scrape
sounds.ref: A rasping low-mid scrape, as though something were dragged across a ridged surface
sounds.blurb: A short rasp made of six or seven separate steps rather than one smooth sound.
sounds.how: The sample and hold is clocked from the modulation generator at its fastest, about twenty-two times a second, and its stepped output is cabled to the high-pass CUTOFF FREQ socket. Each step jumps the high-pass to a new random height, so a band of noise is dragged up and down in lumps instead of sliding. The whole thing lasts about three hundred milliseconds, which is long enough for six or seven steps.

steps.title: Noise, and nothing else
steps.why:
The steps are the interest in this sound, so the source is plain broadband noise with no pitch in it.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) noise: the fourth position disconnects Oscillator 1 (a VCO, voltage-controlled oscillator) and puts the noise generator in its place, so VCO1 LEVEL becomes the noise level.
- VCO1 LEVEL 9, VCO2 LEVEL 0: plenty of noise and nothing from Oscillator 2.
- Listen for: a steady hiss that is the same on every key.

steps.title: A resonant band in the low middle
steps.why:
Both filters are made resonant to leave a narrow band of noise in the low middle, with a hard edge at each end. Those edges are what will make each step heard as a change of colour rather than of volume.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 2.8 · 83 Hz: the high-pass filter (HPF) removes everything below its cutoff. This is where the scrape sits before the steps move it.
- PEAK (HPF) 7: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. It emphasises the bottom edge of the band.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 4.4 · 399 Hz: the low-pass filter (LPF) removes everything above. This is the lid; lower it and the scrape turns dull and distant.
- PEAK (LPF) 6.5: the body of the band. Without it the steps read as hiss rather than a surface.
- FILTER 2: the more aggressive circuit, for a harder edge.
- Listen for: the hiss becomes a dark, hollow roar.

steps.title: Clock the sample and hold as fast as it goes
steps.why:
The sample and hold (S&H) takes a reading each time it is clocked and holds it until the next one. With nothing in S&H IN it reads noise, so every reading is random.
- Cable MG OUT (pulse) → CLOCK: the modulation generator (MG, Korg’s name for the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator) sends a clean on-off pulse to CLOCK.
- FREQUENCY 10 · 22 Hz: its fastest, about twenty-two ticks a second, so steps arrive roughly forty-five milliseconds apart. Slow it and you hear three or four lumps per hit instead of a rasp.
- WAVE FORM (MG) 5 · triangle: the pulse output is an even square at this position.
- Listen for: nothing changes yet. The steps are not going anywhere audible.

steps.title: Send the steps to the high-pass
steps.why:
The steps go to the high-pass cutoff, so the band of noise is dragged up and down in lumps instead of sliding.
- Cable S&H OUT → CUTOFF FREQ (high-pass): this socket takes envelope 2’s place at the high-pass EG2/EXT knob.
- EG2/EXT (HPF mod) 6: now sets how far each step moves the high-pass. At 0 the steps stop and plain noise is left; more makes the jumps wider and harsher.
- Listen for: hold a key. The roar judders from one random colour to the next about twenty times a second.

steps.title: Keep it short
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope that opens the amplifier) cuts the sound down to a short hit, long enough for six or seven steps.
- ATTACK (EG2) 0 · 5 ms: instant.
- HOLD 0.6 · 15 ms: a moment at full before the decay.
- DECAY 5 · 300 ms, SUSTAIN 0: about three hundred milliseconds and then silence, however long the key is held. DECAY is the length of the scrape, and so how many steps get through.
- RELEASE (EG2) 2 · 140 ms.
- VOLUME 10.
- Listen for: tap keys in a rhythm. Each hit is a short rasp you can almost count, and no two sound quite the same.

context.mg.freq: How many steps fit inside each hit, because the modulation generator is clocking the sample and hold. Slow it and you hear three or four lumps; this fast it is a rasp.
context.hpmod.eg2: How far each step moves the high-pass, because the cable replaced envelope 2 at this knob. At 0 the steps stop and a plain noise burst is left.
context.hpf.cutoff: Where the scrape sits before the steps move it.
context.hpf.peak: Emphasis at the bottom edge of the band, which is what turns each step into a change of colour you can hear.
context.lpf.cutoff: The lid. Bring it down and the scrape turns dull and distant.
context.lpf.peak: The body of the band. Without it the steps read as hiss rather than as a surface.
context.eg2.decay: The length of the scrape, and so how many steps get through.

tweaks.hear: The steps separate into three distinct lumps — a ratchet rather than a scrape.
Each step jumps much further and the scrape turns into a random chattering burst.
The scrape runs on for most of a second, which is more of a texture than a hit.
The band sings and each step lands on a recognisable pitch.

sounds.name: Choked Thud
sounds.ref: A blunt mid-range hit that strangles itself as it sounds
sounds.blurb: A hit that starts full and thins out from underneath as it plays, as though it were being smothered.
sounds.how: The main output is cabled round to the external signal processor, and the envelope follower turns the loudness of the synth into a voltage. That voltage goes to the high-pass CUTOFF FREQ socket, so the louder the hit is the more bass the high-pass takes away. The sound therefore chokes itself: full at the front, hollow in the middle, and only allowed back down as it fades.

steps.title: A thin pulse to hit with
steps.why:
A thin pulse is the source. It has plenty of harmonics for the envelope follower to react to, and little enough fundamental that the choking will be obvious.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) Pulse: a pulse wave, thin and nasal next to the default reverse saw.
- PW 7: pulse width, set towards narrow. Nearer 5 gives a squarer, fatter hit that resists the choking.
- SCALE (osc 1) 8′: SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8, VCO2 LEVEL 0: one VCO (voltage-controlled oscillator) only.
- Listen for: a bright, reedy tone.

steps.title: Leave the high-pass room to climb
steps.why:
The filters set up a tone with a body to lose, and leave the high-pass room to climb.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 2.6 · 72 Hz: the high-pass filter (HPF) removes everything below its cutoff. It rests near the bottom, which is the full version of the tone, so the follower has somewhere to push it.
- PEAK (HPF) 6: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. It emphasises the edge that will move.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 5.2 · 687 Hz: the low-pass filter (LPF) sets the top of the hit. Raise it for more edge.
- PEAK (LPF) 7: the body the choke will take away. With it down there is less to lose.
- FILTER 2: the more aggressive circuit, which bites harder at this PEAK.
- Listen for: a honky, resonant mid-range tone.

steps.title: A blunt envelope
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope that opens the amplifier) gives a blunt hit with enough length for the choke to happen inside it.
- ATTACK (EG2) 0 · 5 ms: instant, so the hit starts full.
- HOLD 0.4 · 13 ms: a brief moment at full.
- DECAY 4.6 · 220 ms, SUSTAIN 0: the length of the hit, and so how much of the choke you hear before it is over.
- RELEASE (EG2) 1.8 · 120 ms.
- VOLUME 7.
- Listen for: a short, blunt thud on each key.

steps.title: Let the synth listen to itself
steps.why:
The synth is made to listen to itself. The external signal processor (ESP) turns an incoming sound into control voltages; here the incoming sound is the synth’s own output.
- Cable SIGNAL OUT → SIGNAL IN: the main output goes round into the processor.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 7: preamp gain. The envelope follower then makes a voltage that rises and falls with how loud the synth is. More level drives it harder, so the choking starts sooner.
- Listen for: no change yet. The follower’s voltage is not patched anywhere.

steps.title: Point the follower at the high-pass
steps.why:
The follower is pointed at the high-pass, so the sound chokes itself: the louder it is, the more bass the high-pass takes away.
- Cable ENV OUT → CUTOFF FREQ (high-pass): this socket stands in for envelope 2 at the high-pass EG2/EXT knob.
- EG2/EXT (HPF mod) 6: now the choke amount. At 0 the hit is an ordinary blunt thud; high up it swallows itself.
- Listen for: each hit starts full, goes hollow in the middle, and is allowed back down only as it fades. Turn EG2/EXT to 0 and back to hear the difference.

context.hpmod.eg2: The choke amount, because the CUTOFF FREQ cable replaced envelope 2 at this knob. At 0 the hit is an ordinary blunt thud; high up it swallows itself.
context.esp.level: How hard the output is driven into the follower, which sets how quickly the choking starts.
context.hpf.cutoff: Where the high-pass rests when the sound is quiet — the full version of the tone.
context.lpf.cutoff: The top of the hit. Raise it and there is more edge for the choke to work against.
context.lpf.peak: The body the choke takes away. With it down there is less to lose and the effect is harder to hear.
context.eg2.decay: The length of the hit, and so how much of the choke you hear before it is over.
context.vco1.pw: How thin the source is. Nearer 5 gives a squarer, fatter hit that resists the choking.

tweaks.hear: From a plain thud to a hit that clamps shut on itself before it has finished.
The follower barely reacts and the choking all but disappears.
A longer hit, so the choke has time to release again and the tone swells back at the end.
An octave down: a heavier hit with far more for the high-pass to strip away.

sounds.name: Two-Stage Tick
sounds.ref: A dry tick with a bright second edge arriving a moment behind it
sounds.blurb: One key gives two hits: a dry tick, then a brighter edge about a tenth of a second later.
sounds.how: Both filters are resonating and each is swept by a different envelope. Envelope 2 shoves the high-pass peak up the instant the key goes down, which is the tick. Envelope 1 is cabled to the low-pass CUTOFF FREQ socket, and because envelope 1 has a DELAY stage its sweep arrives about a hundred milliseconds late — a second, brighter edge from the same key.

steps.title: A narrow pulse as the source
steps.why:
Oscillator 2’s narrow pulse is the only source. It is nearly all harmonics and very little fundamental, which gives both filter peaks something to grab.
- WAVE FORM (osc 2) npulse, VCO2 LEVEL 10: Oscillator 2 at full.
- SCALE (osc 2) 4′, PITCH 1.2 · +2.9 st: SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet; 4′ is an octave up. PITCH retunes the source under the filters; it changes the grain of the tick more than its pitch.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) Triangle, VCO1 LEVEL 0: Oscillator 1 is switched out of the mix. VCO stands for voltage-controlled oscillator.
- Listen for: a high, thin buzz.

steps.title: Two peaks, close together
steps.why:
Both filters get high resonance, leaving two resonant edges only a couple of hundred hertz apart, around a kilohertz. Everything after this is a matter of moving one against the other.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 6.4 · 998 Hz, PEAK 8: the high-pass filter (HPF) removes everything below its cutoff. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance; here it rings at the bottom edge of the band.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 6 · 1.2 kHz, PEAK 8.5: the low-pass filter (LPF) removes everything above. Its peak is the top edge, the one envelope 1 will move later.
- FILTER 2: the more aggressive circuit, for a harder ring.
- Listen for: a narrow, whistling tone. With both PEAK knobs down there would be only a faint pulse.

steps.title: Envelope 2 throws the high-pass up
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope) is sent to the high-pass cutoff, so the high-pass peak is thrown up the moment the key goes down. That is the first tick.
- EG2/EXT (HPF mod) 5: the high-pass jumps nearly two octaves and falls back. More makes the first edge brighter and sharper.
- Listen for: a bright flick at the start of each note. For now the envelope still has its default sustain, so the note holds after it.

steps.title: Shape the hit
steps.why:
Envelope 2 is cut down to a hit, but its release is kept long enough to hold the amplifier open for the second edge.
- ATTACK (EG2) 0 · 5 ms: instant.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 4.6 · 220 ms, SUSTAIN 0: a short decay and no held level, so it is a hit rather than a note.
- RELEASE (EG2) 3.2 · 280 ms: kept long on purpose; the amplifier has to still be open when the second sweep arrives.
- VOLUME 10.
- Listen for: a dry tick that dies away quickly.

steps.title: Cable envelope 1 to the low-pass and delay it
steps.why:
Envelope 1 (EG1) is cabled to the low-pass and delayed, so its sweep arrives about a tenth of a second late: a second, brighter edge from the same key.
- Cable EG 1 OUT → CUTOFF FREQ (low-pass): this socket takes envelope 2’s place at the low-pass EG2/EXT knob.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 5.5: now sets how far the low-pass is thrown up, the brightness of the late hit.
- DELAY TIME 4 · 120 ms: the gap between the two edges. At 0 they land together and it collapses into one tick.
- ATTACK (EG1) 1 · 7 ms, RELEASE 2 · 110 ms: the second edge rises quickly.
- Listen for: tap a key. Tick, then a brighter edge just behind it.

context.eg1.delay: The gap between the two edges. At 0 they land together and the sound collapses into one ordinary tick.
context.lpmod.eg2: How far the second edge travels, because the cable replaced envelope 2 at this knob. This is the brightness of the late hit.
context.hpmod.eg2: How far the first edge travels. The two knobs are the two halves of the sound.
context.hpf.cutoff: The bottom edge of the band, and where the first tick starts from before envelope 2 throws it up.
context.lpf.cutoff: The top edge, and where the second edge starts from before envelope 1 throws it up.
context.hpf.peak: The resonance at the bottom edge of the band. With both PEAK knobs down there is nothing but a faint pulse.
context.lpf.peak: The resonance at the top edge — the one envelope 1 moves.
context.eg2.release: Kept long on purpose: the amplifier has to still be open when the second sweep arrives.
context.vco2.pitch: Retunes the source under the filters. It changes the grain of the tick more than its pitch.

tweaks.hear: The second edge slides from a flam to a separate hit a third of a second later.
The late edge turns into a bright chirp that leaps well above the first tick.
The band widens and the first tick gains weight, which makes the two hits sound less alike.
The second edge slides in rather than snapping, turning the pair into a hit followed by a swell.

sounds.name: Falling Ping
sounds.ref: A short bright ping whose pitch drops as it dies
sounds.blurb: A thin, glassy ping a few kilohertz up that slides downward as it fades.
sounds.how: The pitch here belongs to the high-pass filter, not to an oscillator. PEAK is high enough that the filter rings at its cutoff, and envelope 2 throws that cutoff up an octave and a half at the start of every hit and lets it fall back. Noise is the only source: it is there to set the filter ringing and nothing more.

steps.title: Noise as the striker
steps.why:
Noise is the only source. It is the striker: broadband noise has energy at every frequency, so whatever the high-pass is ringing at, there is something there to ring it.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) noise: the fourth position disconnects Oscillator 1 (a VCO, voltage-controlled oscillator) and puts the noise generator in its place.
- VCO1 LEVEL 8, VCO2 LEVEL 0: noise only.
- Listen for: plain hiss. The pitch will come from the filter, not an oscillator.

steps.title: Ring the high-pass a few kilohertz up
steps.why:
The high-pass is made to ring a few kilohertz up, and the low-pass closes the band from above, so the ping has an edge rather than a hiss.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 7.6 · 2.3 kHz: the high-pass filter (HPF) removes everything below its cutoff. This is where the ping rests at the end of its fall, the register of the whole sound.
- PEAK (HPF) 8.8: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. Near the top it emphasises a narrow band at the cutoff, which is the ping’s pitch. With it down only a short hiss is left.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 8.6 · 6.9 kHz, PEAK 8: the low-pass filter (LPF) is the lid over the ping. Bring it down towards the high-pass and it narrows to a single tone.
- FILTER 2: the more aggressive circuit.
- Listen for: a thin, glassy whistle inside the hiss.

steps.title: Let the ring fall
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope) is sent to the high-pass cutoff, so the ringing band starts high and slides back down. The fall is what the ear hears as a ping rather than a tick.
- EG2/EXT (HPF mod) 4.5: the high-pass is pushed up about an octave and a half at the start of each hit. At 0 the pitch sits still and it stops sounding struck; more gives a longer drop.
- Listen for: a short downward chirp at the start of each note. With the envelope’s default sustain it only falls part way for now.

steps.title: A short hit
steps.why:
Envelope 2 is cut down to a short hit. Because the pitch follows the envelope, its decay is also how long the fall takes.
- ATTACK (EG2) 0 · 5 ms: instant.
- HOLD 0.5 · 14 ms: a moment at the top of the fall before it starts, which gives the ping a hard front.
- DECAY 3.4 · 83 ms, SUSTAIN 0: under a fifth of a second and no held level, so each ping is over before the next arrives. Longer makes a slower, zappier fall.
- RELEASE (EG2) 1.6 · 110 ms.
- VOLUME 8.
- Listen for: tap quickly; each tap is a glassy ping that drops as it dies.

context.hpf.peak: The pitch of the ping. With PEAK down there is no ringing band and nothing but a short hiss is left.
context.hpf.cutoff: Where the ping rests at the end of its fall. This sets the register of the whole sound.
context.hpmod.eg2: How far the ping falls. At 0 the pitch sits still and it stops sounding struck.
context.lpf.cutoff: The lid over the ping. Bring it down towards the high-pass and the sound narrows to a single tone.
context.eg2.decay: How long the fall takes, because the pitch follows the envelope.
context.eg2.hold: A moment at the top of the fall before it starts, which gives the ping a hard front.

tweaks.hear: A much longer drop: the ping turns into a short downward whistle.
The whole sound moves down an octave and a half and reads as hollow rather than glassy.
The fall slows right down and each hit becomes a slow slide instead of a ping.
A second ringing edge joins in above the first and the ping gains a metallic beat.

sounds.name: Dust Crackle
sounds.ref: A dry burst of very high crackle, like grit on a hard surface
sounds.blurb: A short burst of crackle right at the top of hearing, with no body underneath it at all.
sounds.how: The output goes round to the external signal processor, and the preamp there is a saturator: driven hard it squares off whatever it is given and throws out new harmonics well above the original. That saturated copy is cabled back into EXT SIGNAL IN, so the filter chain hears its own output again. With the high-pass at the top of its range, only the harmonics the preamp invented survive, and the result flares on each hit and dies with it.

steps.title: Noise to get it started
steps.why:
Noise gets the feedback loop started. It has energy at the top of the range, which is where the high-pass will be listening.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) noise: the fourth position disconnects Oscillator 1 (a VCO, voltage-controlled oscillator) and puts the noise generator in its place.
- VCO1 LEVEL 9: the noise that seeds the loop. Turn it down and there is less for the preamp to work on.
- VCO2 LEVEL 0: nothing from Oscillator 2.
- Listen for: full, bright hiss.

steps.title: Keep only the very top
steps.why:
Only the very top is kept. With no body left, the sound sits above a mix rather than in it.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 10 · 12 kHz: the high-pass filter (HPF) at its maximum removes everything below about twelve kilohertz. Below about 8 the body comes back and it stops being air.
- PEAK (HPF) 6: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. A little at the bottom edge gives the crackle a faint pitch to hang on.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 10 · 18 kHz, PEAK 2: the low-pass filter (LPF) is left wide open so nothing is taken off the top.
- FILTER 2: the more aggressive circuit.
- Listen for: a faint, very high fizz. On small speakers you may barely hear it yet.

steps.title: A short burst
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope that opens the amplifier) makes each hit a short burst. The feedback loop added next dies with the amplifier, so the crackle cannot run on between hits.
- ATTACK (EG2) 0 · 5 ms: instant.
- HOLD 0.4 · 13 ms: a brief moment at full.
- DECAY 3.8 · 110 ms, SUSTAIN 0: about a tenth of a second, then silence. DECAY is the length of the burst.
- RELEASE (EG2) 2 · 140 ms.
- VOLUME 7.
- Listen for: a tiny tick of air on each key.

steps.title: Drive the output into the preamp
steps.why:
The output is driven into the external signal processor (ESP), whose preamp is a saturator: pushed hard, it squares off what it is given and throws out new harmonics well above the original.
- Cable SIGNAL OUT → SIGNAL IN: the synth’s own output goes round into the processor.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 8: how hard the preamp is driven, which is how much grit the loop will make. Low gives a plain noise tick; high gives a dry crackle.
- Listen for: no change yet. The saturated copy is not coming back into the synth.

steps.title: Send the saturated copy back into the filters
steps.why:
The saturated copy is sent back into the filters, closing the loop. Only the harmonics the preamp invented survive the high-pass, so the burst turns to crackle.
- Cable ESP OUT (before the filter) → EXT SIGNAL IN: the processor’s first output carries the preamp signal. EXT SIGNAL IN joins the oscillator mix at the input of the filter chain, so each pass round the loop adds another layer of grit.
- Listen for: each hit now flares into a dry, gritty crackle and dies with the envelope. Turn SIGNAL LEVEL down and up to hear the grit come and go.

context.esp.level: How hard the preamp is driven, which is how much grit the loop makes. Low is a plain noise tick; high is a dry crackle.
context.hpf.cutoff: How high the burst sits. Below about 8 the body comes back and it stops being air.
context.lpf.cutoff: Left wide open so nothing is taken off the top.
context.mix.vco1: The noise that seeds the loop. Turn it down and there is less for the preamp to work on.
context.eg2.decay: The length of the burst, and so how many times the signal goes round the loop.
context.hpf.peak: A little emphasis at the bottom edge, which gives the crackle a faint pitch to hang on.

tweaks.hear: From a clean noise tick to a hard, dry crackle that keeps reshaping itself.
Body comes back underneath and the burst turns into a short rush of air.
The loop runs for most of a second and the crackle builds instead of dying away.
A flat plateau at the front of the burst, which makes it read as harder and more deliberate.

sounds.name: Pluck with a Swelling Tail
sounds.ref: Two envelopes on one amplifier
sounds.blurb: A bright pluck that dies away, then comes back as a slow, darker swell if you keep holding the key.
sounds.how: Envelope 2 plays the pluck: it opens the amplifier and the low-pass for half a second and lets both close again. Envelope 1 is patched from EG 1 OUT into INITIAL GAIN, so it opens the amplifier as well, but its DELAY TIME holds it back until the pluck has faded. It then rises slowly while the low-pass stays closed, so the note returns darker than it started. A delay stage before the attack is what makes this possible, and few synths have one.

steps.title: A sawtooth and a soft square an octave up
steps.why:
A sawtooth gives the pluck its edge, and a quiet square an octave up gives the swell its body once the filter has closed.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) Reverse saw, SCALE 8′: bright and buzzy at normal pitch. SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet.
- VCO1 LEVEL 6.5: VCO stands for voltage-controlled oscillator; this is how much of Oscillator 1 reaches the filters.
- WAVE FORM (osc 2) Square, SCALE 4′, PITCH 0: a hollow tone exactly an octave above.
- VCO2 LEVEL 3.5: kept low. It adds a hollow upper octave, which is what the swell mostly consists of later.
- Listen for: a bright buzz with a faint organ-like octave on top.

steps.title: A low-pass that opens on the pluck only
steps.why:
The low-pass filter (LPF: it removes everything above its cutoff) is set to open only on the pluck. The swell will arrive after envelope 2 has finished, so it only ever hears the resting cutoff.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 5 · 600 Hz: how dark the swell is.
- PEAK (LPF) 2, FILTER 1: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. A little gives the pluck some definition.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 6.5: envelope 2 (EG2) lifts the cutoff more than three octaves at the start of each note. This is how much brighter the pluck is than the swell.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 2.4 · 63 Hz, PEAK 0: the high-pass filter (HPF) only trims the lowest rumble.
- Listen for: notes now start brighter than they hold.

steps.title: Envelope 2: the pluck
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope that opens the amplifier and, here, the low-pass) plays the pluck.
- ATTACK (EG2) 0.5 · 8 ms: near-instant, so the pluck lands on the key.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 5.6 · 500 ms, SUSTAIN 0: about half a second and then silence. DECAY is the length of the pluck; keep it shorter than envelope 1’s delay later, or the two overlap and the gap is lost.
- RELEASE (EG2) 5 · 850 ms: a little ring after short notes.
- VOLUME 8.
- Listen for: hold a key. A bright pluck that has gone quiet well before you let go.

steps.title: Envelope 1 into INITIAL GAIN
steps.why:
Envelope 1 (EG1) is patched into the amplifier too, so two envelopes now open it.
- Cable EG 1 OUT → INITIAL GAIN: INITIAL GAIN adds a voltage to envelope 2 at the amplifier, so envelope 1 can open it on its own.
- EG1/EXT 0: keeps envelope 1 off the oscillator pitch. Turn it up and the swell would come with a rise in pitch.
- Listen for: envelope 1 has no delay yet, so it holds the note open at full straight away and the pluck no longer dies. The next step moves it behind the pluck.

steps.title: Hold envelope 1 back
steps.why:
Envelope 1 is held back until the pluck has faded, then rises slowly. The note comes back darker than it started, because the low-pass has closed by then.
- DELAY TIME 6.2 · 500 ms: keeps envelope 1 at zero for half a second, while the pluck fades. This is the gap between pluck and swell; at 0 the swell starts under the pluck. A delay stage before the attack is rare on a synth.
- ATTACK (EG1) 7 · 1.2 s: how slowly the swell comes back in.
- RELEASE (EG1) 6.5 · 1.8 s: how long the swell takes to fade after you let go.
- Listen for: hold a key for two seconds. Pluck, a moment of near silence, then a dark swell. Short notes end before the swell arrives.

context.eg1.delay: The gap between the pluck and the swell. At 0 the swell starts under the pluck and the gap disappears.
context.eg1.attack: How slowly the swell comes back in.
context.eg1.release: How long the swell takes to fade after you let go.
context.eg2.decay: The length of the pluck. Keep it shorter than the delay, or the two overlap and the gap is lost.
context.lpf.cutoff: How dark the swell is. The pluck is brighter because envelope 2 opens the filter; the swell only ever hears this setting.
context.lpmod.eg2: How much brighter the pluck is than the swell.
context.fmod.eg1: Kept at 0. Turn it up and the swell comes with a rise in pitch.

tweaks.hear: At 0 the pluck is followed straight away by the swell. At 6.2 there is a clear gap between them.
The swell comes back nearly as bright as the pluck, more like an organ than a pad.
The swell arrives slightly sharp, like a note being bent up after it has faded.

sounds.name: Tremolo Mandolin
sounds.ref: In the style of a mandolin played with fast tremolo picking
sounds.blurb: A held note that is picked over and over, about six times a second, on a pair of strings tuned a hair apart.
sounds.how: Envelope 1 is not tied to the keyboard. A cable from the modulation generator’s pulse output into EG1 TRIG IN fires it about six times a second for as long as a key is held, and EG 1 OUT goes into the low-pass CUTOFF FREQ socket, so every firing opens the filter and lets it close again: each one is a new pick on the string. Envelope 2 still opens and closes the amplifier with the key, so nothing sounds between notes.

steps.title: Two sawtooths, slightly apart
steps.why:
A mandolin has two strings to each note, never quite in tune with each other. Two sawtooths at the same octave with a small offset give the same slow beating.
- WAVE FORM Reverse saw on both, SCALE 8′ on both: bright, string-like raw material at the same pitch. SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet.
- PITCH 0.1 · +0.1 st: Oscillator 2 a few cents sharp. More makes the beating faster.
- VCO1 LEVEL 7, VCO2 LEVEL 5.5: both VCOs (voltage-controlled oscillators) in, the second a little lower.
- Listen for: a slow swirl on a held note.

steps.title: A small, dark body
steps.why:
The filters give the string a small, dark body.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 3.5 · 135 Hz, PEAK 1: the high-pass filter (HPF) removes everything below its cutoff; here the weight a mandolin does not have. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 4.4 · 399 Hz, PEAK 2: the low-pass filter (LPF) removes everything above. Resting at about 400 Hz, it keeps the string muffled between picks. Higher sounds brighter between picks.
- FILTER 1: the gentler circuit; the switch covers both filters.
- Listen for: a small, boxy, muffled tone.

steps.title: Envelope 2 holds the note
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope) opens the amplifier for as long as the key is held. The picking will come from somewhere else.
- ATTACK (EG2) 0.5 · 8 ms: quick.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 7 · 1.6 s, SUSTAIN 7: a slow dip to a fairly high held level.
- RELEASE (EG2) 4 · 460 ms: how long the note hangs on after you let go.
- VOLUME 8.5.
- Listen for: a steady held note with nothing moving yet.

steps.title: Fire envelope 1 from the modulation generator
steps.why:
Envelope 1 (EG1) is set to fire from the modulation generator (MG, Korg’s name for the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator) instead of the keyboard, about six times a second.
- Cable MG OUT (pulse) → EG1 TRIG IN: envelope 1 now fires on every cycle of the modulation generator while a key is held.
- FREQUENCY 7.7 · 6.36 Hz: the picking speed. Around 7.7 is a fast tremolo; below 7 it slows to separate strokes.
- WAVE FORM (MG) 5 · triangle: the pulse output is an even square here.
- DELAY 0, ATTACK (EG1) 0 · 3 ms, RELEASE 2.5 · 140 ms: envelope 1 has no sustain knob; it rises while the pulse is high and releases when it drops. A short release makes each firing a quick flick; longer blurs the picks into a shimmer.
- Listen for: no change yet; envelope 1 is not patched anywhere audible.

steps.title: Send envelope 1 to the low-pass
steps.why:
Envelope 1 is sent to the low-pass, so every firing opens the filter and lets it close: each one is a new pick on the string.
- Cable EG 1 OUT → CUTOFF FREQ (low-pass): this socket takes envelope 2’s place at the low-pass EG2/EXT knob.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 6: now sets how hard each pick is. At 6 each firing opens the filter by nearly three octaves.
- Listen for: hold a note and it is picked over and over. Change FREQUENCY to hear the tremolo speed up or break into strokes; nothing sounds between notes, because envelope 2 still controls the amplifier.

context.mg.freq: How fast the picking is. Around 7.7 is a fast tremolo; below 7 it slows to separate strokes.
context.eg1.release: How long each pick rings before the filter closes again. Longer and the picks blur into a shimmer.
context.lpmod.eg2: How hard each pick is. With the cable in, this knob sets how far envelope 1 opens the low-pass, not envelope 2.
context.lpf.cutoff: How muffled the string is between picks.
context.vco2.pitch: The slow beating between the two strings of a pair.
context.eg2.release: How long the note hangs on after you let go.

tweaks.hear: The tremolo turns into separate, deliberate strokes, two or three a second.
Each pick rings into the next and the tremolo turns into a soft shimmer.
Lighter picking, further from the strings.

sounds.name: Koto that Settles in Pitch
sounds.ref: In the style of a Japanese koto
sounds.blurb: A plucked string that starts a little sharp and sinks to its true pitch as it fades.
sounds.how: A plucked string is pulled sharp by the force of the pluck and settles as it dies away. That needs an envelope that decays, sent to pitch, and the K-2 cannot give you one from the front panel: envelope 1 only rises and falls with the key, and envelope 2 has no socket the right way up. The external signal processor can. The synth’s own SIGNAL OUT goes into its SIGNAL IN, and the envelope follower’s ENV OUT, which rises and falls with how loud the note is, goes into FREQ, where the EG1/EXT knob sets how far it bends the pitch.

steps.title: A bright string
steps.why:
A sawtooth carries the string, with a quiet square an octave up for the hard, bright edge a koto has.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) Reverse saw, SCALE 8′: bright and full of harmonics. SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet.
- VCO1 LEVEL 7: VCO stands for voltage-controlled oscillator; this is the main string.
- WAVE FORM (osc 2) Square, SCALE 4′, PITCH 0: a hollow tone exactly an octave above.
- VCO2 LEVEL 2.5: kept quiet, as edge rather than a second note.
- Listen for: a bright, buzzy tone with a thin shine on top.

steps.title: A pluck through both filters
steps.why:
Both filters shape the pluck.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 3.8 · 166 Hz, PEAK 0: the high-pass filter (HPF) removes everything below its cutoff. At about 170 Hz it keeps the string light.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 5.4 · 788 Hz: the low-pass filter (LPF) removes everything above. It rests at about 800 Hz between plucks.
- PEAK (LPF) 2.5: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. A little gives the twang at the front of each note.
- FILTER 1: the gentler circuit.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 5.5: envelope 2 (EG2) opens the low-pass more than two octaves on each pluck. This is how bright the pluck is.
- Listen for: notes start bright and twangy and settle darker.

steps.title: Plucked and left to ring
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope that opens the amplifier) is set as a pluck, left to ring.
- ATTACK (EG2) 0 · 5 ms: instant.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 7.3 · 2.0 s, SUSTAIN 0: about two seconds and then gone, however long the key is held. DECAY is how long each note rings, and later how slowly the pitch settles.
- RELEASE (EG2) 6.8 · 2.5 s: letting go early does not cut the note off.
- VOLUME 9: this also matters for pitch later, because the envelope follower hears the output after VOLUME.
- Listen for: a plucked note ringing for a couple of seconds, but with steady pitch.

steps.title: Let the synth listen to itself
steps.why:
A plucked string starts a little sharp and settles. The K-2’s front panel has no decaying envelope to send to pitch, so the external signal processor (ESP) makes one from the synth’s own output.
- Cable SIGNAL OUT → SIGNAL IN: the main output goes into the processor. Its envelope follower makes a voltage that is high while the note is loud and falls as it fades.
- SIGNAL LEVEL 3: how strongly the follower reacts. Turned up, it holds at full for longer, so the pitch stays sharp until the note is nearly gone.
- Listen for: no change yet. The follower’s voltage is not patched anywhere.

steps.title: Send it to pitch
steps.why:
The follower is sent to pitch, so each note starts sharp and sinks to its true pitch as it fades.
- Cable ENV OUT → FREQ: FREQ takes envelope 1’s place at the frequency modulation EG1/EXT knob.
- EG1/EXT 1.8: how sharp each pluck starts, about a third of a semitone here. Above about 2 it stops sounding like a string and starts sounding like a bend.
- Listen for: play single notes and let them ring. Each one starts slightly sharp and settles as it dies. VOLUME now moves the pitch too: louder gives a sharper start.

context.fmod.eg1: How sharp each pluck starts. Above about 2 it stops sounding like a string and starts sounding like a bend.
context.esp.level: How strongly the envelope follower reacts. Turned up, it holds at full for longer, so the pitch stays sharp until the note is nearly gone.
context.out.volume: This moves the pitch too: the envelope follower hears the output after VOLUME, so a louder setting gives a sharper start.
context.eg2.decay: How long each note rings, and so how slowly the pitch settles.
context.lpmod.eg2: How bright the pluck is.
context.lpf.peak: The twang at the front of each note.

tweaks.hear: At 0 every note is steady from start to finish. At 1.8 each one sinks slightly into tune.
A wide drop on every note, as though the string were pressed behind the bridge and let go.
Shorter notes, and the pitch drops faster to match.

sounds.name: Ring Mod Fifths Pad
sounds.ref: Tuned ring modulation
sounds.blurb: A soft, full organ-like pad that sounds an octave below the key you play.
sounds.how: The ring modulator outputs the sum and the difference of its two inputs. With Oscillator 2 tuned a fifth above Oscillator 1, the frequencies are in the ratio 3 to 2, so the difference is half the note’s frequency and every other product lands on a harmonic of that half. The result is in tune, and pitched an octave below the key. The K-2 puts a ring modulator on Oscillator 2’s waveform switch, so this needs no cables.

steps.title: A triangle into the ring modulator
steps.why:
A triangle on Oscillator 1 is one of the ring modulator’s two inputs, and is also mixed in quietly on its own.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) Triangle: only odd harmonics, and not many of them, which keeps the ring output clean. A sawtooth here would fill it with clangy products.
- SCALE (osc 1) 8′: SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet.
- VCO1 LEVEL 4: a little of the plain triangle. VCO stands for voltage-controlled oscillator. It sits an octave above the pad’s lowest tone once the ring modulator is in.
- Listen for: a soft, flute-like tone.

steps.title: Oscillator 2 to RING, a fifth up
steps.why:
Oscillator 2 is switched to RING, which replaces its output with the two oscillators multiplied together. A ring modulator outputs the sum and difference of its inputs.
- WAVE FORM (osc 2) RING: the ring output now comes through Oscillator 2’s mixer channel.
- SCALE (osc 2) 8′, PITCH 2.9 · +7 st: Oscillator 2 a fifth above Oscillator 1, a ratio of 3 to 2. The difference is then half the note’s frequency and every other product lands on a harmonic of that half, so the pad is in tune and an octave below the key. Move PITCH and it turns into a clang.
- VCO2 LEVEL 6.5: the ring modulator’s level, most of the sound.
- Listen for: the note drops an octave and becomes fuller and more organ-like.

steps.title: Soften the top
steps.why:
The filters soften the top and leave the new low octave alone.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 6 · 1.2 kHz: the low-pass filter (LPF) removes everything above its cutoff, keeping the upper ring products from turning glassy. Higher lets them through.
- PEAK (LPF) 1, FILTER 1: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance; only a touch.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 2: envelope 2 (EG2) brightens the start of each note slightly.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 2 · 48 Hz, PEAK 0: the high-pass filter (HPF) is left almost open, so the low octave comes through.
- Listen for: a softer, rounder pad.

steps.title: Slow in, slow out
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope that opens the amplifier) is set slow at both ends, which is what makes it a pad.
- ATTACK (EG2) 7.5 · 1.4 s: each note fades in over more than a second.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 7 · 1.6 s, SUSTAIN 9: near-full sustain, so held notes stay up.
- RELEASE (EG2) 7.5 · 3.9 s: several seconds of fade after you let go.
- VOLUME 8.5.
- Listen for: notes swell in and hang on, so a slow line overlaps itself.

steps.title: A slow movement in the filter
steps.why:
The modulation generator (MG, Korg’s name for the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator) moves the low-pass slowly, so a held note does not sit perfectly still.
- FREQUENCY 2 · 0.29 Hz: about one cycle every three seconds.
- WAVE FORM (MG) 5 · triangle: a smooth, even sweep.
- MG/T.EXT (LPF mod) 2.5: how far the cutoff moves. More gives an obvious wah.
- Listen for: a held note gently brightening and darkening every few seconds.

context.vco2.pitch: The fifth that makes this work. Move it and the ring products leave the harmonic series and the pad turns into a clang.
context.mix.vco2: The level of the ring modulator, which is most of the sound.
context.mix.vco1: A little of the plain triangle, which sits an octave above the pad’s lowest tone.
context.lpf.cutoff: How soft the pad is. Higher lets the upper ring products through and it becomes glassier.
context.eg2.attack: How slowly each note fades in.
context.lpmod.mg: The slow movement in the tone.

tweaks.hear: At 2.5 the products fall between the harmonics and the pad goes out of tune with itself. At 2.93 it snaps back into a clean chord an octave down.
Only the ring modulator is left: a hollow, reedy tone with no trace of the key you played.
The upper products come through and the pad takes on a glassy edge.

sounds.name: Wordless Singer
sounds.ref: In the style of a wordless solo voice
sounds.blurb: A soft sung line where every note comes out on a slightly different vowel.
sounds.how: The two resonant filters closed in on each other leave a band with a peak at each edge, which the ear hears as a vowel. A singer never repeats a vowel exactly, so the lower edge is moved on every note. TRIG OUT fires the sample and hold each time a key goes down, the sample and hold takes one reading from the noise generator, and its output goes to the high-pass CUTOFF FREQ socket. Each note gets its own vowel and keeps it until the next.

steps.title: Two sawtooths for a voice
steps.why:
A sawtooth has the full set of harmonics a voice has, which gives the filters something to shape into vowels.
- WAVE FORM Reverse saw on both, SCALE 8′ on both: SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet.
- PITCH 0.1 · +0.1 st: the second oscillator a hair sharp.
- VCO1 LEVEL 7, VCO2 LEVEL 3.5: the second VCO (voltage-controlled oscillator) is quieter and just apart, which softens the tone.
- Listen for: a bright buzz with a slight shimmer.

steps.title: Close the two filters in on each other
steps.why:
The two resonant filters are closed in on each other. What is left is a band with a peak at each edge, like the resonances of a mouth and throat, which the ear hears as a vowel.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 5 · 379 Hz: the high-pass filter (HPF) removes everything below its cutoff; this is the lower edge of the band.
- PEAK (HPF) 5: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. How strongly the vowel comes through at the lower edge.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 6.2 · 1.4 kHz: the low-pass filter (LPF) is the upper edge. Lower for a darker “oo”, higher for a brighter “eh”.
- PEAK (LPF) 4.5: past about 7 it whistles.
- FILTER 1: the gentler circuit.
- Listen for: the buzz turns into a vocal “ah”-like tone.

steps.title: A sung note
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope that opens the amplifier) makes each note fade in softly rather than being struck.
- ATTACK (EG2) 4 · 100 ms: about a tenth of a second to fade in.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 6 · 690 ms, SUSTAIN 8.5: a high held level.
- RELEASE (EG2) 4.5 · 630 ms: a short tail after you let go.
- TIME 2: portamento, so the pitch slides between notes like a singer.
- VOLUME 9.
- Listen for: soft note starts and gentle slides between notes.

steps.title: A light vibrato
steps.why:
A light vibrato from the modulation generator (MG, Korg’s name for the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator).
- FREQUENCY 7.3 · 5.13 Hz: about five cycles a second, a natural singing rate.
- WAVE FORM (MG) 5 · triangle: smooth.
- MG/T.EXT (pitch) 1.2: only just on the pitch. Keep it low or it wobbles.
- Listen for: a faint waver on held notes.

steps.title: A new reading on every note
steps.why:
The sample and hold (S&H) takes one reading of the noise generator each time a key goes down, and holds it until the next key.
- Cable TRIG OUT → CLOCK: TRIG OUT carries the trigger that fires the envelopes, so the sample and hold is clocked once per note instead of running freely.
- Listen for: no change yet. The readings are not patched anywhere.

steps.title: Move the lower edge of the band
steps.why:
The random reading moves the lower edge of the band, so every note comes out on a slightly different vowel, as a singer never repeats one exactly.
- Cable S&H OUT → CUTOFF FREQ (high-pass): this socket takes envelope 2’s place at the high-pass EG2/EXT knob.
- EG2/EXT (HPF mod) 4.3: now scales the sample and hold. Each note moves the high-pass up or down by up to about an octave. At 0 every note has the same vowel; more makes the vowels further apart.
- Listen for: play the same note several times. Each one has its own colour and keeps it until the next key.

context.hpmod.eg2: How different one vowel is from the next. With the cable in, this knob scales the sample and hold, not envelope 2. At 0 every note has the same vowel.
context.hpf.cutoff: The average position of the lower edge of the band.
context.lpf.cutoff: The upper edge. Lower for a darker "oo", higher for a brighter "eh".
context.hpf.peak: How strongly the vowel comes through at the lower edge.
context.lpf.peak: How strongly the vowel comes through at the upper edge. Past about 7 it starts to whistle.
context.fmod.mg: Vibrato depth. Keep it low or it wobbles.

tweaks.hear: At 0 every note sounds the same. At 5 the vowels differ more, as though each note were a different word.
The voice darkens towards "oo".
The notes step cleanly instead of sliding, more like an instrument than a voice.

sounds.name: Pedal Steel with a Late Bend
sounds.ref: In the style of Brian Eno and Daniel Lanois — "Apollo"
sounds.blurb: A soft, swelling note that bends up a whole tone once it has settled, the way a pedal steel player presses a pedal.
sounds.how: Envelope 1 is wired to the pitch of both oscillators through the EG1/EXT knob, and it has a DELAY TIME before its attack. Set the knob so that envelope 1 at full is exactly two semitones, and every held note waits, then rises a whole tone and stays there until you let go. Short notes are over before the bend starts. A delay stage before an envelope’s attack is rare on a monosynth, and it is what lets the bend wait for the note to settle.

steps.title: A sawtooth with a quiet square an octave up
steps.why:
A sawtooth gives the steel its bright edge, and a quiet square an octave up adds a little shine on top.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) Reverse saw, SCALE 8′: bright and buzzy at normal pitch. SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet.
- VCO1 LEVEL 7: VCO stands for voltage-controlled oscillator; this is the main tone.
- WAVE FORM (osc 2) Square, SCALE 4′, PITCH 0: a hollow tone exactly an octave above.
- VCO2 LEVEL 3: kept quiet, as shine rather than a second note.
- Listen for: a bright buzz with a thin octave on top.

steps.title: A rounded tone
steps.why:
The filters round the tone off.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 6.2 · 1.4 kHz: the low-pass filter (LPF) removes everything above its cutoff. At about 1.4 kHz the fizz goes but the tone stays clear.
- PEAK (LPF) 2, FILTER 1: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. A little gives some definition; FILTER 1 is the gentler circuit.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 2: envelope 2 (EG2) brightens each note slightly as it starts.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 3 · 95 Hz, PEAK 0: the high-pass filter (HPF) removes everything below its cutoff; here only the lowest rumble.
- Listen for: a warmer, rounder tone.

steps.title: Swell in like a volume pedal
steps.why:
A pedal steel is usually played with a volume pedal, so the note arrives without a pluck. Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope that opens the amplifier) does the same.
- ATTACK (EG2) 5.5 · 320 ms: about a third of a second to swell in. Shorter and each note starts with an edge.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 7.5 · 2.3 s, SUSTAIN 7: a slow ease-off to a steady level.
- RELEASE (EG2) 6 · 1.6 s: notes fade rather than stop.
- VOLUME 8.5.
- Listen for: each note swelling in with no attack of its own.

steps.title: Envelope 1: wait, then rise
steps.why:
Envelope 1 (EG1) is already wired to the pitch of both oscillators through the EG1/EXT knob. Here it is set to wait, then rise. The knob is still at 0, so nothing bends yet.
- DELAY TIME 6.6 · 640 ms: how long each note stays put before the bend. Notes shorter than this are never bent. A delay stage like this is rare on a monosynth.
- ATTACK (EG1) 6.3 · 670 ms: how slowly the bend happens, about two-thirds of a second.
- RELEASE (EG1) 3 · 200 ms: how quickly the pitch falls back after you let go.
- Listen for: no change until the next step turns the depth up.

steps.title: Exactly a whole tone
steps.why:
The depth knob is set so envelope 1 at full is exactly a whole tone. Every held note waits, then rises two semitones and stays there until you let go.
- EG1/EXT 2.9: how far envelope 1 moves the pitch. 2.89 is a whole tone and about 2.04 a semitone; anywhere between sounds out of tune.
- Listen for: hold a note. It swells in, sits for about two-thirds of a second, then bends up to the next note of the scale. Play short notes and they never bend.

context.fmod.eg1: The size of the bend. 2.89 is a whole tone; about 2.04 is a semitone. Anywhere between sounds out of tune.
context.eg1.delay: How long each note stays put before the bend. Notes shorter than this are never bent.
context.eg1.release: How quickly the pitch falls back after you let go.
context.eg2.attack: The volume-pedal swell at the start of each note.

tweaks.hear: The bend is now a semitone, which suits a minor scale.
The bend starts almost at once, so every note, however short, slides up.
A slow, lazy bend that takes a couple of seconds to arrive.

sounds.name: Pad with Changing Colour
sounds.ref: Sample and hold on the filters
sounds.blurb: A slow pad whose tone changes every couple of seconds, each change landing somewhere new.
sounds.how: The sample and hold, clocked by the modulation generator about once every two seconds, sends a new random voltage to TOTAL. A cable in TOTAL takes the modulation generator’s place at every MG/T.EXT knob at once, so one cable moves both filters, each by its own amount. The band between them shifts up or down to a new place and holds there until the next reading.

steps.title: Two sawtooths, gently beating
steps.why:
Two sawtooths at the same octave, a few cents apart, give a slow beat and plenty of harmonics for the filters to pick from.
- WAVE FORM Reverse saw on both, SCALE 8′ on both: SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet.
- PITCH 0.1 · +0.2 st: Oscillator 2 a few cents sharp. More gives a faster, more obvious beat.
- VCO1 LEVEL 6.5, VCO2 LEVEL 6: both VCOs (voltage-controlled oscillators) nearly level, for the thickest beating.
- Listen for: a bright, slowly swirling buzz.

steps.title: A band between the two filters
steps.why:
The two filters leave a band between them, with a slight vowel to it.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 3.8 · 166 Hz: the high-pass filter (HPF) removes everything below its cutoff; the lower edge of the band.
- PEAK (HPF) 3.5: PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance. It sets how strongly each new position sings later; more makes each change more obvious.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 5.8 · 1.0 kHz, PEAK 3.5: the low-pass filter (LPF) removes everything above; the upper edge.
- FILTER 1: the gentler circuit.
- Listen for: the buzz narrows to a slightly vocal mid-range tone.

steps.title: A slow pad envelope
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope that opens the amplifier) is set slow at both ends for a pad.
- ATTACK (EG2) 7.5 · 1.4 s: over a second to fade in.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 7 · 1.6 s, SUSTAIN 9: near-full sustain, so held notes stay up.
- RELEASE (EG2) 7.5 · 3.9 s: several seconds of fade after you let go.
- VOLUME 8.5.
- Listen for: notes swell in and hang on.

steps.title: Clock the sample and hold slowly
steps.why:
The sample and hold (S&H) takes a reading each time it is clocked and holds it until the next. With nothing in S&H IN it reads the noise generator, so each reading is random.
- Cable MG OUT (pulse) → CLOCK: the modulation generator (MG, Korg’s name for the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator) clocks the sample and hold.
- FREQUENCY 3 · 0.50 Hz: a new reading every two seconds. This is how often the colour will change.
- WAVE FORM (MG) 5 · triangle: the pulse output is an even square at this position.
- Listen for: no change yet. The readings are not patched anywhere.

steps.title: Into TOTAL
steps.why:
The random voltage goes to TOTAL, which moves both filters at once, each by its own amount.
- Cable S&H OUT → TOTAL: a cable in TOTAL takes the modulation generator’s place at every MG/T.EXT knob.
- MG/T.EXT (pitch) 0: kept at 0, so the pitch is left alone. Turn it up and the pad becomes a random melody.
- MG/T.EXT (HPF mod) 4.5, (LPF mod) 4: how far the lower and upper edges of the band jump at each change. With both up, the whole band moves together.
- Listen for: hold a chord note. Every couple of seconds the tone jumps to a new colour and holds there.

context.hpmod.mg: How far the lower edge of the band jumps at each change.
context.lpmod.mg: How far the upper edge jumps. With both up, the whole band moves together.
context.fmod.mg: Kept at 0. Turn it up and the pitch jumps at random too, which turns the pad into a random melody.
context.mg.freq: How often the colour changes.
context.eg2.attack: How slowly the pad fades in.
context.hpf.peak: How strongly each new position sings. More PEAK makes each change more obvious.

tweaks.hear: The colour changes about three times a second: a busy, bubbling pad.
Only the low-pass moves, so the changes are in brightness rather than in vowel.
Each new position rings, picking out a different overtone every time.

sounds.name: Pan Pipes
sounds.ref: In the style of Andean pan pipes
sounds.blurb: A hollow, breathy pipe with the air audible around every note.
sounds.how: A pan pipe is a tube closed at the bottom, so it sounds mostly odd harmonics, and that is what a square wave is. The breath comes from Oscillator 1’s fourth waveform position, which swaps the oscillator for the noise generator. That costs the K-2 an oscillator, but the tone only needs one: Oscillator 2 plays the note and Oscillator 1 becomes the air, and both go through the same filters. No cables.

steps.title: Oscillator 2 plays the note
steps.why:
Oscillator 2 plays the note. A pan pipe is a tube closed at the bottom, so it sounds mostly odd harmonics, which is what a square wave is.
- WAVE FORM (osc 2) Square: hollow and woody.
- SCALE (osc 2) 8′, PITCH 0: SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet. 8′ is the same octave Oscillator 1 would be.
- VCO2 LEVEL 7: the pipe tone itself. VCO stands for voltage-controlled oscillator.
- Listen for: Oscillator 1 is still at its default reverse saw and level, so for now you hear a bright saw with the square underneath. The next step changes that.

steps.title: Oscillator 1 becomes the breath
steps.why:
Oscillator 1 becomes the breath. Its fourth waveform position swaps it for the noise generator; that costs an oscillator, but the tone only needs one.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) noise: the noise generator takes Oscillator 1’s place, and both go through the same filters.
- VCO1 LEVEL 6: now the amount of breath. Keep it well below the tone; above about 8 the air starts to cover the note.
- Listen for: the saw is gone and a hollow square sits inside a lot of hiss.

steps.title: Shape the air
steps.why:
The filters shape the air so it sits around the note rather than on top of it.
- CUTOFF (HPF) 4.6 · 288 Hz, PEAK 1: the high-pass filter (HPF) removes everything below its cutoff, taking the low rumble out of the noise without touching the notes. Raise it for thinner, higher breath. PEAK is Korg’s word for resonance.
- CUTOFF (LPF) 6.6 · 1.8 kHz, PEAK 2: the low-pass filter (LPF) removes everything above, keeping the hiss soft. Lower for a softer, more distant pipe.
- FILTER 1: the gentler circuit.
- EG2/EXT (LPF mod) 2.5: envelope 2 (EG2) brightens the start of each note a little, like a puff of air.
- Listen for: the hiss becomes a soft breath around the tone.

steps.title: Blown, not struck
steps.why:
Envelope 2 (EG2, the main envelope that opens the amplifier) makes each note blown, not struck.
- ATTACK (EG2) 3.5 · 72 ms: about 70 ms, so each note starts on the breath. This is how long the air leads the note in.
- HOLD 0, DECAY 5.5 · 460 ms, SUSTAIN 7.5: a slight dip after the start, then a steady level.
- RELEASE (EG2) 4 · 460 ms: stops like a player running out of air.
- VOLUME 9.
- Listen for: a soft, breathy start on each note.

steps.title: A player’s vibrato
steps.why:
A player’s vibrato from the modulation generator (MG, Korg’s name for the LFO, a low-frequency oscillator).
- FREQUENCY 7.3 · 5.13 Hz: about five cycles a second.
- WAVE FORM (MG) 5 · triangle: smooth.
- MG/T.EXT (pitch) 1.3: vibrato depth. More becomes a wobble.
- Listen for: the tone wavers on held notes but the air does not, because noise has no pitch.

context.mix.vco1: The amount of breath. Above about 8 the air starts to cover the note.
context.hpf.cutoff: Takes the low rumble out of the noise. Raise it and the breath gets thinner and higher.
context.lpf.cutoff: How bright the air is. Lower for a softer, more distant pipe.
context.eg2.attack: How long the breath leads each note in.
context.fmod.mg: Vibrato depth.

tweaks.hear: A very breathy pipe, blown hard.
A thinner, reedier tone, closer to a shawm than a pipe.
Each note starts at once, with less of the breath in front of it.

sounds.name: Snarling Driven Riff
sounds.ref: In the style of Daft Punk — "Derezzed"
sounds.blurb: A hard, snarling riff sound that is driven until it tears, with a nasal bite on every note.
sounds.how: Two sawtooths an octave apart are pushed hard into FILTER 2, the circuit that distorts sooner. The high-pass takes out the low rumble and its PEAK adds a nasal honk, while the low-pass has a high PEAK and a quick flick from envelope 2 on every note. The snarl comes from the patch panel: the output goes round to the external signal processor, whose preamp saturates it, and the saturated copy is sent back into the filters through EXT SIGNAL IN. The riff is then heard through two stages of distortion, one inside the filter and one in the loop.

steps.title: Two saws an octave apart, run hot
steps.why:
Two sawtooths an octave apart, both run hot into the filters. The overload thickens and roughens the sound before anything else happens.
- WAVE FORM (osc 1) Reverse saw, SCALE 8′: bright and buzzy at normal pitch. SCALE is Korg’s octave switch, in organ-pipe feet.
- WAVE FORM (osc 2) Reverse saw, SCALE 16′: an octave below, the saw that gives the riff its weight.
- PITCH 0.1 · +0.1 st: a hair sharp, for a little movement.
